dishes.desc: Soft tofu in a fiery, numbing sauce of fermented broad-bean paste and ground Sichuan pepper, created in Chengdu in the 1860s by the pockmarked 'Grandma Chen'. Ordered at virtually every Sichuan restaurant (about ¥20-40); eat it spooned over steamed rice (米饭 mǐfàn).

Diced chicken stir-fried with dried chilies, peanuts and scallions in a sweet-sour 'lychee' sauce, named after the Qing official Ding Baozhen, governor of Sichuan. Far less gloopy than the Western version; a standard ¥25-45 stir-fry at Chengdu home-style restaurants.

Small bowls of noodles with very little sauce, topped with crispy minced pork and preserved greens, named for the shoulder pole (担 dàn) street vendors once carried. Mix thoroughly from the bottom before eating; a small bowl (二两 èr liǎng) costs around ¥10-15 at noodle shops.

Pork belly is first boiled, then sliced thin and 'returned to the wok' with Pixian broad-bean paste and garlic leeks until the slices curl into 'lamp-dish' shapes. Considered the king of Sichuan home cooking; a cheap, rich dish best eaten with lots of rice.

A cold appetizer of thinly sliced beef and offal (despite the name, usually no lung) drenched in red chili oil and numbing pepper, popularized by a Chengdu husband-and-wife team in the 1930s. Order it as a starter or from deli counters selling cold dishes (凉菜 liángcài).

Chaoshou ('folded hands') are Sichuan wontons, and Long Chaoshou on Chunxi Road is Chengdu's most famous 'old brand' shop for them. Choose clear-broth (清汤 qīngtāng) or the spicy red-oil version (红油抄手 hóngyóu chāoshǒu); about ¥15-25 a bowl.

ingredients: bamboo skewers of meat and vegetables
dishes.desc: Chengdu's casual, cheaper cousin of hot pot: grab skewers from the fridge, cook them in a bubbling chili-tallow broth at your table, and pay by the number of sticks counted at the end. A classic late-night meal; ask for 微辣 (wēi là, mildly spicy) if needed.

Braised rabbit heads tossed in chili and numbing pepper, eaten with gloves by prying apart the jaw to get at the cheeks and brain; Chengdu eats tens of millions a year. Sold per head (around ¥10-15) at deli shops; choose spicy (麻辣) or the mild five-spice (五香 wǔxiāng) version.

A street performance and dessert in one: balls of sticky rice dough are thrown against a board with brass bowls, making three loud 'cannon' bangs, before landing in soybean flour and being doused in brown-sugar syrup. Look for it on Jinli and Kuanzhai Alley; cheap, sold in portions of three.

A clear, wobbly jelly made from plant seeds, served chilled with brown-sugar syrup and crunchy toppings — Chengdu's go-to cooler for summer heat and spicy food. Sold at street stalls and hot pot restaurants for a few yuan a bowl.

Leshan's signature snack: skewers of cooked chicken, offal and vegetables soaking in a big clay bowl (钵 bō) of cold, red, numbing chili-oil broth. Pick your sticks and pay per skewer (roughly ¥0.5-1 each); choose the red spicy (红油) or green-pepper (藤椒 téngjiāo) version.

A Leshan bowl of beef and offal in a clear, herb-infused bone broth, named after diners who sat 'with one leg up' on benches at roadside stalls. Eaten any time from breakfast on with a dry chili dip and rice; around ¥15-30 a bowl.

Leshan's famous deli duck: brined and smoked, then fried and brushed with a maltose glaze so the skin becomes glossy, crisp and sweet. Bought by the half or whole duck from takeaway shops and chopped to order — a non-spicy break from Sichuan heat.

Zigong's best-known dish: diced rabbit fried with heaps of dried chilies and peppercorns, then left to cool and eaten cold as a snack or beer food. Sold loose and in vacuum packs everywhere in Zigong and a popular souvenir; expect serious heat.

Tender beef slices poached in a spicy broth over vegetables and finished with a ladle of sizzling oil over chilies and peppercorns; it traces its roots to Zigong's salt-well workers, who cooked the oxen that hauled the brine. Now on Sichuan menus everywhere — order a bowl to share with rice.

A Zigong specialty of beef sliced almost translucent, then slowly baked beside a cow-dung or charcoal fire until dry and fragrant. Eaten as a chewy snack, often tossed in chili oil (麻辣 málà) or plain (五香 wǔxiāng); a classic local gift sold by weight.

The original mala hot pot: a bubbling cauldron of beef-tallow broth loaded with chilies and numbing peppercorns, born among Yangtze dock workers cooking cheap offal. Order tripe (毛肚 máodǔ) and dip everything in sesame oil with garlic; choose a split 'yuanyang' (鸳鸯) pot if you want a mild side.

Chongqing's everyday breakfast: plain noodles in a red, numbing chili-oil base, with no meat in the basic version. Thousands of small shops sell it for around ¥6-10 a bowl; ask for 干溜 (gān liū, dry) or with soup, and say 少辣 (shǎo là) for less heat.
The meaty sibling of xiaomian: noodles topped with soft stewed peas (豌 wān) and savory minced pork (杂酱 zájiàng). Found at the same noodle shops for a few yuan more; a hearty breakfast or lunch.

Crispy morsels of fried chicken hidden in a mountain of dried red chilies, associated with Geleshan in Chongqing. The fun is hunting for the chicken among the chilies (which you don't eat); a shareable main at most Chongqing restaurants.
Slippery, chewy sweet-potato glass noodles in a tangy vinegar and chili broth, topped with crunchy fried soybeans and peanuts. One of Chongqing's most common street snacks, usually under ¥10 a bowl.

A Chongqing jianghu-style stew of silky duck blood curd, tripe and assorted meats in a fiery red broth, originating at Ciqikou old town. Served in a big bowl to share; a good way to try hot pot flavors without ordering a whole hot pot.

Tender fish fillets poached in a sour, gently spicy broth of pickled mustard greens, said to have originated in Jiangjin, Chongqing. Now a nationwide favorite; order a basin to share with rice, often priced by the size of the fish.

A whole fish grilled over charcoal, then served on a tray over a flame, smothered in chili sauce and simmering vegetables; the Wanzhou style (万州烤鱼 Wànzhōu kǎoyú) is the most famous. Pick a fish and flavor (麻辣 málà or 泡椒 pàojiāo pickled chili) and share as a late-night meal.

Bite-size glutinous rice balls filled with black sesame, a beloved Chongqing ('Mountain City') dessert sold at snack shops and old-town stalls. A soothing, cheap palate cleanser after hot pot; sometimes served in sweet fermented rice soup (醪糟 láozāo).

Translucent pleated dumplings of whole shrimp in a thin wheat-starch skin — the benchmark by which every Cantonese teahouse is judged. Order a basket of four at yum cha (morning tea) in Guangzhou; a good skin is thin enough to see the pink shrimp but doesn't tear.
Open-topped steamed dumplings packed with juicy pork and shrimp, crowned with a dot of orange roe. Alongside har gow it's one of the 'four heavenly kings' of dim sum; usually four per steamer basket.

ingredients: shrimp or beef or char siu
dishes.desc: Silky steamed rice sheets rolled around shrimp, beef or barbecued pork and doused in sweet soy sauce. Guangzhou's favourite breakfast — cheap at street stalls (Xiguan-style, often with egg) and served at every dim sum restaurant. Say 'haa1 coeng2' for shrimp or 'ngau4 coeng2' for beef.
Fluffy steamed buns that split open at the top to reveal sweet-savoury Cantonese barbecued pork. A dim sum essential; three to a basket, and also sold from bakery windows for a quick breakfast.

Glossy, smooth egg custard in a flaky or buttery shortcrust shell, created in Guangzhou's department-store tea rooms in the 1920s. Best eaten warm from the oven at yum cha or a bakery; not to be confused with the caramelised Portuguese-style tart of Macau.

Chicken feet deep-fried, braised and steamed until puffy and gelatinous in a black-bean sauce. A beloved dim sum classic in Guangzhou — nibble the skin off the bones and discreetly spit the bones onto your plate. Often listed as 'si6 zap1 fung6 zaau2' (black-bean phoenix claws).

dishes.en: Lo Mai Gai (Lotus Leaf Sticky Rice)
dishes.desc: Glutinous rice stuffed with chicken, Chinese sausage and mushroom, wrapped in a lotus leaf and steamed until fragrant. A filling dim sum item — unwrap the leaf at the table (don't eat it). A smaller version is called 'zan1 zyu1 gai1' (pearl chicken).

Silky Cantonese congee loaded with fish, squid, pork skin, peanuts and crunchy fried dough — originally sold from small boats on Guangzhou's Liwan canals. A classic breakfast or late-night bowl in the old Xiguan district; ask for 'jau4 zaa3 gwai2' (youtiao) on the side.

Whole chicken gently poached until just cooked, then chilled so the skin turns springy and the meat stays silky, served chopped with ginger-scallion oil. The saying in Guangdong is 'no chicken, no feast'; order by the half ('bun3 zek3') or quarter at roast-meat and family restaurants.

Wide rice noodles stir-fried with tender beef over a roaring wok so they pick up smoky 'wok hei' without turning greasy. A Guangzhou late-night staple and the test of a Cantonese chef; the noodles originally come from Shahe, a Guangzhou neighbourhood.

A wobbly steamed buffalo-milk custard with two 'skins' on top, invented in Shunde's Daliang town during the Qing dynasty. Eat it hot or cold at dessert shops like Renxin or Minxin; toppings like red bean or lotus seed are common.

Hot sweetened milk poured onto fresh ginger juice, which sets it into a silky, slightly spicy curd within seconds. A Pearl River Delta dessert from Panyu, Guangzhou; best served warm at traditional dessert shops.

Paper-thin slices of raw freshwater fish laid out on a plate and tossed at the table with a dozen condiments like ginger, shallot, peanuts and oil — Shunde's signature dish. Note that raw freshwater fish carries a parasite (liver fluke) risk; cooked alternatives like fish congee are everywhere in Shunde.

Beef slaughtered that morning is hand-sliced into named cuts and swished for just seconds in a light, clear broth, then dipped in shacha (satay) sauce. Order by cut: try 'diàolóng' (rib-eye) and 'xiōngkǒu yóu' (crunchy brisket fat); finish with beef balls.

Beef pounded by hand with iron mallets into famously bouncy balls — Shantou's proudest snack. Eat them in soup or noodles, or try 'niújīn wán' (beef tendon balls); vacuum packs are the classic souvenir.

Tiny fresh oysters pan-fried with potato-starch batter and egg in lard until crisp at the edges, served with fish sauce. A Chaoshan street-food classic — locals like it crispier than the Taiwanese or Hokkien versions.

Lion-head goose slowly simmered in a spiced soy master stock, sliced and served with garlic vinegar — the centrepiece of Chaoshan feasts. Ask for 'éròu' (meat) for a plate, or try the prized goose liver ('égān') and goose head; braised tofu from the same pot is a cheap side.

Hainan's most famous dish: a free-range chicken from Wenchang poached until tender, chopped, and served with a dip of ginger, garlic and calamansi lime. The ancestor of Hainanese chicken rice — order it with 'jīyóu fàn' (chicken-oil rice).

Thin rice noodles tossed (not in soup) with a thick sweet-salty gravy and a heap of crunchy toppings like peanuts, fried shallots and pickles. Haikou's everyday breakfast, sold at small noodle shops for a few yuan; a bowl of clear soup often comes on the side.

Chunks of free-range chicken simmered in a broth of pure fresh coconut water, which turns sweet and fragrant as it cooks. Drink a bowl of broth first, then eat the chicken with calamansi-soy dip; a hugely popular dinner in Haikou and Sanya.

A meaty mud crab from Hele in Wanning, famous for its rich, orange roe-filled shell, usually simply steamed and dipped in ginger-garlic vinegar. One of Hainan's 'four famous dishes'; priced by weight at seafood markets — Sanya's First Market lets you buy and have it cooked nearby.

Hainan's iconic cooling dessert: a bowl of coconut milk with shaved ice and a mix of beans, taro, jellies, quail eggs and tropical fruit. Sold at street stalls and night markets in Haikou and Sanya for a few yuan — perfect on a hot afternoon.

Round rice noodles dressed with a spiced braising liquor ('lǔshuǐ'), braised meat and crunchy soybeans — Guilin's breakfast of choice. Pay at the counter, take your bowl, and add pickles and chili yourself from the self-serve station; ask for 'yǒu tāng' if you want broth poured over at the end.

Fresh Li River fish pan-fried skin-on, then braised in local Liquan beer with tomatoes and peppers. The signature dish of Yangshuo (in Guilin prefecture) — West Street restaurants display live fish; you pick one and pay by weight.

A savory, bitter-gingery 'soup tea' made by frying and pounding tea leaves with ginger and garlic, then poured over puffed rice and peanuts. A morning ritual of the Yao and Gongcheng area near Guilin; tradition says to drink at least three bowls.

Liuzhou's notorious rice noodle soup in a spicy river-snail broth, famous for the pungent smell of fermented bamboo shoots — it tastes far better than it smells. Order spice level as 'wēi là' (mild) or 'tè là' (extra); add a fried egg or pig's trotter.

Nanning's signature: rice noodles flash-fried with sour bamboo shoots, black beans, garlic and chili, then finished in a hot sour-spicy broth with pork. Legend says it was first made for an old friend with a cold; ask for 'lǎoyǒu miàn' if you want wheat noodles instead.

Chopped duck stir-fried and braised with salt-pickled sour lemons, pickled chili and ginger for a tangy, spicy hit. Originating in Wuming on Nanning's outskirts, it's a staple of local family restaurants — often listed as 'Wǔmíng níngméng yā'.

Hong Kong's favourite bakery bun, named for its crackly sugar-cookie top that looks like a pineapple skin (there is no pineapple in it). Order a bo lo yau (菠蘿油, 'baw-law yow') to get it split warm with a thick slab of cold butter. Best fresh from the oven at a cha chaan teng or bakery, usually HK$8-25.

Strong black tea strained through a cotton 'silk stocking' filter and mixed with evaporated milk, giving it a silky, smooth body. It is the default drink at every cha chaan teng and comes with most set meals. Say 'dung nai chah' (凍奶茶) for iced, or 'chah jau' (茶走) for a version sweetened with condensed milk.

A uniquely Hong Kong mix of coffee and milk tea, named after mandarin ducks, which always appear in pairs. Found on every cha chaan teng menu, hot or iced, for about HK$20-30 or as part of a set meal. Ask for 'dung yoon yeung' (凍鴛鴦) if you want it iced.

Two slices of thick white bread sandwiched with peanut butter (or kaya), dipped in egg and deep-fried, then topped with a pat of butter and golden syrup. A rich cha chaan teng classic for breakfast or afternoon tea, usually HK$25-40. Often shortened to 'sai daw' (西多).

A bubble-shaped waffle cooked in a special honeycomb iron, crispy outside and soft and eggy inside. Sold hot from street stalls across Hong Kong for around HK$20-30; eat it right away while the bubbles are crisp. Modern shops add flavours like chocolate or matcha, or fold it around ice cream.

Plump shrimp-and-pork wontons with springy thin egg noodles in a clear broth flavoured with dried flounder and pork bones. Traditional bowls are small, with the wontons hidden under the noodles to keep them from going soggy, for about HK$35-50. Add a dab of red vinegar or chili oil at the table.

Tender braised beef brisket served over egg noodles in a rich, spiced broth. A staple of Hong Kong noodle shops (often the same ones that sell wonton noodles), costing around HK$45-70. You can also choose ho fun (河粉) rice noodles or ask for 'ngow nahm lo meen' to have them dry with the broth on the side.

Hong Kong's most iconic street snack: springy fried fish balls simmered in a spicy-sweet curry sauce and served on a skewer. Sold from street-side snack shops for about HK$15-25 a stick, often next to siu mai and stuffed peppers. Ask for 'gah lay jup' (more curry sauce) or 'lat' (spicy).

A build-your-own noodle bowl born from Hong Kong's 1950s street carts: pick a noodle type, a soup and three or more toppings such as fish balls, radish, pig skin or curry squid. Shops price per topping, typically HK$40-70 total. Point at the topping list and say the numbers if you can't read it.

Rice cooked to order in a clay pot over charcoal or gas, topped with Chinese sausage, cured meats or chicken, and finished with sweet soy sauce. It's a winter favourite, so expect to wait about 20 minutes; scrape up the crispy rice crust (飯焦, 'fahn jiu') at the bottom. Around HK$60-100 at dai pai dong.

Whole goose roasted until the skin is lacquered and crisp, served chopped with plum sauce at Hong Kong's siu mei (roast meat) shops. Order 'siu ngaw fahn' (燒鵝飯) for goose on rice at about HK$60-90, or ask for the leg (髀, 'bay') for the best piece. Sham Tseng and Central are famous for it.

Crab stir-fried under a mountain of crispy golden garlic and chili, created by boat-dwelling fishermen in Causeway Bay's typhoon shelters. A splurge dish shared at seafood restaurants (often HK$400+ priced by weight); the leftover garlic crumbs are great over rice. Shrimp and squid are cooked the same way.

A chilled dessert soup of fresh mango, pomelo pulp and sago pearls in mango-coconut milk, invented in Hong Kong in the 1980s. Found at dessert shops (糖水舖) and Chinese restaurants for about HK$30-50. A perfect way to cool down on a humid evening.

Fermented tofu deep-fried until puffy and crisp, with a pungent smell you'll notice from down the street. Hong Kong vendors serve it skewered with sweet sauce and chili sauce for around HK$15-25. Look for it at snack stalls in Mong Kok and Sham Shui Po.

Macau's take on the pastel de nata: flaky puff pastry filled with creamy custard and blistered on top until caramelised. Introduced by Lord Stow's Bakery in Coloane in 1989, it's best eaten warm from the oven at around MOP 10-13 each. Margaret's Café e Nata is another famous spot.

A marinated, bone-in fried pork chop stuffed into a crusty Portuguese-style bun, Macau's signature sandwich. Tai Lei Loi Kei in Taipa is the most famous, selling them for roughly MOP 40-60; watch the bone as you bite. Pair it with a milk tea.

Minced beef and pork stir-fried with crispy diced potatoes and soy sauce, considered Macau's national dish of Macanese cuisine. It's home-style comfort food usually served over rice with a fried egg on top, for about MOP 60-100 at Macanese restaurants. The name comes from the English word 'mince'.

Grilled chicken smothered in a rich, mildly spicy sauce of piri-piri chili, coconut and peanuts, a Macanese invention inspired by Portuguese Africa. A centerpiece at Macanese and Portuguese restaurants, usually a half or whole bird (MOP 150-300) to share. Mop up the sauce with bread or rice.

Layers of sweetened whipped cream and finely crushed Marie biscuits that look like sawdust, which is what both 'serradura' and the Chinese name mean. Served chilled in cups at Macanese cafés and bakeries for about MOP 25-40. Locals simply call it 'mook hong'.

Crumbly, melt-in-the-mouth cookies made from mung bean flour and ground almonds, pressed in wooden moulds and baked. Macau's number-one souvenir, sold by the box at Koi Kei and Choi Heong Yuen along Rua de São Paulo, with free samples handed out. Look for versions with a sliver of candied pork fat inside.

Sweet, smoky sheets of grilled pork jerky sold by weight on the street leading to the Ruins of St. Paul's, where sellers press free samples on passers-by. Beef (牛肉乾, 'ngow yook gon') and spicy versions are also available, priced per catty (600g). A classic snack and souvenir alongside almond cookies.

Steamed basket dumplings filled with pork and hot broth, born in Shanghai's Nanxiang suburb and Shanghai's signature food. Nibble a hole, sip the soup, then dip in black vinegar with ginger; a basket of 6-10 runs about ¥15-40, and 蟹粉小笼 (xièfěn, crab roe) is the luxury variant.

Juicy pork buns pan-fried in big flat pans until the bottoms are crisp and golden, then topped with sesame and scallion. A classic Shanghai breakfast sold by the 4-pack (about ¥8-15); bite carefully, they squirt hot soup. Locals often call them 生煎 (shēngjiān) for short.

Thin noodles tossed in oil slowly infused with crispy fried scallions plus soy and sugar, a humble Shanghai staple. Found in every noodle shop for around ¥10-20; mix thoroughly before eating, and add a fried pork chop or egg if you want more.

The classic breakfast pair: long golden deep-fried dough sticks dunked in hot soy milk. One of Shanghai's 'four heavenly kings' of breakfast (四大金刚); ask for 甜 (tián, sweet) or 咸 (xián, savory) soy milk. A set costs only a few yuan.

A fist-sized ball of steamed glutinous rice wrapped tightly around a crunchy piece of youtiao plus fillings like pork floss and pickles. A grab-and-go Shanghai breakfast from street stalls for about ¥5-10; specify sweet (甜) or savory (咸).

Cubes of pork belly slowly braised in soy sauce, Shaoxing wine and rock sugar until glossy, sweet and meltingly tender. Shanghai's version (本帮红烧肉) is notably sweet and dark; it is a home-style dish on nearly every local restaurant menu and best eaten with plain rice.

A crispy deep-fried pork chop served with chewy fried rice-cake slices, all glazed in a sweet savory sauce. An old-school Shanghai snack shop favorite (around ¥20-30), famously served on Huanghe Road and in old lane-house eateries.

Poached chicken chilled and marinated in Shaoxing rice wine, served cold as a classic Shanghainese appetizer. Look for it among the cold dishes (冷菜) at the start of a meal; the meat is silky with a fragrant boozy flavor.

A warm, lightly boozy dessert soup of fermented sweet rice with tiny chewy rice balls, often with egg ribbons and osmanthus. Common at Shanghai snack shops and dessert counters for under ¥15; it is mild enough to eat at breakfast.

Nanjing's most famous dish: duck cured in salt and spices then gently poached, served cold with pale, tender, juicy meat. Buy it by weight (半只 bàn zhī = half a duck) from deli counters all over the city; osmanthus season gives the prized 桂花鸭 (guìhuā yā).

Nanjing's signature street bowl: glass noodles in duck broth with cubes of duck blood, offal and tofu puffs, topped with cilantro. About ¥15-25 everywhere in the city; pair it with a crispy 鸭油烧饼 (duck-fat sesame flatbread).

Suzhou's showpiece banquet dish: a mandarin fish scored into a lattice, deep-fried so it fans out like a squirrel's tail, and drenched in sweet-and-sour sauce. Order it for a group at classic Suzhou restaurants such as Songhelou; expect ¥150+ for a whole fish.

Suzhou-style noodles (苏式汤面) in a clear, rich broth topped with a slab of slow-braised pork belly that melts into the soup. Suzhou locals eat noodles for breakfast, and the seasonal 'first bowl' (头汤面) of the morning is prized; about ¥15-30.

The world's most famous fried rice, from Yangzhou: fluffy grains coated in egg and studded with shrimp, ham and vegetables. In Yangzhou the official recipe is protected and richer than versions abroad; it appears on most local menus as 扬州炒饭 for around ¥20-50.

Huge, tender pork meatballs gently stewed so they are soft enough to eat with a spoon, a pillar of Yangzhou's Huaiyang cuisine. Look for the crab version 蟹粉狮子头 (xièfěn shīzitóu) in autumn; usually served one per person in a small pot.

Pressed tofu cut into hair-fine threads and simmered in rich chicken broth with shrimp and ham, a showcase of Yangzhou knife skills. It is a staple of the Yangzhou morning tea (早茶) spread at places like Fuchun Teahouse.

An oversized, paper-thin dumpling filled almost entirely with hot crab-and-pork soup, which you drink through a straw. A highlight of Yangzhou morning tea; the saying is 'lift gently, move slowly, open a window, then sip'. Pricey (¥30+ each) and best in crab season.

Wuxi's signature dish: pork ribs braised in soy and lots of sugar until dark, sticky, sweet and falling off the bone. Sold in restaurants and as boxed take-home souvenirs; also called 酱排骨 (jiàng páigǔ).

dishes.en: West Lake Fish in Vinegar Gravy
dishes.desc: Hangzhou's most famous dish: a grass carp briefly poached and covered in a glossy sweet-sour vinegar sauce. Served at classic lakeside restaurants such as Lou Wai Lou; it is divisive (mild, bony fish) but a must-try for its fame.

Thick squares of pork belly slow-braised in Shaoxing wine and soy until jiggly and rich, named after poet Su Dongpo who governed Hangzhou. Usually served one square per person in a small clay pot; pair with rice to soak up the sauce.

Tiny, delicate river shrimp stir-fried with fresh leaves of Hangzhou's famous Longjing (Dragon Well) green tea. Light and subtly fragrant; best in spring when the new tea is picked, and found on most Hangzhou restaurant menus.

A stuffed whole chicken wrapped in lotus leaves and sealed in clay or dough, then baked for hours until extremely tender. Cracking the crust open at the table is part of the fun; order ahead at traditional Hangzhou restaurants, and share among several people.
Hangzhou's everyday noodle soup with sliced pork, crunchy bamboo shoots and salty pickled greens (雪菜). Eaten at all hours in local noodle shops like Kuiyuan Guan for around ¥15-30.

Soft glutinous rice balls filled with molten black sesame and lard, served in a sweet broth, Ningbo's most famous food. Bite gently as the filling is hot; the old Gangyagou (缸鸭狗) shop in Ningbo is the classic spot, about ¥10-20 a bowl.

Fermented tofu deep-fried until crisp outside and soft inside, pungent to smell but savory to eat, a famous Shaoxing street snack. Sold on skewers or in paper cups around Lu Xun's hometown for a few yuan; add chili sauce.

dishes.en: Pork Belly with Preserved Mustard Greens
dishes.desc: Slices of pork belly steamed over Shaoxing's dried, fermented mustard greens, which soak up the fat and turn savory-sweet. A home-style Shaoxing classic best with rice and a glass of local yellow wine (黄酒).

The signature dish of Huizhou cuisine: mandarin fish lightly fermented in brine for days, then braised, giving a funky aroma but firm, flaky, savory flesh. Ordered in nearly every restaurant around Huangshan and Tunxi old street; a whole fish costs roughly ¥100-200.

Tofu fermented until it grows a fluffy white mold coat, then pan-fried until golden and served with chili sauce. A Huizhou specialty seen on street stalls in Tunxi and the ancient villages around Huangshan; it tastes mild and creamy, somewhat like cheese.

Small, round, flaky baked pastries filled with preserved mustard greens and pork fat, coated in sesame; also called 蟹壳黄 (xièkéhuáng, 'crab shell yellow') for their color. Sold hot or boxed as souvenirs all over Huangshan and Tunxi.

Hefei's (old name Luzhou) famous roast duck with crisp skin and juicy meat, chopped and served with its sauce. The Luzhou Roast Duck shop chain is a local institution; pair it with 鸭油烧饼 (duck-oil flatbread) and a bowl of duck blood soup.

Beijing's signature dish: lacquered duck roasted until the skin is glassy-crisp, carved tableside and rolled in thin pancakes with sweet bean sauce, scallion and cucumber. Order a whole (整只 zhěng zhī) or half (半只 bàn zhī) duck at famous houses like Quanjude or Siji Minfu; expect roughly ¥200-300 for a whole bird.

Thick wheat noodles topped with a salty, dark sauce of fried soybean paste and diced pork, served with a spread of crunchy vegetable toppings (菜码 càimǎ) you mix in yourself. Old-Beijing noodle shops sell a bowl for about ¥20-35; stir it all together thoroughly before eating.

Old Beijing's hot pot: paper-thin lamb slices swished briefly in a mild broth in a charcoal-fired copper pot, then dipped in a rich sesame sauce. It's a winter favorite at Donglaishun and hutong shops; order the hand-cut lamb (手切羊肉 shǒuqiē yángròu) for the classic experience.

A sour, funky, grayish drink made from the fermented leftovers of mung bean starch production, famously loved by old Beijingers and dreaded by newcomers. It's drunk hot at breakfast with crunchy fried dough rings (焦圈 jiāoquān) and salty pickles; a bowl costs just a few yuan at Huguosi or snack shops.

A hearty Beijing street dish of pork intestines, lung and fried tofu stewed in a soy-and-spice broth, served with chunks of wheat flatbread soaked in the broth. Hole-in-the-wall shops sell bowls for around ¥20-30; ask for no lung (不要肺 bú yào fèi) if you're squeamish.

A Muslim-Beijing snack of beef or lamb tripe blanched for just seconds so it stays crunchy, then dipped in sesame sauce. Shops like Baodu Feng serve different cuts by name; locals pronounce it with an 'r' ending (bàodǔr) and pair it with a sesame flatbread.

Despite its name ('stir-fried liver'), this is a thick, glossy garlicky stew of pork liver and intestine eaten as breakfast. The classic pairing is with small steamed buns at Yaoji Chaogan near Gulou; old-timers sip it straight from the rim of the bowl without a spoon.

Skewers of tart hawthorn berries dipped in hard, glass-like sugar syrup, an iconic winter street snack on hutong corners and in tourist streets like Nanluoguxiang. Vendors also do strawberries, grapes and tangerines; a stick costs about ¥5-15.

A soft glutinous rice roll filled with red bean paste and coated in toasted soybean flour, named for how it looks like a donkey rolling in the dust. Find it at old-Beijing snack shops like Huguosi Xiaochi, often alongside pea-flour cake (豌豆黄 wāndòuhuáng).

Tianjin's beloved breakfast crepe: mung bean batter spread on a griddle, topped with egg and sauces, then folded around a crunchy youtiao or fried crisp. Tianjin purists insist on mung bean flour and no extra fillings like lettuce or sausage; street carts charge about ¥6-12.

Tianjin's most famous brand of juicy pork steamed buns, each pleated with at least 18 folds, dating to the 1850s. The name means 'dog ignores him,' after the founder's nickname; the flagship on Shandong Road is touristy and pricey, so many locals point visitors to neighborhood bun shops instead.

Tianjin's signature souvenir snack: large, crunchy deep-fried dough twists layered with sweet fillings like osmanthus and candied fruit. Guifaxiang's 'Eighteenth Street' shops are the famous name; they're sold boxed at Tianjin station and along Ancient Culture Street.

A classic of Shandong (Lu) cuisine from Jinan: pork intestine blanched, fried and braised in a glossy sauce balancing sweet, sour, salty and spicy notes. It's a banquet staple at old Jinan restaurants like Huifeng Lou; order one plate to share.

Jinan's everyday comfort food: thick slabs of pork belly tied with straw and braised in soy until meltingly tender, served over rice with sauce poured on. Fast-food style shops let you add braised eggs, tofu or meatballs from the pot; a plate is about ¥15-25.

A whole Yellow River carp scored, deep-fried so the head and tail curl upward, and drenched in sweet-and-sour sauce. It's one of the best-known Lu cuisine dishes and a centerpiece at Jinan restaurants; a whole fish is meant for sharing.

Despite the name meaning 'sweet foam,' this Jinan breakfast porridge is savory: millet flour simmered with peanuts, vermicelli, greens and tofu skin, spiced with five-spice and pepper. Locals pair a bowl (about ¥3-5) with youtiao at breakfast stalls.

Qingdao's signature seafood plate: small local clams flash-fried with chili, garlic and scallions, eaten with plenty of Tsingtao beer. Locals call clams 'gala' in dialect; sold by the jin (500 g) at seafood stalls around Pichaiyuan and Yunxiao Road for roughly ¥30-50.

Large, juicy boiled dumplings filled with whipped Spanish mackerel, a Qingdao specialty especially in spring when the fish are in season. Dumpling houses like Chuanyunlou sell them by the plate or by the liang; they're often bigger than standard jiaozi.

Zhengzhou's signature dish: wide, chewy hand-stretched noodles in a rich milky lamb-bone broth with lamb, kelp and tofu skin. Order 羊肉烩面 (yángròu huìmiàn) at chains like Heji or Xiaoji; a bowl is around ¥20-30, with chili oil and garlic on the table.

Henan's essential breakfast: a thick, peppery-hot soup with gluten, vermicelli and meat, famously from Xiaoyao Town. Locals often ask for half hulatang and half tofu pudding (两掺 liǎngchān) and eat it with fried dough or pan-fried buns; about ¥5-8 a bowl.

Kaifeng's famous thin-skinned soup dumplings, filled with pork and hot broth and served in steamers right out of the kitchen. Kaifeng Diyilou is the historic name; bite a small hole and sip the soup first, and order by the steamer (笼 lóng).

A Kaifeng specialty of whole hen slow-cooked in a long-aged master stock, served cold or at room temperature with firm meat and golden skin. Huang Jiaxiang is the famous old shop, and it's also sold by weight at the night market.

dishes.en: Sweet & Sour Carp with Crispy Noodles
dishes.desc: A Kaifeng banquet classic: soft-braised sweet-and-sour carp topped with a nest of hair-thin deep-fried noodles that soak up the sauce. Its full name is 糖醋软熘鲤鱼焙面; order it at old restaurants like Youyixin to share at the table.

ingredients: mung bean or sweet potato starch jelly
dishes.desc: A Kaifeng night-market staple: cubes of starch jelly fried on a big griddle until crispy-edged, then seasoned with bean paste, garlic and scallions. Look for it at Gulou or Xisi night markets for around ¥10-15 a plate.

The heart of Northeastern home cooking: boiled dumplings with fillings like pork and sauerkraut (猪肉酸菜 zhūròu suāncài), ordered by the liang (两, about 6 dumplings) at dumpling houses. Shenyang's century-old Laobian Jiaozi (老边饺子) is famous; dip in vinegar with raw garlic on the side.

Harbin's signature dish: thin slices of pork in a crackly potato-starch batter, double-fried and tossed in a tangy sweet-and-sour glaze. Invented in Harbin for Russian guests, it's on nearly every Northeastern menu; the old-style version is pale golden, while Liaoning versions often use ketchup.

A smoky, garlicky Russian-style sausage with a reddish casing, Harbin's most popular food souvenir. Qiulin and Shangzhi are the famous brands; buy it by weight to eat with dalieba bread and a Harbin beer.

A rich, creamy milk popsicle sold from the windows of the historic Modern Hotel (Madier) on Central Street since 1906. Eating one outdoors in minus-20 Harbin winter is a local rite; they cost about ¥5-10.

A huge, round, dense Russian-style loaf (from Russian 'khleb') baked in Harbin since the early 1900s. Qiulin's bakery is the classic place to buy one; it keeps well for days, making it a popular travel snack and souvenir.

One of the 'big four stews' of Northeastern cuisine: a young chicken braised with wild hazel mushrooms and glass noodles in a big pot. Often served in an iron pot (铁锅炖 tiěguō dùn) with cornbread stuck to the sides; portions are huge, so order one for a group.

A homestyle Northeastern stir-fry of eggplant, potato and green pepper, each fried then glazed in a savory garlic-soy sauce. It's cheap, filling and on virtually every Dongbei menu, making it a go-to vegetarian order (about ¥20-30).

Shenyang's favorite street snack: chicken carcasses braised, smoked, fried or grilled, then picked apart by hand over beer. Order smoked (熏鸡架 xūn jījià) or fried (炸鸡架 zhá jījià) at street stalls for about ¥10-15 each.

Dalian's signature street snack: cubes of sweet potato starch jelly fried on an iron griddle until crispy outside and chewy inside, then dressed with sesame sauce and garlic water. Sold at stalls and food streets all over Dalian for about ¥5-10 a portion.

Chopped slow-stewed meat stuffed into a crisp griddled baiji flatbread, often called the world's oldest sandwich. In the Muslim Quarter it is filled with beef or lamb (niúròu / yángròu jiāmó); elsewhere in Xi'an the classic is pork (làzhī ròujiāmó). Around 10-20 RMB, eaten on the go any time of day.

Belt-wide hand-slapped noodles topped with chili flakes and garlic, then doused with smoking-hot oil; famous for having one of the most complex characters in Chinese. Many shops simply write it as 'biangbiang面' or sell it as yóupō miàn (oil-splashed noodles). Ask for a mixed topping bowl (sān hé yī) for tomato-egg, braised pork and oil-splash in one.

Xi'an's signature Hui dish: you tear a dense flatbread into pea-sized pieces yourself, then the kitchen cooks them in rich lamb broth. Smaller pieces mean the bread soaks up more soup; eat it with sweet pickled garlic. About 25-40 RMB; beef version is niúròu pàomó.

Chewy, slippery cold sheet noodles tossed in chili oil, vinegar and garlic, a summer staple sold everywhere in Xi'an. Ask for májiàng (sesame paste) or Qínzhèn mǐpí (rice-flour version); usually 8-15 RMB and often paired with a roujiamo.

dishes.en: Steamed Sticky Rice and Date Cake
dishes.desc: Layers of glutinous rice, jujubes and beans steamed for hours in a huge pot and sliced out by weight from street carts, a classic Muslim Quarter breakfast sweet. Sold by the portion (a few RMB), usually on a paper plate or bamboo stick.

Golden pan-fried cakes made from persimmon dough and filled with osmanthus-scented sugar and nuts, a Muslim Quarter street-stall favorite. Eat them hot but carefully as the filling is molten; roughly 5-10 RMB each.

Hand-pulled noodles in clear beef broth, defined by 'one clear, two white, three red, four green, five yellow' (broth, radish, chili oil, herbs, noodles). Locals call it niúròu miàn or just 'niú dà' and eat it for breakfast; choose a thickness such as máoxì (thread-thin), èrxì or kuān (wide). Around 10-20 RMB.

Whole grains of highland barley or oats lightly fermented into a sweet, slightly boozy cooling snack, sold in bowls from Lanzhou street stalls and night markets. Often eaten in summer; ask for it iced.

Chunks of bone-in lamb simply boiled and eaten with your hands, dipped in salt, garlic or chili vinegar; Ningxia's prized Tān yáng (Tan sheep) makes Yinchuan's version famous. Ordered by the jin (500 g) at Hui restaurants.

A spicy bowl of mixed lamb offal in rich broth that is Yinchuan's go-to Hui breakfast, often eaten with a flatbread. Small shops sell it from early morning for around 15-25 RMB; ask for less chili with 'shǎo là'.

Hui-style tea served in a lidded 'three-cannon' cup (sānpàotái) packed with dried fruits, goji and rock sugar; staff keep refilling the hot water. Standard at Ningxia and Gansu Hui restaurants alongside lamb dishes.

Chunks of lamb and fat grilled over charcoal and showered with cumin and chili; in Xinjiang they are bigger and juicier than anywhere else in China (Uyghur: kawap). Ordered by the stick at night markets, a few RMB each; say 'bú là' if you want no chili.

A huge platter of spicy chicken and potato stew born in northern Xinjiang, finished with wide belt noodles (dài miàn) to soak up the sauce. Meant for sharing among 2-4 people; ask to 'jiā miàn' (add noodles).

Rice cooked in lamb fat with sweet carrots and onions and topped with a hunk of lamb, the centerpiece of Uyghur cooking (Uyghur: polo). Often cooked in giant woks and sold by lunchtime until gone; also just called zhuāfàn.

Chewy hand-pulled noodles topped with a stir-fry of lamb, tomatoes and peppers (Uyghur: leghmen; also called lātiáozi). Xinjiang's everyday lunch; many places offer free extra noodles (jiā miàn) when you finish.

Square or pillow-shaped pastries filled with lamb, fat and onion and baked against the walls of a tandoor oven (Uyghur: samsa). Sold hot from street ovens, especially around Kashgar's old town, for a few RMB each.

Round tandoor-baked flatbread stamped with patterns, eaten at every meal in Xinjiang (Uyghur: nan). Comes in many sizes, from huge thin wheels to small thick girde nan; buy it hot from bakeries for a few RMB.

ingredients: lamb lung filled with flour batter
lamb intestine stuffed with rice and liver
dishes.desc: A Uyghur night-market classic (Uyghur: öpke-hésip): lamb lung filled with a flour batter and intestines stuffed with rice, sliced and doused with chili sauce. Look for the steaming stalls in Kashgar's night market; priced by the plate.

A lightly fizzy, honey-sweet fermented drink introduced by Russian and Tatar communities and sold everywhere in Urumqi in summer. Barely alcoholic; vendors sell it chilled by the cup or bottle alongside skewers.
Roasted highland barley flour kneaded by hand with butter tea into dough balls, the staple food of Tibet (Tibetan: tsampa). Try it at Tibetan teahouses in Lhasa, usually alongside butter tea.
Salty tea churned with yak butter, drunk all day across Tibet to fight cold and altitude (Tibetan: po cha). Hosts refill your cup constantly; leave it full when you have had enough.
Sweet milky tea poured by the thermos in Lhasa's crowded teahouses (Tibetan: cha ngarmo), where locals linger for hours. Very cheap, a few RMB per pot; pairs with Tibetan noodles.

Steamed or fried dumplings filled with yak meat (Tibetan: momo); Chinese menus list them as zàngshì bāozi or simply mómo. Sold by the plate in Lhasa teahouses and restaurants with a chili dipping sauce.
A simple bowl of noodles in yak-bone broth topped with minced yak meat, Lhasa's everyday breakfast (Tibetan: thukpa). Eaten in teahouses with sweet tea; a bowl is typically under 15 RMB.

Changsha's version is jet-black: fermented tofu deep-fried until puffy, then punctured and filled with garlicky chili sauce. It's the city's signature street snack, sold by the bowl of 4-6 pieces at stalls around Pozi Street and Taiping Street.

dishes.en: Steamed Fish Head with Chopped Chili
dishes.desc: A huge carp head steamed under a blanket of red (and often green) pickled chopped chilies — Hunan's most famous restaurant dish. When the fish is gone, order noodles to toss in the spicy juices left on the platter.
Crayfish braised in a fiery, numbing sauce, eaten with gloves late into the night at Changsha's summer night markets. Sold by the jin (500 g); peak season is May to August.

Chewy glutinous rice patties fried in oil and caramelized in brown sugar syrup — Changsha's classic sweet street snack. Cheap and sold hot in small paper bowls; eat them fast before the sugar hardens.

Locals start the day with a bowl of slippery round rice noodles in clear broth, topped with a 'mazi' (码子) of your choice such as braised pork or beef. Help yourself to the chili and pickles on the table.

The everyday Hunan home-style dish: sliced pork wok-fried with blistered fresh green chilies. Ubiquitous on Changsha menus (also listed as 农家小炒肉, 'farmhouse stir-fried pork') and best eaten with lots of rice.
Glossy cubes of pork belly braised with caramelized sugar and chilies but no soy sauce, said to be Chairman Mao's favorite. A staple at Hunan restaurants; one plate is plenty to share.

The king of Wuhan's 过早 (guòzǎo, 'breakfast out') culture: springy noodles tossed with thick sesame paste and pickles, eaten on the go. A bowl costs only a few yuan; stir well before eating and pair it with 蛋酒 (egg rice wine) or soy milk.

A crisp mung-bean-and-egg crepe pan-fried over a layer of savory glutinous rice studded with pork and mushrooms, cut into squares. A guozao breakfast staple, famous at Hubu Alley (户部巷); ask for 三鲜豆皮 (sānxiān, 'three fresh').

A savory ring-shaped fritter, thick at the rim and thin and crisp in the middle, deep-fried in a special ladle. One of the classic Wuhan breakfast bites, usually eaten alongside hot dry noodles or a bowl of hutangfen.
Thin rice noodles in a thick, peppery broth made from small river fish cooked down for hours. A beloved guozao breakfast; dunk a 油条 (fried dough stick) into it the way locals do.
Duck necks braised in a sweet, numbing-spicy master stock and gnawed as a snack with beer. Wuhan's Jingwu Road (精武鸭脖) made them famous nationwide; buy by weight at chain shops and train stations.

dishes.en: Lotus Root and Pork Rib Soup
dishes.desc: Hubei's signature comfort soup: chunks of starchy Hubei lotus root simmered with pork ribs for hours in a clay pot until the root turns pink and stringy. Ordered at almost every Wuhan family meal, especially in autumn and winter.
A delicate whole Wuchang bream steamed with ginger and scallions, made famous by a line in a Mao poem. A classic banquet dish at Wuhan restaurants, priced per fish.
Xiamen's signature noodle soup with a rich, nutty, mildly spicy shacha broth. You choose your own toppings (shrimp, squid, intestines, tofu puffs) from a display and pay per item.

Little cold aspic cups made by boiling marine peanut worms until their collagen sets, served with garlic vinegar and chili sauce. A Minnan specialty, sold in Xiamen's Zhongshan Road and Gulangyu as well as Quanzhou's Anhai.

Plump little oysters fried in a gooey starch batter with eggs and chives, finished with a sweet-spicy sauce. A must-try Minnan snack at Xiamen and Quanzhou stalls; locally also called 蚵仔煎 (ô-á-chian in Hokkien).

Peeled peanuts simmered until meltingly soft in a light sweet milky soup, eaten hot or cold. A classic Xiamen dessert (and breakfast with a fried dough stick); Huangzehe (黄则和) on Zhongshan Road is the famous spot.

A paper-thin crepe rolled around stir-fried shredded vegetables, meat, peanut powder and seaweed. Hugely popular in Quanzhou; in Xiamen it's usually called 薄饼 (báobǐng), traditionally eaten around Qingming festival.

Ultra-fine wheat noodles cooked to a silky, porridge-like soup in seafood stock, with add-ons like intestine, oysters or braised egg. Quanzhou's quintessential breakfast — tear in a fried dough stick (油条) the local way.

Fuzhou's legendary luxury soup, slow-simmered in a Shaoxing wine jar with abalone, sea cucumber, fish maw and more — so fragrant even a monk would jump the wall for it. Expensive; many Fuzhou restaurants sell individual-portion pots.
Bouncy fish balls with a juicy minced-pork center, served in clear soup. Fuzhou's most iconic snack; order a bowl alongside 肉燕 or 拌面 at any small eatery.
Fuzhou's unique wontons whose wrappers (燕皮, yànpí) are made from pork pounded thin with sweet potato starch, said to look like swallows' tails. Served in soup; often ordered with fish balls as 鱼丸肉燕.

Yunnan's signature dish: a bowl of scalding, oil-capped broth arrives with a tray of raw meats, vegetables and rice noodles that you add yourself so they cook in the soup. Add the meat and egg first, then greens, then noodles; sets range from about 15 RMB to 60+ RMB for deluxe versions.

Chicken steamed in a Jianshui clay pot with a central chimney, so the condensed steam becomes a clear, intensely flavored broth with no added water. A classic Kunming banquet dish; one pot serves 2-4 and often comes with medicinal herbs like sanqi.

Flaky pastry filled with sweet jam made from Yunnan's edible roses, sold fresh from bakery windows all over the province. A few RMB each and the go-to edible souvenir; Kunming and the old towns of Dali and Lijiang have them everywhere.

A flat disc of pounded rice cake toasted over charcoal, brushed with sauces and folded around fillings like a Yunnan burrito. A morning street-stall staple for 5-10 RMB; ask for 'jiā yóutiáo' to add a fried dough stick.

Yunnan is China's wild mushroom capital, and in the rainy season (roughly June-September) Kunming restaurants serve hot pots loaded with a dozen foraged varieties. Staff time the boiling for you: wait the full 15-20 minutes before eating, as undercooked wild mushrooms can be toxic.

A thin sheet of Bai cow's milk cheese, stretched and dried on bamboo poles, then grilled on a stick until crisp and brushed with rose jam. A Dali old-town street classic for around 5-10 RMB; also served pan-fried as a dish.

Fresh fish from Erhai Lake simmered in a clay pot with a rich stock of chicken, ham, mushrooms and tofu. A signature Bai dish of Dali, best shared at lakeside restaurants; priced by the fish's weight.

ingredients: or brown sugar and rose paste (sweet version)
dishes.desc: A round flatbread baked between two layers of charcoal fire, crispy outside and soft within, from the Bai village of Xizhou near Dali. Choose savory (xián de, with ham and scallion) or sweet (tián de, with sugar and rose); about 5-10 RMB.

The Bai people's welcome ritual: three cups served in sequence, a bitter roasted tea, a sweet tea with cheese and walnuts, then an aftertaste tea with honey and peppercorn. Often part of a performance in Dali and Xizhou; a symbol of 'first bitter, then sweet, then reflection'.
A dense, layered, pan-fried Naxi flatbread, sometimes sold to tourists as 'Chinese pizza'. Comes sweet with brown sugar or savory with ham and scallion; a cheap breakfast throughout Lijiang Old Town.

A Naxi snack made from local black chickpeas set into a jelly, served cold in strips with chili and vinegar or pan-fried hot in cubes. A Lijiang Old Town street staple for a few RMB; ask for 'liáng de' (cold) or 'rè de' / 'jiān de' (hot, fried).

Lijiang's signature hot pot: salty, smoky cured pork ribs simmered into a rich broth before you add vegetables and mushrooms. Restaurants all over the old town specialize in it; ordered by the jin (half kilo) of ribs, ideal for warming up on cold highland nights.

Guizhou's most famous dish, from the Miao people: a whole fish cooked tableside in a tangy, fermented red sour broth. Served as a shared hot pot priced by the fish's weight; add vegetables and noodles once the fish is gone.

ingredients: shredded vegetables (radish, cucumber, kelp, bean sprouts)
dishes.desc: Guiyang's signature snack: tiny crepes you fill yourself with dozens of shredded vegetables, roll into a 'swaddled baby' shape, then spoon in tangy chili dipping soup. Around 10-20 RMB for a set with unlimited wrappers.

Guiyang's classic breakfast noodle: springy egg noodles in red chili broth topped with braised pork intestine, silky pig blood and crunchy pork bits. The name is a pun for 'long-lasting prosperity'; about 15-20 RMB a bowl.
Rice noodles in a clear, rich beef broth piled with sliced beef, from Guiyang's Huaxi district. A favorite breakfast across the city; add pickled greens and chili at the counter, about 15-25 RMB.

ingredients: chili dip (zhe'ergen, scallion, soy sauce, vinegar)
dishes.desc: Small squares of fermented tofu grilled until puffy, then split open and stuffed with a spicy, sour dip. Named for the couples who once shared them at street stalls in wartime Guiyang; a few RMB for a plate.
Tender pig's trotters slow-braised in spiced soy stock, the must-eat in Qingyan Ancient Town on Guiyang's outskirts. Sold by the piece from shopfronts along the old streets; dip in dry chili powder.

Honey-glazed roast pork with a sticky, charred red edge, hung in the window of every siu mei shop. Order it over rice as 叉烧饭 (caa1 siu1 faan6) for a cheap lunch, or ask for 半肥瘦 (half fatty, half lean) for the best texture.
Roast pork belly with a crackling, blistered skin and juicy layered meat, sold by weight at siu mei counters. Dip it in mustard or sugar, or order a two-meat combo plate (双拼饭) with char siu.
Whole fish steamed just until done, then topped with shredded scallion and sizzling oil and soy. The test of a good Cantonese kitchen; ask for 清蒸 (steamed) with any live fish from the tank.

Soups simmered for hours with meat, vegetables and medicinal herbs — a cornerstone of Cantonese home cooking. Restaurants offer a daily 例汤 (soup of the day), and some shops sell individual steamed soups (炖汤) in small pots.
Smooth rice porridge with salted lean pork and creamy century egg — the most popular congee in Guangdong. Eat it for breakfast with a 油条 (fried dough stick) or rice noodle roll.

dishes.en: Molten Salted Egg Custard Bun (Lau Sa Bao)
dishes.desc: Steamed buns that ooze a hot, sweet-salty golden salted-egg-yolk custard when bitten — 'flowing sand'. Bite carefully; often shaped like piglets or other cute animals.

dishes.en: Steamed Spare Ribs with Black Bean
dishes.desc: Bite-sized spare ribs steamed in small dishes with fermented black beans and garlic. A core dim sum order; the same dish over rice in a claypot is 排骨饭.
Savoury cake of shredded radish and rice flour studded with sausage and dried shrimp, pan-fried in slices until crisp. A dim sum staple and a must-eat at Chinese New Year (糕 sounds like 'rising').
Flaky round pastries filled with sweet winter melon paste — a famous Guangzhou bakery item, with Lianxianglou (莲香楼) claiming its invention. Buy them warm from old bakeries as gifts.
The classic Cantonese 糖水 (sweet soup): adzuki beans simmered until creamy with tangerine peel. Served hot or cold at dessert shops and as a free dessert at restaurants.
Thin slices of tender local beef flash-fried with heaps of fresh chilies and coriander — a staple on every Hunan restaurant menu. Order it with plenty of rice; it's fiery and smoky.
A classic of Xiang cuisine: poached young chicken stir-fried with chili, ginger and vinegar for a hot-sour tang. Famously served at state banquets; found at traditional Hunan restaurants.
Smoked and cured Hunan meats steamed together until the fat turns translucent. A deeply savory winter classic best eaten with rice.
Spicy stir-fried snails you slurp ('suo') out of the shell — a Changsha night-market staple with beer. Ordered by the plate or bowl at late-night stalls.
A Tujia minority dry hot pot of three meats (often cured pork, tripe and trotters) cooked together with chili. The signature meal in Zhangjiajie.
Soup-filled pork dumplings from Wuhan's famous Sijimei shop, part of the city's 'guozao' breakfast ritual. Sip the broth before eating.
Pork meatballs rolled in glutinous rice and steamed until the grains glisten like pearls. A classic Hubei festive dish.
Hubei's (Qianjiang-style) crayfish braised in oil, chili and beer — summer street food all over Wuhan. Order by the jin with beer.
Rice noodles cooked to order in a small copper pot with minced pork and pickles — Kunming's everyday breakfast noodle. Cheaper and more local than crossing-the-bridge.
Stir-fried slices of erkuai rice cake with pork and vegetables; legend says it 'saved the emperor.' Ask for 'chao erkuai' anywhere in Yunnan.
Little puffy tofu squares grilled on a wire rack and dunked in chili salt; locals count them with corn kernels. A must in Jianshui's old town.
Sweet sticky rice steamed inside a hollowed pineapple — a Dai minority favorite in Xishuangbanna.
Whole fish stuffed with herbs, tied with lemongrass and grilled over charcoal. The signature Dai dish.

Tender fish slices poached and buried under a sizzling slick of chili oil and dried chilies; the dish was born in Chongqing's Yubei district in the 1980s. Order by the bowl to share; eat the fish, leave the oil.

Chicken gizzards, hearts and intestines stir-fried with pickled chilies and ginger until sour, crunchy and fiery. Hugely popular as a cheap dry-pot or hot-pot style meal across Chongqing; say 'jīzá' to any roadside restaurant.
A bowl of fresh, plain tofu pudding eaten with a spicy dipping sauce and steamed rice, the classic Chongqing workers' meal. Very cheap; refills of rice are often free.
Crisp fried dough twists from Ciqikou Ancient Town, sold in sweet, spicy and numbing flavors. The quintessential Chongqing edible souvenir; free samples line the old street.
Rice noodles in rich mutton bone broth topped with thin slices of lamb and plenty of chili oil, Zunyi's signature breakfast. Add mint and garlic sprouts from the table; shops open at dawn.
Guizhou's version of spicy chicken: chunks braised in a garlicky ciba chili paste, eaten first dry then with broth as a hot pot. Unlike Chongqing's crispy laziji, it's saucy and aromatic.
A shallow cast-iron griddle on which you grill tofu, potatoes, meat and vegetables, dipping them in dry chili powder. A beloved social snack-meal across Guizhou, especially in Guiyang and Liupanshui.
Small cubes of tofu grilled until crisp outside and molten inside, dipped in chili sauce. A Guizhou street-food star; also served on laoguo griddles.

Crunchy roots of fish mint (houttuynia) dressed with chili and vinegar — a bitter, peppery flavor locals adore and visitors find challenging. Zheergen appears in nearly every Guizhou dish; try it straight here.

A silky, thickened fish soup said to date to the Southern Song dynasty, when a widow named Song served it to Emperor Gaozong. Tangy with a dash of vinegar, it's a fixture at Hangzhou restaurants like Louwailou; order a small bowl to share.

A youtiao and scallions wrapped in a thin pancake, pressed on a griddle and brushed with sweet sauce. Legend says it mocks the traitor Qin Hui; it's a cheap Hangzhou breakfast snack sold near Hefang Street.

China's most famous green tea, grown in the hills around West Lake, with a toasty-chestnut flavor. Visit Longjing or Meijiawu tea villages to drink it fresh; Mingqian (pre-April) harvest is the priciest.
Ningbo's famously smooth rice cake slices, most often stir-fried with pickled greens and pork (xuecai rousi chao niangao) or in soup. Look for the Cihu brand.

dishes.en: Yellow Croaker Soup with Pickled Greens
dishes.desc: Whole yellow croaker simmered in a milky broth with tangy pickled greens. A defining dish of Ningbo seafood cuisine.
Amber rice wine aged in clay jars, best drunk warm. Order a bowl of Huadiao or Jiafan in a Shaoxing tavern like Xianheng Jiudian.
Broad beans simmered with star anise until chewy and savory — the drinking snack immortalized in Lu Xun's story 'Kong Yiji'. Sold at Xianheng tavern with a bowl of rice wine.
Steamed sticky rice topped with crunchy fried dough bits, pork floss and gravy, eaten with a bowl of sweet soy milk. The essential Wenzhou breakfast.
China's most famous dry-cured ham, deeply savory and used to season soups and braises across the Jiangnan region. Buy whole or sliced in Jinhua.
Soy-marinated sticky rice with fatty pork wrapped in bamboo leaves — the benchmark zongzi, made famous by the Wufangzhai brand. Sold hot at service stations and shops all over Zhejiang.
A layered iron pot of pork, tofu, bamboo shoots and egg dumplings slow-cooked together, linked to scholar Hu Shi. A hearty Huizhou centerpiece shared at the table.
Salt-cured pork steamed on a wooden cutting board, which perfumes the meat. A rustic Huizhou classic served sliced on the board.
A famous green tea from Yellow Mountain with downy leaf tips and an orchid-like aroma. Sold everywhere in Tunxi; try a glass in a teahouse.
Crescent dumplings with rice-flour skins filled with pork and tofu, then deep-fried golden. From Sanhe ancient town near Hefei and sold at street stalls citywide.
A spicy, peppery beef soup with glass noodles and tofu, eaten with flatbread for breakfast. Huainan-style shops are ubiquitous across Anhui.
Duck braised in a clay pot with lots of old ginger and sesame oil — warming and aromatic. A Minnan classic; shops in Xiamen and Quanzhou sell it by the half or whole bird.
Soy-braised sticky rice dumplings stuffed with pork, chestnut and egg yolk, served hot with sweet chili and peanut sauce. Sold year-round at Xiamen and Quanzhou stalls.
Rice batter is splashed onto the edge of a hot wok, dried into sheets, then scraped into a seafood broth. Fuzhou's iconic breakfast, eaten with fried oyster cakes.
A puffy, deep-fried UFO-shaped fritter stuffed with oysters and pork. A cheap Fuzhou street breakfast, best paired with dingbian hu.
Scored pork pieces fried so they curl like lychees, glazed in sweet-sour sauce. A Fuzhou banquet and home classic on most local menus.
Tiny wontons with paper-thin skins and pounded pork filling in a clear broth — the star of Shaxian snack shops found in every Chinese city. Order with peanut noodles for a classic combo.
Flaky round pastries filled with sweet mung bean paste — Xiamen's go-to souvenir. Bought fresh-baked on Zhongshan Road and Gulangyu.
Tender beef pieces coated in starch and poached in a peppery, thickened broth. A beloved Quanzhou snack often eaten with fried dough or rice.
A famous floral oolong from Anxi county near Quanzhou, brewed gongfu-style in tiny cups. Tea shops across Xiamen and Quanzhou offer free tastings.
A flat disc of cold noodles smeared with peanut and sweet sauces, then rolled around fried tofu or five-spice roll and eaten by hand. Zhangzhou's signature street snack.

A rustic winter stew of fatty pork, blood sausage and Northeastern sour cabbage, originally cooked on the day a family slaughtered its pig. Served in big shared bowls at homestyle Dongbei restaurants; dip the pork in garlic soy sauce.
One of the 'four great stews' of the Northeast: slow-braised pork belly with thick, slippery sweet-potato noodles that soak up the gravy. A cheap, filling staple on every Dongbei menu.
Thin slices of boiled pork belly simmered with tangy fermented Chinese cabbage, often with glass noodles; also served as a hot pot (酸菜白肉锅). The sour broth cuts the fat — a classic winter warmer.
Goose (or fish, chicken, ribs) stewed in a giant iron cauldron set into the table, with cornbread cakes stuck to the rim to steam. A group feast; order 铁锅炖 and pick your main protein.
The Northeast's signature night-market snack: a sheet of cold noodles griddled with egg, brushed with sweet-spicy sauce, wrapped around a sausage and cut into bites. About ¥6–12; add 加肠 for sausage.

Chewy buckwheat noodles in an icy, tangy-sweet beef broth topped with beef, kimchi, pear and egg — the signature dish of the Korean-Chinese community in Yanbian. Eaten year-round, even in deep winter.
Huge pork spine and rib bones braised in soy and spices until the meat falls off; you're handed plastic gloves and a straw to suck out the marrow. Great with beer.
Wide hand-pulled noodles topped with chili flakes and garlic, then splashed with sizzling oil at the table. Shaanxi's everyday noodle; add vinegar and stir.
Thin noodles in a tart, chili-red broth topped with braised pork and colorful garnishes, served in small bowls so people order several. A Shaanxi classic for birthdays and festivals.
A pork-based paomo: chunks of flatbread soaked in rich broth with cleaned pork large intestine. Like lamb paomo, you tear the bread yourself; eat with sweet pickled garlic.
Xi'an's Hui-style hulatang: a thick, peppery broth full of beef meatballs and vegetables, eaten with flatbread for breakfast. Milder and chunkier than Henan's version.
Ningxia's famed braised young lamb, slow-cooked with chili and garlic and served on a big platter. Tender, barely gamy — Ningxia's tan sheep is prized across China.
Lamb, potatoes and peppers dry-sizzled in an iron pan and served still crackling. Qinghai's signature restaurant dish.
Big chunks of lamb hung in the naan tandoor and roasted until crisp outside, juicy inside (Uyghur: tonur kawap). Sold by the skewer at bazaars; much larger than regular chuanr.
A whole lamb glazed with egg and spices and roasted in a giant pit oven — Xinjiang's feast centerpiece. Restaurants and bazaars sell it by the jin (500 g).
Steamed Uyghur dumplings (pitir manta) with skins so thin the juicy lamb-and-onion filling shows through. Sold by the steamer basket at morning bazaar stalls.
Thick, chewy rice noodles stir-fried in a fiery red sauce — Urumqi's cult street food. Order 微辣 (mild) if you're not a chili fiend; even that's hot.
Dense slabs of walnuts, raisins and dried fruit bound in grape syrup (Uyghur: matang), sliced off by weight from carts. Agree on the weight and price before cutting.
Yak meat strips air-dried in the cold plateau wind and eaten raw-cured with chili dip (Tibetan: sha kampo). Sold everywhere in Lhasa as a snack and souvenir.
Thick, tangy set yogurt (Tibetan: sho), central to the Shoton 'Yogurt Festival'. Served in bowls at teahouses — add sugar to taste.
Tibetan chang: a cloudy, mildly sour, low-alcohol barley brew served in teahouses and at every festival. Hosts will refill your cup — leave it full when you've had enough.
Slivered pork stir-fried in the sweet, sour and garlicky "fish-fragrant" sauce, which contains no fish at all. One of the most ordered dishes in China and a reliable rice companion.
Small pork dumplings served in a sweet garlicky soy sauce with red chili oil, a famous Chengdu snack since the 1890s. Order at Zhong Shuijiao shops or snack halls, often as part of a sampler.
Savory tofu pudding in a thickened broth topped with meat, crunchy soybeans and chili oil. Leshan's signature breakfast; Niuhua town's version (牛华豆腐脑) is the most famous.
Thick, very sour yogurt from yak milk (Tibetan 'sho'), served in bowls with sugar to sprinkle on top. Celebrated at the Shoton (Yogurt) Festival; ¥10-20 at Lhasa teahouses.
Wuhan's breakfast shaomai are stuffed with peppery, lard-rich glutinous rice rather than shrimp — very different from Cantonese siu mai. A core 过早 item, often eaten with 热干面.
Smoky cured pork stir-fried with crunchy, pungent fish-mint root, the quintessential Guizhou flavor. Found on every Guiyang home-style menu.
Rice noodles topped with chunks of chicken fried in ciba chili, a Guiyang breakfast that locals swear by. ¥15-20; also comes with 面 (wheat noodles) if you ask.
Glossy, honey-lacquered barbecued pork hung in the window of every siu mei shop. Order 叉燒飯 (char siu over rice) for about HK$45-60, or ask for 半肥瘦 (half fat, half lean) for the juiciest cut.
Roast pork belly with a crackling, blistered skin, chopped to order at siu mei counters. Great as 雙拼飯 (two-meat rice) with char siu; dip in mustard.
The quintessential cha chaan teng breakfast: instant noodles (公仔麵) topped with fried Spam and a sunny-side egg. Usually part of a 早餐 set with toast and milk tea.
Fried pork chop over egg fried rice, smothered in tomato sauce (or cream sauce) and baked; the signature cha chaan teng hot dish. About HK$60-80 with a drink.
A warm pineapple bun split and stuffed with a thick slab of cold butter - Hong Kong's ultimate indulgence. Best fresh from the oven at places like Kam Wah Cafe.
Yellow-wrapped fish paste dumplings sold on skewers or in paper cups, doused in soy sauce and chili oil. Different from dim sum siu mai; a few dollars at street stalls.
Thick, starchy street soup with glass noodles standing in for shark fin. Season with red vinegar and white pepper; about HK$20 a bowl.
Chewy steamed rice-flour pudding set in little porcelain bowls, eaten on two bamboo skewers. Classic old-school street snack.
Strong black tea with a pile of lemon slices you smash with a long spoon. Hong Kong's most ordered cold drink; add HK$2-3 for 'cold' with a set meal.

dishes.en: Shredded Pork in Sweet Bean Sauce
dishes.desc: Slivers of pork stir-fried in sweet bean sauce, served over raw scallion shreds and wrapped in thin tofu skins or pancakes like a budget Peking duck. On almost every Beijing home-style menu for about 30-50 RMB.

Literally 'lamb scorpion' because the chunks of spine look like scorpion tails; braised in a spiced broth and gnawed with gloves, then the broth is used as hot pot. A winter favorite in Beijing; priced by the jin of bones.
Thick, juicy beef patties in a pan-fried dough shell, shaped like the bronze nails on Forbidden City gates. Bite carefully - they are full of hot juice. A Hui Muslim Beijing staple.
Crisp, golden fried glutinous cakes stuffed with sweet red bean paste, one of Tianjin's 'Three Treasures' of snacks (with Goubuli and Guifaxiang mahua). Named after the narrow Erduoyan Lane.

dishes.en: Tianjin Crispy Crepe Strips in Gravy
dishes.desc: Strips of mung-bean crepe soaked in a thick, savory gravy with sesame paste, fermented tofu and chili. A uniquely Tianjin breakfast, also written 锅巴菜 - Dafulai is the famous shop.

dishes.en: Corn Cakes with Stewed Small Fish
dishes.desc: Small fish braised in an iron pot whose sides are slapped with cornmeal cakes that crisp in the steam. A beloved Tianjin home-style dish found in local restaurants.
The flagship Lu (Shandong) cuisine dish: sea cucumber braised in a glossy scallion-infused sauce. Pricey; order at classic Jinan restaurants like Jufenglou.
A whole chicken braised so tender the meat falls off the bone, sold vacuum-packed at every Shandong train station. The classic gift from Shandong.
A spiral, flaky scallion-oil pastry baked crisp, Jinan's signature breakfast bread. Often eaten with a raw egg poked into the center or with tianmo porridge.
Grilled skewers finished by the diner on a small table-top charcoal stove, then wrapped in thin flour pancakes with scallions and dipping powder. Went viral in 2023 and draws crowds nightly.
Qingdao's famous beer, drunk fresh from the tap - locals buy draft beer in plastic bags (dai zhuang pijiu) to take away. Pair it with spicy clams.
A glossy red whole chicken braised in an old master stock, from Daokou town in Hua County. One of China's famous 'four great chickens'; sold in Zhengzhou stores and stations.
A flaky flatbread puffed on a griddle, then torn open and filled with beaten egg, lettuce and sauce. Born in Henan, now a breakfast staple everywhere for 5-8 RMB; add sausage (jiachang).
A 24-course banquet in which every dish is soupy and served in sequence like flowing water, dating to the Tang dynasty. Try it at Zhenbutong restaurant in Luoyang.

Small whole river shrimp flash-fried in very hot oil, then glazed in a glossy sweet-soy sauce so the shells turn crisp and edible. A benbang (old Shanghai) classic on nearly every local restaurant menu; eat it shell and all.

A milky, slow-simmered soup of cured and fresh pork with spring bamboo shoots — the name means 'salted, slow-bubbled, fresh'. Best in spring (March–April) when bamboo shoots are in season; usually ordered as a shared pot for the table.
Bite-sized ribs fried and reduced in a sticky, dark sweet-and-sour glaze, usually served at room temperature as a cold starter. One of the most-ordered Shanghai home-style dishes; great with beer.
Despite the name it isn't smoked: thick fish steaks are deep-fried and soaked in a sweet, spiced soy marinade. A staple cold appetizer (冷菜) at Shanghai restaurants and deli counters, sold by weight.

Flaky, coiled dough with scallions and lard, pan-fried then finished in the oven until crisp outside and layered inside. Famous street-stall breakfast in Shanghai (A Da's stall had hour-long queues); a few yuan each.

A flaky Suzhou-style pastry stuffed with juicy pork, served hot from the oven. Around Mid-Autumn Festival Shanghai has long queues for them (e.g. at Guangming Village on Huaihai Rd); best eaten immediately.
Rice cooked with chopped bok choy and salted pork in lard — humble, fragrant and very Shanghainese. Often sold with a pork chop or a bowl of 'chicken-duck blood soup' at cafeteria-style shops.
A pounded, breadcrumbed pork chop fried golden and dipped in Shanghai's tangy Worcestershire-style 'spicy soy' (辣酱油). A haipai classic — the place Xianderen (鲜得来) and old cafés are famous for it.
Pan-fried beef dumplings with crisp bottoms and juicy filling — Nanjing's Muslim-influenced specialty (Li Ji Qingzhen is famous). Pair with duck blood vermicelli soup.
Small taro pieces in a thick, translucent ruby-colored syrup scented with osmanthus. Nanjing's best-known dessert, especially in autumn.
Shredded paddy eel stir-fried in a thick soy sauce, then topped with garlic and sizzling hot oil at the table — 'xiangyou' means 'noisy oil'. A Suzhou/Shanghai classic.
Kunshan's famous noodles in a rich, dark broth made with fish, topped with fried fish or braised duck. One of China's 'top ten noodles'; try it in Kunshan or Suzhou.

Steamed hairy crabs from Yangcheng Lake near Suzhou, prized for rich golden roe. Season is roughly late September–December (females first, males later); dip in ginger vinegar and drink warm yellow wine.
A fluffy steamed bun filled with diced chicken, pork and bamboo shoot in sweet soy. Signature of Yangzhou morning tea (早茶) at Fuchun or Ye Chun teahouses.
Wuxi's famous hollow fried gluten balls stuffed with pork and braised in sweet soy. A Wuxi home-style classic; dry gluten puffs are a popular souvenir.
Salt-cured pork hock pressed into a pink, translucent terrine with jelly, sliced and dipped in Zhenjiang black vinegar with ginger. Zhenjiang's famous breakfast/teahouse dish.
Noodles cooked with a small wooden lid floating in the big pot — Zhenjiang's iconic everyday noodle. Ask for toppings like pork (肉丝) or eel (长鱼).
Silky flat rice noodles in clear pork or beef broth, the everyday breakfast of Shantou and Chaozhou. Choose toppings like beef balls, pork liver or fish balls; a bowl costs about ¥10-20.
Squares of rice-flour sheet in a starchy broth topped with braised pork, offal and egg. A classic Chaoshan breakfast; look for stalls also selling lu (braised) goose and pork.
Raw crab, shrimp, clams or mantis shrimp steeped in a garlicky soy-chili marinade - nicknamed 'Chaoshan poison' for being addictive. Best at late-night seafood joints; ask for 生腌虾蛄 for mantis shrimp.
Rice cooked to a loose porridge in a claypot with fresh shrimp, crab or eel, a favorite late-night meal (宵夜). One pot feeds 2-4; prices vary with the seafood you pick.
Large, duck-like stuffed glutinous rice balls served in clear sweet syrup - Chaozhou's famous tangyuan. A must-try sweet in the old town.
Tiny cups of strong Phoenix Dancong oolong brewed in the Chaoshan gongfu ritual. Offered everywhere; join locals at any shop for a cup.
One of Hainan's 'four famous dishes': tender muscovy duck from Qionghai, poached and served with lime-chili dip.
Wanning's black goat, stewed or roasted, another of Hainan's four famous dishes. Often cooked with coconut milk.
Rice noodles in a tangy sour-sweet sauce with dried squid and peanuts. The go-to noodle in Sanya.
Sour, spicy broth made from rice-wine lees; eaten as a seafood hot pot or noodle soup. A Wenchang specialty now trendy all over Hainan.
Haikou's laid-back tea-house culture: a cheap pot of tea with small plates of snacks for hours. Try in old arcade streets.
Slices of pork belly layered with Lipu taro and steamed in a fermented-tofu sauce. A Guilin banquet must.
Sweet-sour-spicy pickled fruits and vegetables sold in jars on Nanning streets.
Zhuang festival rice dyed five colors with plants, sold at markets.
Macanese creation of chicken baked in a coconut curry sauce - despite the name it's not Portuguese. A must-try at Macanese restaurants.
Portuguese salt cod, served many ways. Available at all Portuguese restaurants in Macau.
Silky congee with crab, a Macau late-night favourite.
Lacquered roast duck stuffed with aromatics and hung beside char siu in siu mei shops. Ordered by the quarter or half, chopped on the bone, with plum sauce or over rice or rice noodles.

A whole young pig roasted until the skin turns into a thin, glassy crackling — a centrepiece at Cantonese weddings and banquets. Many restaurants and siu mei shops sell it by the plate, served with hoisin and sugar for dipping.
Whole chicken poached in a sweet, star-anise-scented soy master stock until the skin turns glossy brown. A siu mei shop staple served chopped over rice or noodles.

Young pigeon marinated, scalded and deep-fried until the skin crackles and the meat stays pink and juicy. A Cantonese restaurant classic, often ordered whole and eaten with your hands, with salt-pepper and lemon on the side.

A whole chicken air-dried then fried so the skin turns paper-thin and crackly while the meat stays moist — a fixture of Cantonese banquets. Usually served half or whole with prawn crackers and spiced salt.

A Hakka dish from eastern Guangdong in which a whole chicken is wrapped in paper and baked in hot rock salt, giving silky, aromatic meat. Widely sold in Guangzhou; many shops now offer a quicker steamed 'salt-baked' version, often torn by hand (手撕).
A Guangzhou cold dish named after Baiyun Mountain: trotters boiled, chilled and pickled in sweet vinegar until crunchy and tangy. A popular appetiser at Cantonese restaurants and dim sum houses.
Beef brisket slow-braised in chu hou sauce, a fermented soybean paste invented in Foshan. Served in claypots or over rice, and also a classic street-stall filling with daikon.
A pot of mixed beef offal and radish simmering in spiced broth, snipped into a paper cup with scissors at Guangzhou street stalls. Point to the pieces you want and add mustard or chilli sauce.

Sweet-savoury air-dried sausages (腊肠 laap6 coeng2), cured pork belly and duck that hang in Guangzhou shops through winter. Most often steamed over rice or in claypot rice; a seasonal favourite before Chinese New Year.

Chicken flash-cooked in a scorching claypot so it sizzles ('ze ze') at the table, finished with a splash of rice wine. A Guangzhou late-night favourite; the same method is used for eel, frog and vegetables.
The original Cantonese sweet and sour pork: crisp battered pork in a glossy pineapple sauce. Found on nearly every Cantonese menu; also called 菠萝咕噜肉 when made with pineapple.
Despite the name, a Cantonese dish of fried spare ribs in a sticky, tangy sweet glaze. A crowd-pleaser on family-style menus.

dishes.en: Pork Belly with Preserved Mustard Greens
dishes.desc: Pork belly slices layered over sweet preserved mui choi and steamed until meltingly soft, then turned out dome-up. A Hakka dish from eastern Guangdong that's a home-style staple in Guangzhou restaurants; eat it with plain rice.
Tofu squares stuffed with seasoned minced pork and pan-fried, then braised or served in broth. A Hakka classic widely found in Guangdong home-style restaurants.

Fresh crab wok-fried with heaps of ginger and scallion — the classic Cantonese way to let seafood shine. Pick your crab from the tank and expect market price by weight; the same sauce is used for lobster.
Live shrimp briefly poached in boiling water and served whole with a soy-chilli dip — Cantonese cooking at its simplest. Order by the jin (500 g) at seafood restaurants and peel at the table.
Lightly battered squid fried and tossed with salt, pepper, garlic and chilli. The 椒盐 (salt-and-pepper) treatment is also popular with shrimp, tofu and pork ribs.
Scallops on the half shell steamed with a mound of golden garlic and glass noodles. A standard at Guangdong seafood restaurants and night-market seafood stalls, usually sold per piece.
Shrimp folded into softly set, barely cooked scrambled eggs — a gentle Cantonese home-style dish. Great over rice; the same egg style appears in 滑蛋牛肉 with beef.
Eggs whisked with water and steamed into a wobbly, silky savoury custard, finished with soy sauce. A home-style comfort dish often topped with minced pork, clams or dried scallop.

dishes.en: Steamed Pork Patty with Salted Fish
dishes.desc: A flat patty of hand-chopped pork steamed with a slice of pungent salted fish on top. Cantonese comfort food served with white rice; a common 'set rice' (蒸饭) option.
Tender sliced beef wok-tossed in oyster sauce, a sauce invented in Guangdong. Often served with greens; a dependable order at any Cantonese restaurant.
Crisp lettuce quickly blanched or stir-fried and drizzled with oyster sauce. The default vegetable side at Cantonese restaurants; 生菜 sounds like 'growing wealth', so it's popular at New Year.
Tender flowering greens blanched and dressed with oil and soy or oyster sauce. The simplest and most common green vegetable at congee shops, dim sum houses and restaurants; also try gai lan (芥兰).
A refined Buddhist dish from Dinghu Mountain near Zhaoqing: a dozen kinds of mushroom, fungus and vegetables braised in a light glossy sauce. Found on upscale Cantonese and vegetarian menus.
A braised mix of vegetables, tofu skin, fungus and noodles, traditionally eaten on the first day of Chinese New Year. Standard vegetarian option on Cantonese menus.
Cubes of soft tofu fried until crisp outside and custardy inside, then tossed with salt, pepper, garlic and chilli. A popular vegetarian-friendly order at Cantonese eateries.
A whole winter melon hollowed out, sometimes carved, and steamed with a rich broth of seafood and ham inside. A summer banquet showpiece; usually needs ordering in advance.

dishes.en: Pig's Trotters in Sweet Ginger Vinegar
