dishes.desc: Trotters, hard-boiled eggs and ginger stewed in sweet black vinegar — traditionally made for new mothers and shared with visitors to celebrate a birth. Sold by the bowl at Guangzhou dessert and snack shops.
Raw slices of fish poached directly in boiling congee so they stay silky. 生滚 means 'cooked to order' — the style used for most Cantonese congees, from beef to pork liver.
A Guangzhou congee with pork liver, kidney and meatballs; the name means 'passing the imperial exams' after a scholar who ate it. A classic at old-school congee shops.
Congee loaded with mixed pork innards cooked to order. A cheap, hearty breakfast at Guangzhou and Shunde congee stalls.
Wide, slippery rice noodles named after the Shahe area of Guangzhou where they originated — the 'ho fun' of 'beef chow fun'. Ordered in soup with beef, fish balls or brisket, or stir-fried.
The saucy sibling of dry-fried beef ho fun: rice noodles fried then smothered in a glossy beef and egg gravy. A noodle-shop staple; also 滑蛋牛河 with silky egg.
Thin egg noodles tossed in a hot wok with soy sauce, bean sprouts and scallions. A cheap breakfast staple at dim sum halls and noodle shops.
Noodles pan-fried into a cake crisp and golden on both sides, then topped with a seafood or meat gravy. Also called 煎面 or 'Hong Kong-style chow mein' abroad.
Spongy, pre-fried e-fu noodles braised dry with mushrooms and yellow chives. A must at Cantonese banquets and birthdays, where long noodles symbolise longevity.
Springy egg noodles tossed (捞) in ginger-scallion oil and oyster sauce, with broth on the side. A simple noodle-shop order; add char siu or brisket on top.
Thick, round, chewy rice noodles traditionally served in broth topped with roast goose or char siu. A Guangzhou and Pearl River Delta noodle-shop staple, especially around festivals.
Paper-thin, translucent rice sheets from Chencun in Shunde, steamed and served with soy and garlic or topped with beef or ribs. Silkier than cheung fun; widely eaten across Guangdong.
Flaky, buttery pastry packed with sweet BBQ pork, baked golden and sprinkled with sesame. A favourite baked item on the dim sum cart.
Fluffy steamed buns filled with sweet egg custard. A dim sum dessert loved by kids; don't confuse it with the molten 流沙包.
Like turnip cake but made with chunks of taro, steamed and often pan-fried. Popular on dim sum menus and at New Year.
A translucent, springy sweet cake with crunchy bits of fresh water chestnut, often pan-fried. A classic dim sum sweet, especially around New Year.
A fluffy, caramel-coloured steamed sponge cake served in big wedges at dim sum. Not too sweet — a good finisher with tea.
Football-shaped glutinous rice dumplings, fried until crisp and chewy, filled with savoury pork. A fried dim sum classic; slightly sweet dough with salty filling.
Mashed taro shaped around a savoury pork filling and deep-fried, forming a lacy honeycomb crust. Eat it hot; also called 蜂巢芋角 (honeycomb taro puff).
Thin, crackly fried rolls filled with pork, shrimp and vegetables. A dim sum and festival staple, served with Worcestershire or sweet chilli sauce.
Tofu-skin wrapped around shrimp and pork, then fried and/or steamed in an oyster gravy. Fried versions are 鲜虾腐皮卷 (crispy shrimp rolls); steamed ones are 鲜竹卷.
Soft tofu-skin rolls stuffed with pork and vegetables, steamed in a savoury gravy. A common steamer basket on dim sum menus.
Bouncy steamed beef meatballs flavoured with tangerine peel and coriander, sitting on bean curd skin. Served with Worcestershire sauce at dim sum.
A smaller, single-serve version of lo mai gai — sticky rice with chicken and mushrooms steamed in lotus leaf. Easier for one person to finish.
Bundles of chicken, fish maw, ham and taro tied in tofu skin and steamed in sauce. An old-school dim sum item still served in Guangzhou teahouses.
Tender honeycomb beef tripe steamed with ginger, chilli and spices. A classic 'adventurous' dim sum dish; also order 牛百叶 (beef omasum) for a crunchier tripe.
Translucent crystal-skin dumplings packed with garlic chives and shrimp, often pan-fried. A green, fragrant counterpoint to har gow.
One large dumpling filled with meat, seafood and gelled stock, served in its own bowl of broth. An indulgent dim sum item — pierce it and drink the soup with a spoon.
Translucent half-moon dumplings with a chunky pork, peanut and vegetable filling — the Guangzhou original made famous by 'Sister E' (娥姐粉果) in the 1920s. Different from the Teochew style.
Dumplings steamed then fried on one side to a crisp golden base. Served at many dim sum halls with red vinegar.
A fist-sized steamed bun stuffed with chicken, pork, sausage and half an egg — a whole meal in one. Also called 鸡球大包; a traditional dim sum cart item.
Soft steamed buns filled with smooth sweet lotus seed paste; peach-shaped ones (寿桃包) are served at birthdays for longevity.
A crispy fried dough stick wrapped in a slippery rice noodle sheet and drizzled with sweet soy. A Guangzhou dim sum breakfast pairing of crunchy and silky.
A modern dim sum hit: pink-red rice noodle roll wrapped around a crunchy fried netting with whole shrimp. Now on most Guangzhou dim sum menus.
Springy hand-beaten mud carp balls, steamed or fried. A Pearl River Delta favourite on dim sum and congee shop menus.
A Shunde showpiece: the fish skin is removed whole, stuffed with its own seasoned meat and fried so it looks intact. Order at Shunde restaurants that specialise in river fish.
Golden pan-fried fish cakes from Jun'an town in Shunde, springy and fragrant with tangerine peel. Sold at Shunde markets and restaurants as a snack or side.
Blanched crunchy fish skin tossed with peanuts, coriander, ginger and soy. A Shunde/Guangzhou snack served at congee shops and as a cold starter.
A Shunde specialty: buffalo milk and egg white stir-fried into soft, snowy curds, often with crab or shrimp. Shows off Shunde's famous dairy; mildly sweet and savoury.
A fermented, translucent white rice cake from Lunjiao in Shunde, springy with a honeycomb crumb and gently sweet-sour. Sold in dim sum halls and bakeries; similar to 白糖糕.
Steamed fermented rice flour cake, white, springy and lightly sweet. A traditional snack sold at dim sum halls and street stalls.
Little puddings of rice flour and sugar steamed in ceramic bowls, often with red beans, eaten on a bamboo stick. A nostalgic street snack across Guangdong.
Many thin layers of steamed sweet dough with salted egg yolk between them. A traditional dim sum sweet.
Chilled squares of white coconut jelly, sometimes layered with red bean. A light, cooling end to dim sum.
Clear, fragrant jelly set with osmanthus flowers and goji berries. A delicate, refreshing dim sum dessert.
Smooth mango pudding, often shaped in a fish mould and topped with evaporated milk. A dim sum dessert favourite.
Flaky golden pastries filled with creamy durian, baked or fried. A modern dim sum dessert hit; mild enough for durian beginners.
Soft, chewy glutinous rice balls stuffed with peanut-sesame-sugar and rolled in coconut. Sold at bakeries and dim sum houses; also the name of a famous Guangdong lychee variety.
Hollow fried balls of glutinous rice coated in sesame, chewy inside and crisp outside. A dim sum staple and New Year treat — Jiujiang in Foshan makes a famous giant version.
Light, brittle ribbons of fried egg dough drizzled with maltose syrup. A traditional Cantonese New Year and dim sum snack.
Puffy, chewy fried bread rounds, savoury-sweet with five-spice and fermented tofu. Eaten for breakfast with congee in Guangzhou, alongside youtiao and 牛脷酥.
Long, oval fried dough named for its ox-tongue shape, crisp outside and soft within, slightly sweet. A classic congee-shop side in Guangzhou.
Despite the name, no chicken: a crunchy, sweet-salty biscuit with fermented bean curd, pork fat and sesame, created in Guangzhou. A traditional souvenir from old bakeries.
Flaky pastry wrapped around century egg, sweet lotus paste and pickled ginger. A Guangzhou teahouse speciality balancing sweet, savoury and sour.
A crumbly biscuit from Foshan with candied pork fat, sesame and peanuts, said to have been invented by a blind fortune-teller in the Qing dynasty. A classic Foshan souvenir.
Crescent-shaped fried pastries with a crimped edge, filled with crushed peanuts, sesame and coconut. A must-have Chinese New Year snack in Guangdong, symbolising wealth.
Fried or steamed rice with roast meats and seafood, wrapped in a lotus leaf and steamed to absorb its fragrance. A Guangzhou classic on restaurant and dim sum menus.
Sweet mung bean soup, believed to clear summer heat; the Guangzhou version often includes kelp (海带). Eaten hot or chilled at dessert shops.
Thick, nutty black sesame paste served hot as a sweet soup. A staple of every Cantonese dessert shop; sometimes with glutinous rice balls.
A smooth, fragrant sweet soup of ground apricot kernels and rice, served hot. Ordered at dessert shops, sometimes with a swirl of egg white.
Sweet potato chunks simmered in a gingery brown-sugar syrup. Humble, warming home-style sweet soup found at dessert stalls.

dishes.en: Bean Curd and Ginkgo Sweet Soup
dishes.pron: foo jook bahk gwaw tong sui
dishes.desc: Silky dissolved bean curd sheets with ginkgo nuts and barley, often with a beaten egg. A classic Cantonese dessert shop soup.
Chewy glutinous rice balls in brown sugar syrup rolled in crushed peanuts and sesame — the name means 'sugar won't fall off'. A traditional Dongguan/Guangzhou street dessert.
Sago pearls in sweet coconut milk, often with taro (芋头西米露). Served hot or iced at dessert shops.
Double-boiled papaya with silky snow fungus — a nourishing, beauty-boosting Cantonese dessert. Sometimes served inside a hollowed papaya.
Wobbly silken tofu pudding served warm with ginger or brown sugar syrup. Eaten as a dessert or breakfast snack across Guangdong; in Guangzhou it's always sweet.
Bitter herbal brews sold from cauldrons at Guangzhou's herbal tea shops to 'cool' the body, with a UNESCO-recognised tradition. Try 廿四味 (24-flavour) if brave, or sweeter 菊花茶 (chrysanthemum tea).
A lightly sweet cooling drink brewed from sugarcane, cogon root and carrot. Sold chilled by the cup at herbal tea and dessert shops.

dishes.en: Smoked Bamboo Shoots with Cured Pork
dishes.desc: Smoky Hunan bacon stir-fried with chewy smoked bamboo shoots and chili. A rustic home-style favorite on most local menus.
Finely chopped dried pickled vegetables from western Hunan stir-fried with chili, often with minced pork. A cheap, salty side that makes rice disappear.
Duck marinated, pressed flat and dried with chili and spices — chewy, very spicy and sold vacuum-packed or by weight. A popular snack and souvenir in Changsha.
Chopped duck stir-fried with chili, then finished with fresh duck blood that coats every piece. A bold southern Hunan specialty found in Xiang restaurants.
Beef tripe sliced as fine as hair and stir-fried hot and sour. A celebrated Changsha classic prized for its crunch.
Thin-stemmed cauliflower charred in a sizzling dry pot with pork belly and chilies, kept hot at the table over a flame. Ubiquitous at Hunan restaurants.
Braised then fried pork intestines served in a tabletop dry pot with chili. Rich and chewy — a favorite with beer.
Charred green chilies pounded in a mortar with century eggs and garlic. A smoky, punchy cold dish on most Changsha menus.

dishes.en: Pickled Long Beans with Minced Pork
dishes.desc: Sour pickled beans stir-fried with minced pork and chili — a cheap, addictive rice topper. Also spooned onto Changsha rice noodles.
Cabbage torn by hand and wok-fried with dried chilies and a splash of vinegar. A cheap, smoky vegetable side ordered at nearly every Hunan meal.
Hunan's famous lotus seeds simmered in a light rock-sugar syrup. A classic sweet finish at banquets and dessert shops.
Crispy deep-fried rice-flour cakes studded with scallion, sold hot at street stalls. A cheap savory counterpart to sugar-oil baba.
Smooth tofu-like pork blood served in a bowl with chili and crunchy toppings. A traditional Changsha snack, especially around Pozi Street.
A pair of glutinous rice balls — one sweet, one savory — made famous by the Huogongdian restaurant. Order them alongside stinky tofu for a classic Changsha snack spread.
Fluffy steamed buns from a century-old Changsha shop, with sweet-savory char siu or mixed fillings. A typical breakfast grab.

ingredients: pea or mung bean starch jelly
dishes.desc: Cool starch jelly scraped into strands and drenched in chili and vinegar. A refreshing summer street snack.
Sliced crunchy peaches and young ginger tossed with perilla, sugar and chili. A sweet-sour-spicy summer snack sold in cups on Changsha streets.
Round rice noodles in rich beef broth topped with spicy braised beef — originally from Changde but sold all over Hunan for breakfast. Ask for 'hongshao' (braised) or 'qingdun' (clear-stewed).
Rows of little bowls of steamed meats, vegetables and tofu you pick from a counter and eat with rice. A cheap, fast lunch found all over Changsha.
Not real tofu but soft rice jelly cut into cubes and served cold or warm with spicy toppings. A popular western Hunan street snack in Zhangjiajie and Fenghuang.
Dried betel nut husks chewed as a stimulant snack, sold in packs at every Hunan convenience store. Strong and astringent — try one piece only.
Wuhan's take on shaomai, filled with peppery soy-seasoned glutinous rice. Often eaten wrapped in a fried flatbread as 'youbing bao shaomei'.
Fried glutinous rice balls coated in sesame — the name means 'happy lumps.' A sweet breakfast snack at Wuhan stalls.
A slab of hot sticky rice wrapped around a fried dough stick, sweet with sugar or savory with pickles. A filling, cheap Wuhan breakfast.
Sweet fermented rice wine with egg ribbons, drunk hot alongside hot dry noodles. Only lightly alcoholic.
Thin crepes made from rice and bean batter, cut into strips and pan-fried or served in soup. A local breakfast and home-style dish.
Flaky, oil-rich baked flatbread from Wuhan's breakfast stalls, eaten plain or with tea.
A deep-fried crescent dumpling shaped like a rooster's comb, filled with peppery pork. A classic Wuhan breakfast item.
Meat, fish and vegetables coated in seasoned rice flour and steamed — a famous Hubei banquet trio from Xiantao.

dishes.en: Purple Choy Sum with Cured Pork
dishes.desc: Wuhan's prized purple flowering greens stir-fried with smoky cured pork — a winter seasonal favorite.
Yangtze longsnout catfish braised in soy until silky and gelatinous. A prized Hubei fish dish.
Semi-dried fish chunks fried then simmered in a sweet-spicy glaze. A home-style Hubei favorite.
A smooth steamed fish cake with a golden egg top, sliced and served in hot pots or banquets. Originally from Jingzhou.
Lotus root slices sandwiching minced pork, battered and fried. Hubei is lotus country, and this is a common snack and side.
Sweet fermented rice soup with little glutinous balls and osmanthus, thickened slightly. A warming Wuhan dessert.
Eel strips fried crisp and coated in sweet-sour sauce — a time-honored Wuhan restaurant dish.
Little tadpole-shaped rice jelly drops in iced brown sugar syrup — despite the name, no shrimp. A summer street drink.
Not dumplings but crisp fried patties of shredded radish in rice batter, served with chili. Yichang's signature street snack.
Small whole potatoes slowly pan-fried until crisp, then dusted with chili and cumin. A cheap street snack in western Hubei.
Rice noodles topped with soft tofu pudding and savory meat sauce — a silky Kunming classic.
Cold rice noodles tossed with shredded chicken in a tangy chili dressing — a Dali summer favorite.
Thick rice threads (ersi) pan-braised with soy and pork — Yunnan's chewy alternative to mixian.
A warm, thick yellow pea porridge eaten for breakfast, often with fried dough or rice noodles dipped in. Very cheap and filling.
Steamed buns with flaky layered dough and savory ham or sweet fillings — a Kunming breakfast classic.
Sweet-salty mooncakes filled with diced Xuanwei ham and honey, sold year-round. A beloved souvenir.
Yunnan's prized dry-cured ham, sliced and steamed, fried with vegetables, or folded into buns and mooncakes.
Air-dried salted beef, often fried in oil until crispy, from Hui Muslim communities. Served as a side or snack.
Three ingredients — pork, dark pickled greens and green chili — finely chopped and stir-fried. A cheap home-style rice topper.
Duck roasted over pine wood for a crisp skin and smoky aroma, sold by the half or whole around Kunming.
Prized wild termite mushrooms slow-fried and preserved in chili oil — eaten with noodles or rice, and sold in jars as a souvenir.
Wild bolete that turns blue when touched, stir-fried with garlic during the rainy season. Must be thoroughly cooked — only eat it at reputable restaurants.
Rough mashed potatoes fried with pickled greens and chili — soft enough for grandma to eat. On nearly every Yunnan menu.
Fried potato chunks tossed with chili, mint and scallion, sold by the cup at street stalls everywhere in Yunnan.
Soft steamed rice sheets rolled up and doused with sauces — a cheap breakfast or snack.
Wobbly clear jelly from fig seeds in brown sugar syrup — a cooling summer dessert. Not actually papaya.
A Kunming summer dessert of cool sweet rice with fruits and syrup, sold at snack shops.
Sweet-tart tamarind drink served cold in restaurants across Yunnan — the classic pairing with spicy food. Also sold as tamarind candy (suanjiao gao).
Yunnan's famous aged and fermented tea, pressed into cakes. Tea shops will happily let you sample before buying.
A Dai dish of rice noodles and beef dipped in a sour or bitter herb sauce. Lime-based versions are milder for first-timers.
Chicken feet pounded with lime, chili and herbs — a sour, fiery Dai snack.
Meat, fish or vegetables wrapped in banana leaves with herbs and grilled over coals. Choose your filling at Dai barbecue stalls.
Dai dipping sauces served with raw and blanched vegetables. Every Dai meal comes with one.
Sticky rice cooked inside a fresh bamboo tube for a subtle fragrance; you crack the tube open to eat. A minority specialty sold at markets.
Shredded chicken tossed with lime, chili and herbs — sour and fiery. Popular at Dai restaurants.
Deep-fried bamboo worms with a crunchy, nutty taste — the most accessible of Yunnan's edible insects.
A Bai specialty of blowtorched pork skin and raw pork dipped in sour chili sauce. Adventurous only; check the source.
Plums intricately carved and preserved in honey — a Bai snack and souvenir.
A puffy fried flatbread said to be named for Western tourists. Eaten with honey or yak butter tea.
Naxi rice-and-blood sausage, sliced and pan-fried — a classic in Lijiang's old town.
Layered meats and vegetables stewed in a clay pot heated with charcoal — Tengchong's hearty local hot pot.

A Jianghu-style dish from Nanshan where chicken is cooked in mountain spring water, then stir-fried spicy or simmered in broth. Dozens of restaurants line the Nanshan hillside road; ordered per whole bird.

Live fish cooked in a bubbling red sauce of pickled chilies and peppercorns, from Laifeng town in Bishan. A classic of Chongqing's rustic 'Jianghu cuisine'; you pick the fish and pay by the jin (500 g).
Silky fish pieces braised in a spicy-sour pickled chili sauce, named after Tai'an town in Tongnan. Another Jianghu fish classic, usually sold by weight.
Small crucian carp simmered in a numbing-spicy pot, originally from a highway stop in Dazu. Served like a mini hot pot; add tofu or vegetables once the fish is gone.
Duck pieces braised in beer with chilies and spices until glossy and tender. A common home-style Jianghu dish at casual Chongqing restaurants; often served as a dry pot.
Chopped chicken stir-fried with a mountain of fresh green chilies and green peppercorns, fragrant rather than red-hot. Popular since the 1990s Jianghu boom; good with plain rice.
Chicken and soft baby taro stewed in a spicy red broth served in a big pot. A Chongqing comfort classic; the taro soaking up the chili broth is the best part.
Rooster chunks braised in a fiery, oily pot; once the chicken is eaten, broth is added and it becomes a hot pot. Shops with a big red 'Shāo Jīgōng' sign are everywhere in Chongqing.
A dry pot of spicy stir-fried chicken that is turned into a hot pot with broth once you've eaten down the meat, credited to Chongqing. Chains sell it across China; order by size of pot.
A Liangping-origin spicy chicken pot served like a hot pot, with vegetables and noodles added later. Inexpensive, hearty and popular with groups.
Chicken stewed in an iron wok over a wood fire built into the table, with corn cakes stuck to the wok's rim. A rustic outskirts-of-town experience in Chongqing.
Chicken and soft pork intestines braised together in a spicy pot, a Chongqing Jianghu favorite served as a dry pot that turns into hot pot. For adventurous eaters.

dishes.en: Old Duck Soup with Pickled Radish
dishes.desc: A clear, sour, gently flavored duck soup made with pickled radish, often eaten as a non-spicy hot pot. A great option when you need a break from mala.
Tiny bamboo steamers of spiced, rice-flour-coated ribs, beef or intestines, a Wanzhou street-food classic. Order several baskets of different meats with chili and coriander.
Salted, pressed and smoked duck from Baishiyi town, sold whole or chopped at deli counters. A traditional Chongqing souvenir food, eaten cold with drinks.
Chongqing xiaomian topped with chunks of spicy braised beef, a standard noodle-shop order. Ask for 'gān liū' (dry) or soup, and 'wēilà' if you want milder spice.
Spicy noodles topped with a savory minced-pork sauce, a staple at every Chongqing noodle stall. Different from Beijing zhajiangmian; often ordered as 'zájiàng xiǎomiàn' for breakfast.
Pork wontons drenched in a heavily numbing red oil, a Chongqing favorite made famous by local chain Lao Ma Chaoshou. Cheap and filling for breakfast or late night.
Pig brain grilled in a foil tray with chili, garlic and scallions until custardy, a famous Chongqing late-night street snack. Found at barbecue stalls; for the adventurous.
A chewy sweet potato starch sheet grilled flat, brushed with chili sauce and folded around fillings. Ubiquitous at Chongqing night-market barbecue stalls for a few yuan.
Sweet fermented rice wine fried with lard, nuts and brown sugar, a warming traditional Chongqing breakfast. Often sold with a poached egg added.
Crisp blocks of puffed rice bound with sugar, peanuts and sesame, a famous specialty of Jiangjin. Sold boxed as gifts in Chongqing.
Thin, soft slices of sweet rice cake studded with walnut, a century-old specialty from Hechuan. A popular boxed Chongqing gift.
Crunchy fried broad beans coated in a 'strange flavor' mix of sweet, salty, spicy and numbing. A classic Chongqing packaged snack, great with beer.
Salty, crunchy pickled mustard tuber from Fuling, eaten with congee, noodles and rice all over China. Comes in small sachets everywhere; it's the original Zha cai.
Fish sliced and cooked so fast in a pickled-chili broth it seems to 'jump into the water', keeping it extremely tender. A Jianghu dish served at casual Chongqing fish houses.
A trendy Chongqing hot pot combining bullfrog and fish head in a spicy broth. Order a half-and-half pot at the specialty chains; the frog cooks in minutes.
Chongqing's own light lager, the standard pairing with hot pot and barbecue. Ask for it chilled ('bīng de') at any restaurant.
A herbal-tinged Chinese cola created in Chongqing in the 1980s and recently revived. A fun nostalgic drink to cool down after hot pot.
Wide noodles served in soft tofu pudding and eaten by dipping into a chili sauce. A Zunyi breakfast staple dating back to the 1940s.
Golden steamed rice cakes wrapped in bamboo leaves and sweetened with brown sugar, a Zunyi specialty. Eaten steamed or pan-fried in slices.
Zunyi's open-topped steamed dumplings, named for their resemblance to a broom head; a local cousin of siu mai. Ordered by the steamer basket at teahouses.

A Miao and Dong specialty from southeast Guizhou where the bitter broth is made from partly digested grass in the cow's stomach, eaten with beef and offal. Famous as an adventurous local delicacy; locals swear it aids digestion.
A thick, creamy hot pot broth made from mashed kidney beans and pickled greens, a cozy Guiyang favorite. Dip ingredients into a chili-zheergen sauce.
Hollow deep-fried tofu balls slit open and stuffed with spicy sauce and zheergen, a classic Guiyang snack (also called 'Lei's tofu balls'). Eat them hot from the fryer.
Mashed potato cakes pan-fried crisp and dusted with chili powder, a ubiquitous Guizhou street snack. Cheap and filling.
Thin rice-flour crepes rolled around crunchy pickles and vegetables and doused with sour-spicy sauce, an Anshun-origin snack found all over Guiyang. Similar to silk dolls but pre-rolled.
Glutinous rice cake slices in a sweet translucent lotus-root starch porridge with rose sugar, a Guiyang breakfast classic. Sold from morning stalls alongside chang wang noodles.
Rice stir-fried with whatever is on hand — pickles, cured pork, zheergen, potatoes — into a mixed-up 'strange' fried rice. A Guiyang night-market and student favorite.
A scoop of steamed sticky rice packed with crunchy fried dough, pickles and spicy minced pork, a grab-and-go Guiyang breakfast. Cheap and very filling.
Thick rice-noodle sheets snipped with scissors straight into your bowl and topped with sauces and pickles. A Guiyang street snack eaten cold or warm.
Rice noodle sheets chopped ('duó') into small pieces and tossed in sour-spicy sauce, a nostalgic Guiyang snack. Look for it at old-town stalls.
Fish from the Wujiang River cooked in a spicy, sour chili broth, popular across northern Guizhou. Sold by weight at riverside restaurants.
A sweet icy slush drink sold from Guiyang street stalls, perfect after spicy food. Often mixed with fruit or bean jelly.
Juice from the vitamin-C-packed 'chestnut rose' fruit, a Guizhou specialty with a tart, astringent taste. Sold bottled everywhere in the province.
China's most famous sauce-aroma baijiu, distilled in Maotai town near Zunyi. Powerful and pricey; try a small shot or visit the distillery town.
A delicate, curly green tea from Duyun, ranked among China's famous teas. Buy loose leaf in Guiyang tea shops.
Chewy maltose candy flavored with rose, pulled and sold by vendors in Qingyan Ancient Town near Guiyang. Watch it being made and buy a bag.
Beef cooked in the Miao red sour soup (fermented tomato and chili), a sibling of the famous sour soup fish. Served as a hot pot in Kaili and Guiyang.
Tender spring bamboo shoots braised in soy sauce and sugar until glossy and sweet-savory. A seasonal Hangzhou classic in March–May; ask for it when shoots are fresh.
Thin tofu skin rolled around minced pork and fried so crisp it 'rings' when bitten. A classic Hangzhou starter, dipped in sweet bean sauce or spiced salt.
A clear, delicate broth with slippery water shield leaves from West Lake, garnished with ham and chicken. A light palate-cleanser at Hangzhou banquets and restaurants.
Tiny ear-shaped pinches of dough simmered in a light broth with shrimp and ham. A comforting Hangzhou snack at old-style restaurants like Zhiweiguan.
A hollowed orange stuffed with crab meat and roe and steamed so the citrus perfumes the crab. An elegant autumn dish on Hangzhou restaurant menus during hairy-crab season.
Duck cured in soy sauce and air-dried until mahogany, then steamed and sliced. Hung outside homes in winter, it's served cold as a salty-sweet appetizer.
Pink, flower-shaped steamed rice cakes filled with red bean paste, once given to soldiers wishing for victory. Sold warm from stalls and bakeries around Hangzhou.

dishes.en: West Lake Lotus Root Starch Pudding
dishes.desc: Lotus root starch whisked with hot water into a translucent, jelly-like pudding topped with osmanthus and nuts. A Hangzhou specialty sold by the bowl near West Lake and as a boxed souvenir.
Noodles in a rich broth topped with stir-fried river shrimp and crispy-fried eel strips. The signature of Hangzhou's century-old Kuiyuanguan noodle shop.

dishes.en: Lotus Leaf Steamed Pork with Rice Powder
dishes.desc: Pork belly coated in spiced rice powder, wrapped in lotus leaf and steamed until meltingly tender. One of the classic 'West Lake Ten Scenes' dishes in Hangzhou.

dishes.en: Old Duck and Dried Bamboo Shoot Casserole
dishes.desc: A slow-simmered clay pot of old duck, dried bamboo shoots and ham, giving a deep, savory broth. A staple of Hangzhou home-style restaurants, especially in cooler months.
A big carp head stewed with tofu in a bubbling clay pot until the broth turns rich. A classic Hangzhou family dish; one pot feeds a table.
Lotus root stuffed with glutinous rice, simmered in sugar syrup and drizzled with osmanthus. Served sliced and cold as a sweet starter across Hangzhou.
Minced pork wrapped in thin tofu sheets and simmered in broth, often served with vermicelli. A Huzhou specialty found all over Zhejiang.
A crisp flatbread stuffed with pork and preserved greens, baked on the wall of a barrel oven. Originating in Lishui's Jinyun county, its stalls are everywhere in Zhejiang.
Raw swimming crab cured in strong brine and eaten cold, prized for its jelly-like orange roe. Very salty — Ningbo locals eat it with plain rice.
Noodles in a rich fish broth with pan-fried yellow croaker and pickled greens. A favorite lunch at Ningbo noodle shops.
Short, crunchy fried dough sticks, often flavored with seaweed or sesame. A traditional Ningbo snack sold in bags at old shops on Chenghuang Temple streets.
A flaky, crisp square biscuit of many layers, sweet with a hint of seaweed. A souvenir from Xikou, Chiang Kai-shek's hometown near Ningbo.
Poached chicken cured in fragrant Shaoxing wine lees and served cold. A boozy, aromatic appetizer typical of Shaoxing.
Pungent fermented tofu skins, usually steamed, part of Shaoxing's beloved 'mei' (fermented) foods. Strong-smelling but savory; pairs with rice wine.
Irregular, springy fish-paste strips in a light broth sharpened with vinegar and pepper. A cheap, beloved Wenzhou street snack.
Lamp-shaped fritters of rice-soy batter stuffed with radish, pork and egg, deep-fried in a ladle. A crispy Wenzhou street snack.
Delicate, translucent-skinned wontons in broth with egg ribbons and seaweed; Changren is the famous old shop. A quick snack any time of day.
Small, crunchy baked pastries filled with preserved mustard greens and pork fat, coated in sesame. A popular Jinhua snack and souvenir.
Tender mountain bamboo shoots from Shexian braised with cured pork. A spring delicacy on Huangshan menus.
Chicken simmered with stone-ear lichen picked from Huangshan's cliffs. A restorative mountain soup in Tunxi and Yellow Mountain area restaurants.
A flat savory pie pressed under a hot stone on a griddle until crisp, filled with preserved greens and pork. A popular snack in Huizhou old towns like Tunxi Old Street.
A green tea with distinctive long, flat leaves from the Taiping area near Huangshan. Smooth and floral; one of China's ten famous teas.
A rich braise of seafood, meats and vegetables named after the Hefei-born Qing statesman Li Hongzhang. A signature on Hefei restaurant menus.
Spiced braised goose from Wushan near Hefei, once sent as tribute. Bought sliced from takeaway shops and eaten cold.
Flaky flatbread brushed with duck fat and scallions, baked crisp — often paired with Luzhou roast duck. A Hefei breakfast staple.
A clear, deeply flavored soup from slow-cooked old hen, from Feixi county near Hefei. Restaurants specializing in it are all over Hefei.
Wide noodles slapped on a board, served in a spicy beef sauce. Originally from Taihe county, these noodle shops are found all over Anhui.
A whole chicken fried then braised with spices until tender — one of China's four famous chickens. Sold whole at Anhui deli counters and stations.
A small round baked bread with a hole in the middle, named after general Qi Jiguang whose soldiers carried them on strings. Split and stuffed with fillings at Fuzhou stalls.
Fried pork ribs tossed in a sweet-sour sauce with a splash of rice wine. A favorite Fuzhou dish of the sweet-and-sour school.
Chicken cooked with red fermented rice wine lees, giving a rosy color and fruity aroma. Red lees (hongzao) is the signature seasoning of Fuzhou cooking.
Steamed taro mashed with lard and sugar into a rich, hot paste topped with dried fruits. A Fuzhou dessert served at the end of banquets — careful, it's very hot inside.
Fluffy, sweet-savory dried pork floss, a Fuzhou specialty since the Qing dynasty. Sprinkle on congee or buy in tins as a souvenir.
Springy slivers of starch-coated pork poached in a tangy, peppery broth. Fuding-style shops are all over Fujian for a quick, cheap meal.
Springy noodles tossed in rich peanut sauce and soy. The cheap, filling staple of Shaxian Xiaochi shops, eaten alongside wonton soup.
Small pleated pork dumplings steamed in bamboo baskets, often eaten with peanut sauce. A Shaxian snack shop standby.
Little clay jars of soup slow-steamed with pork ribs, chicken or herbs. Pick a jar from the steamer at any Shaxian shop.
Pork and water chestnut seasoned with five-spice, wrapped in tofu skin and deep-fried. A popular Xiamen snack, cut into slices and dipped in sweet chili sauce.
A clear, cooling jelly made from seaweed, served icy with syrup. A refreshing Xiamen summer treat, often part of si guo tang.
A shaved-ice dessert bowl where you pick toppings like jellies, beans and fruit. Found at dessert shops across southern Fujian on hot days.
A thick, fluffy griddle pancake folded around crushed peanuts and sugar. Sold by the wedge at Xiamen street stalls.
Steamed rice-and-radish cake, sliced and pan-fried until crisp. A Minnan breakfast and street snack, especially popular around Lunar New Year.
A big square of pork sealed in a pot and slow-steamed with mushrooms until melting. A banquet must from Tong'an district of Xiamen.
Soft glutinous rice balls rolled in peanut or sesame powder. Gulangyu's famous Ye family stall draws long lines of tourists.
Noodles in a thick, savory gravy-like broth loaded with pork, seafood and egg. A southern Fujian festive staple, served at weddings and local noodle shops.
Springy fish-paste rolls from the fishing town of Chongwu, sliced and fried or added to soups. A Quanzhou-area specialty and souvenir.
Pork marinated in vinegar, battered and fried crisp. A Quanzhou snack added to noodle soups or eaten on its own.
A seafood congee loaded with oysters, shrimp and pork, its name possibly from the cat-like noise of a stall owner. A Zhangzhou late-night and breakfast favorite.
A 'chaotic stew' of pork, potatoes, eggplant, beans, corn and whatever vegetables are on hand. Huge portions — one bowl feeds several people.
Fried sweet potato chunks coated in hot caramel that pulls into long golden threads as you lift each piece. Dip quickly in the bowl of cold water provided to set the sugar before eating.
Battered, deep-fried pork pieces quickly tossed in a glossy savory-sweet sauce with peppers. A cousin of guo bao rou that's saltier and less sour.
Wide, chewy translucent starch sheets tossed with shredded vegetables and a sesame-garlic-vinegar dressing. A refreshing cold dish to balance heavy Dongbei stews.

Chewy yellow buns of sticky millet/rice dough filled with sweet red bean paste, traditionally made in big batches and frozen for winter. Steamed and dipped in sugar; sold at markets and breakfast stalls.
Pears frozen solid outdoors until black, then thawed in cold water so the inside turns into icy, juicy sorbet. A Harbin winter classic — fancy restaurants now serve it peeled and sliced.
Harbin's Russian-heritage borscht, made tomato-red rather than beet-red, served at old Russian-style restaurants along Central Street with big Russian bread. Order alongside 红肠 and 大列巴.
Thin, flaky layered flatbread stuffed with sliced smoked pork, made famous by the century-old Li Liangui (李连贵) brand. A filling lunch for about ¥15–25.
Rice topped with vegetables, meat and a fried egg in a sizzling stone bowl; stir in chili paste and let a crispy crust form. Ubiquitous in Yanji and Korean-Chinese restaurants across the Northeast.
Korean-style sticky rice pounded with mallets, cut into squares and rolled in roasted soybean powder. Watch vendors pound it fresh at Yanji's Xishi market.
Korean-style sundae: pork intestine stuffed with rice, blood and noodles, sliced and dipped in salted shrimp or spicy sauce. A cheap market snack in Yanji.
Spicy fermented napa cabbage made by Yanbian's Korean-Chinese families, served free as a side and sold by weight in markets. Also used in kimchi fried rice and stews.
Balls of red bean paste wrapped in whipped egg white and fried into feather-light puffs, then dusted with sugar. A classic Dongbei banquet dessert; eat them hot.
Shenyang's century-old dumpling brand, famous for its pre-cooked 'simmered' filling that makes them extra juicy. Order a mixed steamer to try several fillings.
A Hui Muslim shaomai house dating to 1796, serving open-topped beef dumplings with paper-thin wrappers. A Shenyang time-honored brand (老字号).
Fresh Dalian oysters battered and deep-fried until crisp, dipped in pepper salt. A classic Liaodong seafood appetizer.
Quick-stir-fried 'sea intestine' (a marine spoon worm) with chives and savory sauce, poured over rice. A pricey but beloved Dalian/Bohai seafood specialty.
Fried salted fish eaten with pan-crisped cornmeal cakes — humble fishermen's food turned nostalgic Dalian restaurant favorite.
River fish stewed with tofu and glass noodles in soybean paste, named after a roadside village near Harbin. Big portions meant for sharing.

dishes.en: Green Chili with Dried Tofu Sheets
dishes.desc: Thin, chewy Northeastern tofu sheets stir-fried with mildly hot green peppers. A cheap everyday side dish on every Dongbei menu.
A platter of raw scallions, cucumbers, lettuce and radishes dipped into salty fermented soybean paste (often fried with egg). The quintessential Dongbei side dish.

Pick skewers or ingredients from a fridge, pay by weight, and they're cooked in a milky bone broth finished with sesame paste — creamier and sweeter than the Sichuan original. Harbin's Yang Guofu and Zhang Liang chains started here.
Thick noodles squeezed by hand from fermented corn dough straight into broth, a Manchu-origin specialty of Liaoning. Mildly sour and comforting.
Clear lamb broth with tender sliced mutton and glass noodles, served with a small flatbread you dip or eat on the side — unlike paomo, no crumbling. A popular Xi'an breakfast.
Tiny steamed sticky-rice cakes on sticks, smoothed flat like a mirror and sprinkled with sugar and colorful sweet powders. A cheap Muslim Quarter snack.
An ancient flatbread baked on hot river pebbles, leaving dimpled crispy surfaces. Sold as a travel snack and souvenir in Xi'an.
Smoky-sweet chilled plum juice ladled from big jars in the Muslim Quarter — the ideal partner to greasy roujiamo or skewers. Ask for 冰的 (iced).
Xi'an's beloved local orange soda in a glass bottle, a must with roujiamo and liangpi (the 'Shaanxi trio' 三秦套餐). Return the bottle to the shop.
A milky, low-alcohol rice wine flavored with osmanthus, served warm or cold in Xi'an since the Tang dynasty. Sweet and easy to drink with dumpling banquets.
Coarse flour stirred into a dense paste, cut into pieces and doused in spicy vinegar sauce — peasant food from the Guanzhong plain. Also made into 'fish' shapes (水围城, 搅团鱼鱼).
Extra-long, belt-wide noodles served in hot water, dipped strand by strand into a spicy tomato-egg sauce. One noodle can fill the bowl.
The Gansu/Qinghai cousin of liangpi: thick, jiggly steamed wheat sheets cut into strips and dressed with chili, vinegar and garlic. Lanzhou's 高担酿皮 stall is famous.
A thick, sweet soup of slow-cooked grey peas and jujubes, eaten hot or cold. Classic Lanzhou street dessert after a bowl of beef noodles.
Hot milk with sweet fermented rice, swirled egg and dried fruits — Lanzhou's night-market comfort drink (try Zhengning Road night market).
Noodles in a cooling, sour broth fermented from vegetables — a summer favorite in Gansu and Shaanxi. Tangy and light.
Hand-torn square noodles stir-fried with meat, peppers and tomato in Hui Muslim noodle shops across the Northwest. Hearty and cheap.
A whole pear stewed in rock-sugar syrup and served hot in its juice — a traditional Lanzhou winter remedy for coughs.
Ningxia tan lamb steamed plain to showcase its mild, sweet meat, dipped in salt and garlic. Yinchuan restaurants list it next to hand-pulled lamb.
A bowl of mixed little things — fried meatballs, sliced meat, noodles and tofu — in hot broth. A beloved Yinchuan breakfast and night-market dish.
Fine, springy noodles made with wormwood-seed powder, served in a lamb soup with diced meat. A Yinchuan breakfast staple.
Golden fried rounds of dough eaten by Hui Muslims at festivals and with tea. Slightly sweet; sold at mosques and Hui bakeries.
Thin strands of dough looped and deep-fried into crispy nests, a Hui festival snack served with eight-treasure tea.
Thick, set yogurt sold in bowls at Xining markets, often topped with sugar. Rich and tangy — spoon it straight from the bowl.
A thin, layered pan-fried pancake whose funny name comes from how the cook drizzles oil around the rim. Eaten with milk tea or yogurt in Xining.
Small noodle squares pinched straight into lamb broth — 'ga' means 'little' in Qinghai dialect. Everyday food in Xining's Muslim noodle shops.
Small lamb-filled wonton-style dumplings (Uyghur: chuchure) in a light, tangy broth. A warming breakfast or light meal.
Short pulled noodles in a hearty tomato-lamb soup (Uyghur: suyuqash). Cheap, comforting and found in every Uyghur canteen.
Noodles chopped into tiny cubes and stir-fried with lamb and vegetables, eaten with a spoon. A Uyghur canteen staple alongside laghman.
Cold poached chicken tossed with tingly green Sichuan pepper oil and lots of onion — a Xinjiang Hui and Han favorite. Often served with wide noodles.
Big slabs of lamb hung on iron racks and roasted over a pit fire until smoky and crisp — a specialty from Xinjiang's sheep country.
Lamb stewed in individual enamel mugs lined up over a coal fire — a Kashgar breakfast classic. Pour the broth over torn naan.
A Kazakh dish of boiled meat (often horse) laid over flat noodles with onions, eaten by hand. Look for it in Kazakh restaurants.
Kazakh smoked horse sausage (kazy), sliced and served cold or in stews; sold in Urumqi's bazaars as a souvenir.
Springy yellow noodles served cold with vinegar, garlic and chili (Uyghur: sériq ash) — a summer bazaar snack, often paired with 凉粉.
Lamb feet braised and coated in a dark, numbing chili sauce — gnawing these is a classic Urumqi late-night snack with beer.
Tower-shaped steamed buns of paper-thin layers brushed with lamb fat; soft and rich. Eaten for breakfast with milk tea or with pilaf.
Noodle dough pinched off in thumb-sized pieces straight into a tomato-lamb broth. Home-style comfort food in Xinjiang's Hui and Han restaurants.
Unwrapped sticky rice dumplings drowned in thick yogurt and syrup, sold from carts in summer. A uniquely Xinjiang sweet snack.
Rich, eggy ice cream (Uyghur: maroji) churned in a spinning drum on ice and scooped into bowls in Kashgar's old town. A few yuan a bowl.
Pomegranates pressed by hand on the spot at street carts all over southern Xinjiang. Kashgar's pomegranates are famously sweet.
Kazakh and Uyghur milk tea brewed from brick tea with milk and salt — drunk with naan at breakfast and nearly every meal.
Eggs (sometimes pigeon or goose) slow-roasted in hot sand or embers until the white turns brown and nutty, sold at Kashgar's bazaars.
Lamb kidney skewers grilled with cumin and chili — a favorite offal item at Xinjiang barbecue stalls alongside 羊肉串 and 烤羊肝.
Gyuma: intestine filled with blood and barley flour, boiled and sliced, often served alongside 面肠 (flour sausage) and 肉肠 at market stalls.
Crunchy twisted or shaped fried pastries (Tibetan: khapse), also called 炸果子, made in large batches for Losar (Tibetan New Year). Sold at Barkhor-area shops.
Droma desi: buttery rice mixed with tiny sweet silverweed roots, raisins and sugar — an auspicious Losar dish found in Tibetan restaurants.
Chicken simmered with wild mushrooms in a hand-carved soapstone pot from Medog — a Nyingchi specialty that's hugely popular in Lhasa. Drink the broth first, then add vegetables.
Small free-range highland pigs prized for lean, flavorful meat, often roasted whole or grilled in Nyingchi and Lhasa restaurants.
Rock-hard cubes of dried yak cheese (Tibetan: chura/chhurpi), sucked slowly like candy for hours. Also crumbled into dumplings and tsampa; sold on strings at markets.
Round pan-cooked or fried flatbread (Tibetan: balep), eaten with butter tea or sweet tea for breakfast. Cheap at Lhasa teahouses.
Half-moon bread pockets stuffed with seasoned yak meat and cabbage, pan-fried until golden. A filling street snack around the Barkhor.
Thenthuk: flat noodle pieces pulled and torn into yak broth with vegetables — the Tibetan everyday noodle soup, distinct from round-noodle thukpa.
Hot pot built around sliced fresh yak meat in a rich bone broth — a favorite way to warm up on chilly Lhasa evenings.
Boiled lamb or mutton ribs served in a heap and eaten by hand with a fiery chili-tomato dip (sepen). Typical of Tibetan restaurants and nomad homes.
Glass noodles braised with minced pork and chili bean paste; the bits of meat clinging to the noodles look like ants on twigs. A cheap home-style staple on almost every Sichuan restaurant menu.

Cold poached chicken shredded (traditionally beaten with a stick, hence the name) and doused in a nutty, numbing chili-sesame sauce. Originated in Leshan's Hanyang Ba and sold by weight at deli counters.
Chunks of duck braised with springy konjac in a red chili-bean sauce, a classic Chengdu home-style dish. A similar version with pork ribs (魔芋烧排骨) is also common.
Silky fried eggplant tossed in the sweet-sour-spicy yuxiang sauce. Often vegetarian but ask, as some kitchens add minced pork.
Green beans fried until blistered and wrinkled, then tossed with preserved mustard greens and chilies. Usually includes a little minced pork; say 不要肉 (bú yào ròu) for a vegetarian version.
A banquet classic: duck marinated, smoked over tea leaves and camphor twigs, steamed, then deep-fried for crisp skin. Non-spicy and sold by the half or whole at Chengdu restaurants and deli counters.
Chilled noodles topped with shredded chicken and a sweet-sour-spicy sauce, a summer street snack in Chengdu. Plain 凉面 (liángmiàn) without chicken is cheaper and sold everywhere.
Paper-thin slices of poached pork belly draped over cucumber and drenched in garlicky sweet chili sauce. A classic Sichuan cold starter.
Cold poached chicken bathed in a pool of fragrant red chili oil, numbing pepper and peanuts; the name literally means "saliva chicken". A standard starter at Sichuan restaurants.
Beef sliced so thin light shines through it, then dried and fried into a crisp, spicy-sweet jerky. Originally from Dazhou, now sold vacuum-packed as a souvenir snack in Chengdu.
A whole pork knuckle simmered until meltingly tender, served in its broth with a spicy dipping sauce. Associated with poet Su Dongpo's hometown Meishan, near Chengdu; good for sharing.
Beef coated in spiced ground rice and steamed in small bamboo baskets until tender. A Chengdu snack often stuffed into a guokui flatbread.

dishes.en: Steamed Pork Belly with Preserved Greens
dishes.desc: Slices of fatty pork belly steamed over preserved mustard greens, then flipped onto the plate. A rich, non-spicy banquet and home-cooking staple across Sichuan and Chongqing.

dishes.en: Sweet Steamed Pork with Sticky Rice
dishes.desc: Pork belly slices sandwiched with red bean paste and steamed over sweet sticky rice. A celebratory dish served at rural banquets and family feasts.

Cabbage hearts served in a broth so clear it looks like plain water but is a labor-intensive stock of chicken, ham and duck. A showpiece of non-spicy Sichuan banquet cooking found at upscale Chengdu restaurants; not actually vegetarian.
A whole fish braised in Pixian chili bean paste with a touch of sweet and sour. Often made with crucian carp (豆瓣鲫鱼).
Crosshatch-scored pork kidney flash-fried over a roaring flame with pickled chilies so it stays crisp-tender. A classic of Sichuan home-style restaurants.
Julienned potato quick-fried so it stays crunchy, with vinegar and chilies. A cheap vegetarian side ordered with nearly every meal.
A thick soup whose sourness comes from vinegar and heat from white pepper rather than chili. A comforting starter served across Sichuan.
Strips of paddy eel dry-fried until chewy and fragrant with chilies and celery. A Chengdu home-style favorite with beer.
Soft glutinous rice balls filled with black sesame or other sweet fillings, a century-old Chengdu brand. Served in hot water with a sesame dipping sauce.
Delicate steamed pork buns from a Chengdu brand dating to 1914. A good breakfast or snack in the city's old-style snack halls.
Thick, chewy hand-rolled noodles coated in a sweet soy and chili oil sauce. A cheap vegetarian Chengdu snack served in small bowls.
A flaky pan-baked flatbread layered with peppery minced pork, from Juntun near Chengdu. Street stalls also split plain guokui and stuff them with fillings like spicy beef or rabbit.

ingredients: fillings like sesame, cream or pork floss
dishes.desc: Small folded pancakes cooked in mini pans and filled with sweet or savory fillings. A classic Chengdu street snack; pick fillings from the stall's list.
Glutinous rice balls fried in caramelized brown sugar, rolled in sesame and sold on skewers. A beloved cheap Chengdu street snack, best eaten hot.
Cold starch jelly noodles with a sauce so fiery it supposedly makes you cry, hence the name. A Chengdu tourist-street favorite in places like Jinli.
Thick strips of pea-starch jelly in a savory-spicy sauce, originally from Nanchong. Sold cold at snack shops all over Chengdu.
Chewy sweet-potato starch noodles in a spicy, sour broth topped with braised intestine. A favorite Chengdu breakfast, often paired with a guokui flatbread.
A "hot pot for one": pick ingredients from a fridge, they are boiled in spicy broth and served in a bowl. Priced by weight; choose spice level 微辣 (mild) to 特辣 (extra).
Pig trotters slow-stewed with white beans into a milky, non-spicy soup, dipped in chili sauce. A Chengdu late-night comfort food.
Glutinous rice dumplings filled with sweet sesame or savory pork and steamed in leaves. A classic snack in Chengdu and Leshan.
Fried or steamed sticky rice cakes drizzled with brown sugar syrup and dusted with soybean powder. The go-to dessert to cool down after hot pot.
Huge thin sheets of hand-pulled dough, as wide as a "blanket", in a spicy broth. Often served with braised intestine (肥肠铺盖面) in Chengdu noodle shops.
Dry noodles tossed with so much oil they could supposedly catch fire, topped with preserved greens and peanuts. Originally from Yibin, now sold at noodle shops across Sichuan.
Crinkle-cut fried potatoes tossed with chili, numbing pepper and herbs. A cheap Chengdu street snack sold in paper cups.
A round fried pastry stuffed with peppery minced beef, crisp outside and juicy inside. Classic Chengdu street food, best eaten straight from the pan.
Tea served in a lidded bowl with a saucer, refilled by attendants with long-spouted kettles. The heart of Chengdu teahouse culture, e.g. in People's Park.
Chengdu's summer-night ritual of cold beer with spicy cold dishes and braised snacks at outdoor tables. Ask for 冷淡杯 at riverside and street-side stalls.
Exceptionally smooth tofu from Xiba town near Leshan, cooked in dozens of styles from stuffed to braised. Order a set tofu banquet at Leshan restaurants.
Fresh rabbit stir-fried with a mountain of fresh and pickled chilies, a fiery pillar of Zigong's salt-merchant cuisine (盐帮菜). Served sizzling in a wok.
Firm-yet-tender fresh tofu pudding from Fushun county, eaten with a fiery chili dip and rice. A cheap, filling Zigong meal.
Small pieces of chicken quick-fried with fresh chilies and pickled ginger, a defining Zigong dish. Fragrant, spicy and slightly sour.
Beef cubes fried in chili oil and eaten at room temperature, sibling to Zigong's cold-eaten rabbit. Sold in jars and bags as a souvenir snack.
Pork knuckle slow-braised until gelatinous with soybeans, from Niufo town near Zigong. A rich, non-spicy salt-gang classic.
Silky pork wontons served in a puddle of red chili oil. Found in every noodle shop; 清汤抄手 is the non-spicy broth version.
Potato chunks pan-fried until crusty and tossed with spices. A common Chongqing street snack.
Sesame-filled rice balls served over shaved ice with brown sugar syrup. A summer dessert often eaten to soothe the mouth after hot pot.
Little rice-paste drops shaped like shrimp, floated in iced brown sugar water. A refreshing summer street dessert with no actual shrimp.
A "dry hot pot": choose ingredients and they are stir-fried together in a fiery mala sauce. Priced by weight; specify spice level.
A wobbly white chilled rice cake drizzled with brown sugar syrup. A summer dessert that cools the mouth after spicy food.
Crisp-fried pork slices in a sweet-sour sauce, a non-spicy classic of Chongqing cooking. A good choice for spice-averse travelers.
Ruffled beef tripe, the must-order item in Chongqing hot pot. Swish it in the boiling broth for about 15 seconds (七上八下, dip up and down) and eat.
Long, crunchy duck intestines, another classic hot pot order. Cook only a few seconds until they curl.
A hot pot split into spicy and mild halves, the safe choice for spice beginners. Ask for 鸳鸯锅 when ordering; some purist Chongqing shops only serve spicy.
Cubes of silky lamb-blood tofu and glass noodles in a hot, sour-spicy broth, often with torn flatbread. A cheap (¥10-15) Muslim Quarter breakfast and snack.
Little cat-ear pasta shells rolled with the thumb, simmered or stir-fried with meat and diced vegetables. A homey Guanzhong staple; order 烩麻食 (soupy) or 炒麻食 (stir-fried), about ¥15.

A huge, dense, slow-baked wheat round like a helmet, sold in wedges; Shaanxi's 'eight oddities' joke that 'the bread is like a pot lid'. Keeps for days; shops in Qianxian and Xi'an sell it by the jin.
A tall steamed coil of paper-thin oily dough strands that unwinds like golden thread, a Tang-era Xi'an pastry. Usually eaten with Peking-duck-style sauce and scallion at old restaurants.

dishes.en: Xi'an Spiced Cured Beef and Lamb
dishes.desc: Hui-style beef and lamb cured then simmered in spiced stock until rosy and firm; sliced cold or stuffed into a mo as 腊牛肉夹馍. Buy by weight at Muslim Quarter counters.
Paomo bread cooked in a wok with meat, noodles and vegetables until the broth is almost absorbed, saucier and drier than the soup version. Ask for it at any paomo house.
Glutinous rice cooked and pressed into a block, sliced with a thin wire and drizzled with honey and osmanthus syrup, served chilled. A summer Muslim Quarter dessert, about ¥5-8.

dishes.en: Savory Flour Tea with Fried Dough Twists
dishes.desc: A thick, savory porridge of toasted flour and fat poured over broken fried twists, a Hui breakfast in Xi'an. Not to be confused with Guilin's tea-based youcha.
Xi'an's own retro orange soda since 1948, in a glass bottle, and the classic order alongside roujiamo and liangpi. Ask for 'yì píng Bīngfēng'.

A whole chicken boiled, steamed, then deep-fried until golden and so tender it falls apart, named for its gourd-like shape; a Tang-dynasty 'number one dish of Chang'an'. Order at old Xi'an restaurants.
A whole pork knuckle with its bone 'handle', boiled, fried and steamed until meltingly soft, served with scallion and sweet sauce. A Dali County banquet classic now on Shaanxi restaurant menus.
Coarsely grated potato tossed in flour, steamed, then stir-fried with garlic and chili, a Northern Shaanxi farmhouse dish. A cheap side at Shaanbei-style restaurants in Xi'an.
Silky steamed rice-flour sheets cut into ribbons and served warm with chili oil, garlic and vinegar, the southern Shaanxi cousin of cold liangpi. Ask for 'rè mǐpí' to get it warm; about ¥8.
Gansu-Ningxia's version of liangpi: chewy wheat-starch sheets cut into strips with spongy gluten, dressed with chili, vinegar and garlic. Lanzhou's 'gāodàn' (shoulder-pole) style is famous; ¥6-10.
Short noodles rolled between the palms into little fish shapes, then stir-fried or served in soup. A Hexi Corridor specialty found in Lanzhou noodle shops.
Fine golden pulled noodles topped with braised sauce, served with a plate of sliced spiced donkey meat. Gansu's Dunhuang signature, also served in Lanzhou.
Lamb fried then braised with chilies and potato until golden and tender; Jingyuan County's version is a protected Gansu product. Shared from a big plate; order with noodles (面) to soak up the sauce.

Gansu-style malatang that went viral in 2024: ingredients are boiled then topped with fragrant Gansu chili and hot oil, eaten with chewy potato starch noodles. Pick items from the fridge; priced by weight.
Short, hand-rolled noodles stir-fried or soupy with lamb, tomato and chilies, one of Yinchuan's signature everyday noodles. Ask for 'yángròu cuōmiàn' at Hui noodle shops; ¥15-25.
Yinchuan's own hot pot with a thick, spicy-savory 'paste' broth, a night-out favorite since the 2000s. Order lamb and veggies to dip; ¥60-100 per person.
Thin griddle pancakes shredded and stir-fried with lamb and vegetables until slightly crispy, a Yinchuan specialty. Hearty and cheap at local Hui eateries.
Rolled and steamed oat-flour noodle twists dressed cold with garlic, chili and vinegar, a southern Ningxia farm dish. Nutty and healthy-tasting; a common side in Yinchuan.
Tender braised lamb piled on torn nan that soaks up the gravy, called 'tawa kawap' in Uyghur. A big sharing platter for groups; ¥80-150.

dishes.en: Xinjiang Starch Jelly and Lamb Soup
dishes.desc: A Hui-Xinjiang breakfast soup of lamb and tomato with cubes of slippery starch jelly, traditionally paired with youtazi. Tangy and warming.
Xinjiang's ubiquitous fresh salad, named for its onion (皮牙子), chili and red tomato, served to cut through rich lamb dishes. Order it alongside skewers or pilaf.
Thick, tangy homemade yogurt sold in bowls with a spoonful of honey or sugar, sometimes with raisins. Ask for 'shǒugōng suānnǎi' (handmade); a great antidote to spicy food.
A dense brick of nuts and dried fruit bound with syrup, hacked off giant slabs by street vendors (hence the nickname 切糕 'cut cake'). Always agree on weight and price before they cut.
A dark, moist 'black cake' studded with walnuts and raisins, called 'bakkali' in Uyghur. A festive bakery item, often sold by the slice.
Smoked horse-meat sausage (Kazakh 'qazy'), sliced and served cold or steamed, a winter delicacy of Xinjiang's Kazakhs. Found in Urumqi markets and Kazakh restaurants.
Boiled horse meat or lamb sliced over flat noodles with onion and a cup of broth, the Kazakh 'naryn' or beshbarmak. Served at Kazakh restaurants in Urumqi.
Xinjiang's famous big-bottled lager, nicknamed 'big red Wusu' and notorious for its strength. The default drink with barbecue skewers.
Lamb kebab meat taken off the skewers and stir-fried with peppers and onion, an Urumqi bar staple often paired with noodles (炒烤肉拌面). Smoky and spicy.
A puffy, round tandoor-baked bun filled with fatty lamb and onion, Uyghur 'pamirdin', larger and softer than samsa. Look for it at Kashgar bakeries in the morning.
Finely chopped raw yak meat mixed with chili and spices, eaten with tsampa or momos. A traditional dish at Tibetan restaurants; only order where it's fresh.
Flat noodle pieces pulled straight into a yak broth with vegetables, Tibetan 'thenthuk'. A heartier alternative to thukpa on chilly Lhasa evenings.
Crunchy deep-fried pastries twisted into knots and ears, made in huge batches for Losar (Tibetan New Year). Sold in Lhasa markets around the festival.
A noodle-dumpling soup eaten two days before Losar, with dough balls hiding chili, salt or wool that 'tell your fortune'. Seasonal; look for it in late winter.
Rice cooked with butter, sugar, raisins and tiny 'ginseng fruit' roots (droma), Tibetan 'dresil', served at Losar and celebrations. Found on traditional Tibetan restaurant menus year-round.
A thick, flat skillet bread ('balep korkun') eaten for breakfast with butter tea or sweet tea. Often sold fresh from Lhasa bakeries and teahouses.
A lager brewed with Tibetan highland barley, billed as the world's highest brewery. Go easy at altitude.
Small, lean free-range pigs from Nyingchi roasted until the skin crackles, a southeastern Tibetan specialty. Order on Lhasa barbecue and Kongpo restaurant menus.
Chunky potatoes deep-fried then tossed with chili and spices, a ubiquitous Lhasa street snack. Sold by the cup near the Barkhor; ¥5-10.

Chopped chicken stir-fried with heaps of chili and aromatics, then served sizzling in a small pot over a burner. Hunan restaurants offer many 干锅 versions — try 干锅肥肠 (intestines) or 干锅牛蛙 (bullfrog) too.
Bite-sized pieces of young chicken fried crisp then tossed with dried chili and numbing peppercorn. A traditional Hunan dish with a drier, smokier heat than its Sichuan cousins.

Chopped duck fried with chilies, then finished with its own fresh blood, which coats every piece in a dark, savory glaze. Famous from Shaoyang and Wugang (武冈血鸭); found in Hunan home-style restaurants in Changsha.
A silky tofu dish named after Hunan governor Tan Yankai (谭延闿, styled Zu'an), whose private chef created it. A refined, non-spicy Hunan classic served at heritage restaurants like 玉楼东.
Finely chopped sun-dried pickled vegetables from western Hunan (湘西), stir-fried with chili and often egg. Salty, sour and savory — a cheap rice companion on almost every Hunan menu.
Chicken gizzards, hearts and livers stir-fried with pickled chili and sour radish — crunchy, sour and hot. A beloved Hunan home-style dish and a cheap order at local eateries.
Slices of firm, smoky Hunan dried tofu (famously from Youxian, 攸县香干) stir-fried with pork and chili. Hearty and cheap; ask for 攸县香干 for the classic version.
Translucent strips of pea-starch jelly served hot in a peppery broth or cold with chili and vinegar. An old Changsha snack sold at 火宫殿 and small stalls; slippery and refreshing.

A thick, nutty 'tea' made by grinding tea leaves with sesame, peanuts, beans and ginger, then adding hot water. A rustic Hunan tradition (especially Taojiang and Anhua) served in teahouses with small snacks.
Steamed sweet glutinous rice packed with lotus seeds, dates and candied fruit, glossy with lard and sugar. A traditional Changsha dessert served at 火宫殿 and at festivals.
Little chewy rice-flour pearls served in a savory broth with scallions and a dab of chili. An old Changsha snack traditionally sold from street carts and at 火宫殿.
Balls of mashed tofu, pork and pig's blood, smoked until dark and firm, then sliced and stir-fried with chili and garlic. A Shaoyang specialty seen on Hunan home-style menus in Changsha.
Small, slightly sour-sweet pancakes of fermented rice batter griddled in a round mold until golden on one side and fluffy on the other. A cheap Wuhan breakfast snack sold from street griddles.
Wide strips cut from a rice-and-mung-bean crepe, wok-fried with beef or eggs until crispy at the edges. A Wuhan specialty; ask for 牛肉炒豆丝 (with beef) or 汤豆丝 (in soup).
A uniquely Wuhan carb-on-carb breakfast: sticky-rice shaomai stuffed inside a freshly fried flatbread. Famous at long-running guozao stalls; very filling and cheap.
A thin, crunchy flatbread stuffed with meat and baked against the wall of a clay oven, originally from Gong'an in Hubei. Ubiquitous in Wuhan; try 牛肉锅盔 (beef) or 霉干菜锅盔 (preserved greens).
A smooth steamed loaf of pureed fish and pork fat with a golden egg-yolk top, sliced and often served in a hot pot. A Hubei banquet staple, essential at weddings and New Year (鱼糕丸子).

dishes.en: Hongshan Purple Choy Sum with Cured Pork
dishes.desc: Wuhan's famous purple-red choy sum (洪山菜薹), sweet after frost, stir-fried with smoky cured pork. A winter-spring seasonal must; ask for 清炒 for a vegetarian version.
Snow-white, extremely tender fish balls that float in light broth — a showcase of Hubei's freshwater fish cooking. Common at Hubei restaurants; also served alongside fish cake as 鱼糕丸子.
Slender young lotus shoots stir-fried or pickled with chili and vinegar — crisp, juicy and refreshing. A Hubei summer specialty from the lake country.
Cooled, oil-tossed noodles dressed with sesame paste, vinegar and chili — the summer stand-in for hot dry noodles. Sold at breakfast stalls and night markets when Wuhan's heat sets in.
Noodles in a fiery, beef-tallow-red broth topped with beef and offal, from Xiangyang in north Hubei. Locals call it 牛油面 and drink it at breakfast with a cup of sweet 黄酒.
Paper-thin slices of prized local clam blanched at the table in boiling clear chicken broth. One of Fuzhou's most famous banquet dishes; pricey but a true Min-cuisine classic.

dishes.en: Sea Snail Slices with Wine Lees
dishes.desc: Crisp-tender slices of sea whelk quickly stir-fried with white rice-wine lees. A refined Fuzhou classic that shows off Min cuisine's love of 糟 (wine lees).
Rice batter is splashed onto the hot rim of a wok, then scraped into a seafood broth as silky flakes. Fuzhou's quintessential breakfast (also called 鼎边糊), eaten with 海蛎饼 or 光饼.

Springy noodles tossed with peanut sauce or scallion oil and a dash of shrimp-flavored soy. Fuzhou locals pair it with a bowl of 扁肉 soup — the classic 拌面扁肉 combo, also sold at Shaxian snack shops (沙县小吃) everywhere.
Fujian's name for tiny wontons whose filling is pork pounded into a springy paste, served in clear broth. Order 拌面扁肉 at any Shaxian or Fuzhou snack shop for a cheap, quick meal.
Super-thin Putian (Xinghua) rice vermicelli stir-fried with seafood, pork and vegetables. A Fujian staple at Putian-cuisine restaurants, which are common in every Fujian city.
Thick noodles simmered in a rich, slightly thickened seafood broth loaded with clams, shrimp and pork. A hearty Putian specialty sold at Putian restaurants across Fujian.
Fuzhou is the birthplace of jasmine tea, where green tea is scented layer by layer with fresh jasmine blossoms. Order it in teahouses or buy some as a souvenir.
A plump steamed dumpling with a taro-and-starch skin wrapping pork, shrimp and mushrooms. A traditional Xiamen snack, served with sweet chili sauce.
Flaky little pastries filled with sweet mung bean paste, Xiamen's classic souvenir snack. Gulangyu island shops sell many flavors and let you taste before buying.
Soft glutinous rice balls rolled in ground peanut-sugar and sesame. Gulangyu's family-run 叶氏麻糍 is famous; join the queue for a fresh box.
Delicate vegetarian pastries made by Xiamen's Nanputuo Temple, filled with mung bean or date paste. Buy them at the temple shop after visiting.
Deep-fried glutinous rice balls coated in sesame with a sweet filling, shaped a bit like dates (枣). A southern Fujian festival and street snack.
Chicken feet braised in a sweet-savory spiced soy sauce until tender and glossy, from Honglai town in Quanzhou. A famous Quanzhou snack sold by weight.
A soft, fluffy rice-flour cake steamed in a small bowl until it splits open on top 'like a smile'. A Quanzhou breakfast and festival treat sold at morning stalls.
Chilled rice noodles tossed with sweet soy, vinegar, garlic water, chili and crunchy vegetables. A summer street snack sold from glass cases at markets for ¥6-10.
Rice noodles in clear bone broth topped with slices of tender pressed pork. A staple Kunming breakfast; you can usually add 帽子 màozi (extra toppings) for a few yuan more.
Silky ersi noodles in rich broth topped with fall-apart stewed pork leg, a specialty of Weishan county south of Dali. Look for 耙肉饵丝 signs in Dali old town and Xiaguan.
A steamed bun with a layered, lard-flaky dough, filled with ham and pork or sweet fillings. A Kunming breakfast classic (¥2-4 each).
A firm, tofu-like fresh goat cheese from the Sani/Yi people, sliced and pan-fried or steamed with ham. Order 炸乳饼 or 乳饼夹火腿 at Yunnan restaurants (¥20-35).
Fried rice with shredded ganba mushroom, a dark, intensely savory wild fungus that's one of Yunnan's priciest. A summer-to-autumn specialty at Kunming mushroom restaurants.
Thin slices of chilled boiled beef from Kunming's Hui Muslim kitchens, dipped in a chili sauce. A typical starter at halal (清真) restaurants.
Crunchy deep-fried bamboo larvae seasoned with salt and chili, a Yunnan delicacy often eaten with beer. Found at Dai and minority restaurants in Kunming.
Chicken stewed with sour Chinese quince, a tangy Bai dish from Dali. Served at Bai restaurants in Dali old town.
Fish braised with pork skin and chili, then left to set into a savory jelly, a Bai winter dish from around Erhai Lake. Served cold at Dali restaurants.
A light soup of the long, silky Ottelia water plant from Erhai and Lugu lakes with soft taro. A common side at Bai and Naxi restaurants; the stir-fried version is 炒水性杨花 in Lijiang.
Whole fish grilled over charcoal and stuffed with herbs and chili, a Naxi specialty sold along the canals of Lijiang. Often bought from riverside grill stalls in the old town.
Crispy fried whole fish smothered in zaola, Guizhou's tangy fermented chili. A popular restaurant main in Guiyang.
Fried rice with a mishmash of pickles, cured meat, fish mint and chili, hence 'weird'. A cheap Guiyang night-market staple (¥10-15).
Braised (卤) or grilled tofu from Qingyan ancient town outside Guiyang, served with a chili dip. Grab it at street stalls inside the town for a few yuan.
Rice noodles dressed with chili, vinegar and toppings, served hot (烫) or cold (凉) — the cheapest breakfast in Guiyang at about ¥5. Add 脆哨 for crispy pork bits.
Wide noodles in a bowl of hot douhua, dipped into a separate chili sauce bowl, from Zunyi. Popular breakfast or lunch in Guiyang.
Chilled yellow noodles tossed with tangy vinegar and chili, sold with siwawa and cold rice noodles at snack stands. Summer staple (¥6-10).
Little cubes of pork fried until crisp and caramelized, Guiyang's favorite topping for noodles and sticky rice. Also sold by weight at markets as a snack.
Sticky rice scooped and rolled around cuishao, pickles and fried dough, a grab-and-go Guiyang breakfast. Around ¥5-10 from morning stalls.
Small, spongy steamed rice cakes cooked in little bowls, lightly sweet. Sold at Guiyang snack streets for a couple of yuan.
Rice flour steamed in a bamboo cup over a blasting steam pot, then sprinkled with sugar and sesame. A disappearing Guiyang street snack found on old snack streets.
Small round egg pancakes wrapped around savory vegetables and chili sauce, not sweet like the name suggests. A Guiyang street-stall snack.
Whole chicken poached in a sweet master-soy braise until mahogany, a siu mei shop staple. Order a quarter (例牌) or over rice.
Whole roasted piglet with paper-thin crackling skin, served at banquets and sold by the slice in better siu mei shops. Look for it on a 燒味拼盤 (roast meat platter).
Thick, slippery round rice noodles in clear broth topped with chopped roast goose; a classic pairing at siu mei restaurants. Ask for 髀 (bei, leg) for the best cut.
Cantonese chicken scalded, air-dried and fried until the skin shatters like glass, served with spiced salt and prawn crackers. A dinner restaurant favorite, usually ordered by the half (半隻).
Springy bamboo-pressed egg noodles tossed dry and showered with savory dried shrimp roe, served at old-school noodle shops. Comes with a bowl of broth on the side.
Bouncy Chiu Chow-style fish balls and sliced fish cake in light broth over rice noodles (河粉 or 米粉). A cheap everyday lunch around HK$40.
Instant noodles with velvety beef in a peanutty satay broth, a beloved cha chaan teng breakfast. Often ordered as a set with a buttered bun and milk tea.
Macaroni in light chicken broth with strips of ham, a British-influenced cha chaan teng breakfast. Comes in a set with eggs, toast and a drink.
Simple wok-tossed egg noodles with soy sauce and bean sprouts; prized for its 'wok hei' and eaten for breakfast at congee shops. Cheap and fast, around HK$25-35.
Curry-spiced fried rice vermicelli with char siu and shrimp, invented in Hong Kong despite the name. A cha chaan teng and diner staple.
Yunnan-style rice noodles customized by spice level and toppings, made a Hong Kong obsession by chains like TamJai. Pick a soup, a spice level (小辣 mild to 大辣 hot) and toppings.
Wings braised in a sweet soy sauce - the 'Swiss' supposedly a misheard 'sweet'. A Hong Kong-style western (豉油西餐) classic, served with rice or spaghetti.
A tomato-red, Russian-derived soup that's the default starter in cha chaan teng and HK-style western set meals. Order a set and choose 紅湯 (red soup) instead of 白湯 (cream soup).
Tender braised brisket in mild, coconut-tinged HK curry over rice. A lunchtime comfort dish in cha chaan teng and noodle shops.
