dishes.pron: hahm yoo guy lup chow fahn
dishes.desc: Fried rice punched up with pungent salted fish and diced chicken; a dai pai dong and cha chaan teng favorite.
A soft omelette and ham sandwich on crustless white bread, ordered toasted (烘底) or not. Classic cha chaan teng quick breakfast with milk tea.
Thick toast spread with condensed milk and peanut butter (or butter), shorthand from 奶 (milk) + 醬 (sauce) + 多士 (toast). Cheap tea-time snack with milk tea.
Soft bun filled with sweet buttery coconut, topped with two stripes and sesame seeds. Invented in 1950s Hong Kong bakeries; costs a few dollars.
A crusty 'piggy bun' (豬仔包) toasted and drizzled with butter and condensed milk. Sweet cha chaan teng tea-time snack.
Soft bun with a crisp, buttery, cookie-like crust, a cousin of the pineapple bun. A Hong Kong bakery classic despite the name.
A sausage baked inside a soft sweet bun, sold at every Hong Kong bakery. Popular grab-and-go breakfast.
Individual flaky pastry pie with creamy chicken filling, a British legacy sold in Hong Kong bakeries and cafes.
Small tart with a chewy, golden shredded-coconut filling; the egg tart's sidekick in bakery cases.
Flaky pastry filled with sweet winter melon paste, a traditional Cantonese bakery item and classic Hong Kong souvenir.
Eggplant, green peppers and tofu stuffed with fish paste and pan-fried, sold on street skewers. Pick your pieces and ask for soy sauce and chili.
Mixed beef offal and radish simmered in a spiced broth and snipped into cups or onto skewers. Add mustard and chili; a Mong Kok street staple.
Crispy deep-fried pork intestine skewers from the street snack stalls, glazed with sweet sauce and mustard.
Whole squid grilled or fried on a stick and brushed with sweet sauce, sold at street snack shops and night markets.
Thin waffle folded in half with butter, peanut butter, condensed milk and sugar. Sold alongside egg waffles at street stalls.
Silky threads of pulled sugar wrapped around crushed peanuts and coconut, made by hand at street stalls. Eat it fast - it melts in humidity.
Hard malt candy chiseled off a big slab with a hammer and chisel - named after the 'ding ding' sound. Rare today but still found at nostalgic stalls.
Chestnuts roasted in woks of hot black sand, sold in paper bags from street carts in winter. Often sold with roasted sweet potatoes and quail eggs.
River snails wok-fried in black bean and chili sauce, sucked from the shell at dai pai dongs and night food stalls. Great with beer.
Clams wok-tossed with fermented black beans and peppers, a dai pai dong signature. Order with beer and a plate of rice.
Giant mantis shrimp deep-fried and tossed with garlic, chili and spiced salt. Pick one from the tank at seafood restaurants in Sai Kung or Lei Yue Mun; priced by weight.
Crab stir-fried with heaps of ginger and scallions, a seafood restaurant and dai pai dong classic. Ask for 伊麵 (e-fu noodles) underneath to soak up the sauce.
Cantonese-style hot pot with clear or satay broths and hand-made balls, beef and seafood, eaten in winter and late at night. Mix your own dipping sauce with soy, chili, garlic and raw egg.
A layered communal feast in a big basin, from the New Territories walled villages; eaten at Lunar New Year. Pre-order from restaurants or village caterers.
Sweet, thick red bean soup scented with aged tangerine peel, served hot or cold. Often the free dessert at the end of a Cantonese meal.
Mung bean sweet soup, often with kelp; considered cooling in summer. Tong sui shop staple.
A rich mixed-bean and taro sweet soup with coconut milk, served hot or cold at dessert shops.
A thin yellow crepe wrapped around whipped cream and fresh mango. Found at dessert shops like Honeymoon Dessert and in dim sum restaurants.
Bitter black herbal jelly believed to cool the body and clear the skin; served with honey or syrup. Sold at herbal tea shops and Hoi Tin Tong.
Sweet red beans with evaporated milk and syrup over ice, served in a tall glass at bing sutt (冰室) cafes. A retro summer favorite.
Salt-preserved lemon mashed into 7-Up, a cha chaan teng remedy for sore throats and a refreshing drink.
Coke with fresh lemon slices, a cha chaan teng staple; order 熱檸樂 (hot lemon Coke with ginger) as a cold remedy.
Bitter Cantonese herbal infusions sold by the cup from street-front herbal tea shops; try 廿四味 (24-flavor) if brave or 五花茶 (five-flower tea) for something gentler.
Freshly pressed sugarcane juice from juice stalls and herbal tea shops; sweet and grassy, served cold.
A light, cooling herbal brew of sugarcane and cogon grass root, sold chilled at herbal tea shops and in bottles at supermarkets.
A fast, high-heat stir-fry of thin lamb slices and big lengths of scallion, a staple of Beijing's Muslim restaurants. Order it with sesame flatbread (shaobing) to scoop up the juices.

Marinated lamb or beef cooked on a big round iron griddle over wood fire, a Beijing Muslim tradition (famous at Kaorou Ji by Houhai). Diners traditionally stand with one foot on the bench and grill it themselves.
Cold napa cabbage rounds marinated in hot mustard, sugar and vinegar, a sinus-clearing old Beijing cold dish. Classic at Lunar New Year and in old-Beijing (laobeijing) restaurants.
Smooth, pale-yellow squares of sweetened pea purée set into a cake, once a Qing palace snack. Sold chilled at old-style snack shops like Huguosi and in Beijing dessert sets.

dishes.en: Glutinous Rice Balls with Sweet Filling
dishes.desc: Soft white mounds of steamed glutinous rice stuffed with sweet sesame, nut or bean filling, a Hui (Muslim) Beijing snack. Look for them at Huguosi snack bar and Niujie halal shops.
A brittle, golden fried dough ring traditionally eaten with douzhi (fermented mung bean drink) or tucked into a sesame flatbread. A cheap old-Beijing breakfast item.

dishes.en: Fried Starch Slices with Garlic Sauce
dishes.desc: Despite the name ('sausage'), these are slices of starch loaf pan-fried until crisp-edged and dipped in garlic brine. A classic hutong and temple-fair snack.
A round, flaky baked pastry layered with brown sugar and sesame paste, a Tongzhou (Dashunzhai) specialty dating back centuries. Eaten for breakfast with soy milk or douzhi.
Long, open-ended pan-fried dumplings shaped like an old purse (dalian), crisp on the bottom. Often paired with a bowl of beef-blood soup.
Round, layered flatbreads swirled with sesame paste and coated in sesame seeds. The standard side for copper-pot lamb hot pot, tripe and braised dishes across Beijing.
A grey, mashed byproduct of making douzhi, fried in lamb fat and topped with chili oil - an acquired old-Beijing taste. Order in laobeijing restaurants as a side.
Small pinched dough nuggets boiled then stir-fried with meat and vegetables. A hearty Hui Muslim Beijing dish, famous at Huguosi area restaurants.
A chilled, silky almond-milk jelly cut into cubes and served in sweet osmanthus syrup - no tofu involved. A classic Beijing summer dessert.
A smooth, set milk custard curdled with rice wine, from the Qing palace kitchens. Served cold in small bowls at shops like Nailao Wei.
Sweet, thick yogurt sold in a squat white ceramic jar, drunk through a straw on the spot (you return the jar). Found at hutong corner shops for a few RMB.
A nostalgic Beijing orange soda with a polar bear on the bottle, the classic partner to roast duck or lu zhu. Ask for it ice-cold (bing de).
Paper-thin slices of boiled lamb's head meat sprinkled with spiced salt, eaten cold. A Hui Muslim specialty of old Beijing snack streets.
Ear-shaped fried dough soaked in syrup, glossy and chewy. A Beijing halal pastry also called mimahua.
A Manchu-origin sweet of fried dough strands bound with syrup into fluffy blocks. Sold in Beijing pastry shops like Daoxiangcun.
A gift box of eight traditional Manchu-style baked pastries with different fillings. Buy at Daoxiangcun as a souvenir.
Paper-thin white wafers sandwiching honeyed nut filling, a classic Beijing souvenir snack. Found in every souvenir shop near Wangfujing and Qianmen.
Candied preserved fruits - apricots, pears, dates - sold by weight as a Beijing souvenir.
Soft rolls of white kidney bean paste swirled with sweet red bean, an old palace snack. Usually bought alongside wandouhuang and lüdagun.
A thick millet porridge drizzled with sesame paste and spiced salt; locals sip it from the rim without a spoon. A traditional winter breakfast.
A puffy round of fried dough with a brown-sugar layer on top, the Beijing breakfast companion to soy milk or douzhi. Plain version: youbing.
Hand-cut noodles under a thick, savory gravy of pork, egg, wood ear and lily buds. Beijing's other signature noodle after zhajiangmian, often served at birthdays.
Stir-fried pork with scrambled egg (whose yellow flecks resemble osmanthus, muxi) and wood ear. A northern home-style staple, eaten with rice or pancakes.
Small pork meatballs deep-fried until crunchy, dipped in Sichuan pepper salt. A classic old-Beijing restaurant starter and beer snack.
Thin pancakes of shredded zucchini and egg batter, dipped in garlic vinegar. An old-Beijing summer home dish found in laobeijing restaurants.
Tiny cone-shaped steamed buns of fine cornmeal and chestnut flour, refined from a peasant staple into a Qing palace treat. Sold at Fangshan and old-style snack shops.
Silky soft tofu ladled into a bowl and topped with a savory gravy (dalu) of mushrooms and egg. The northern breakfast version is always salty, never sweet.
Small round rice-flour cakes steamed in wooden molds and topped with colorful jams. A nostalgic Tianjin street snack (also called zengr gao).
Flour scalded with boiling water from a huge dragon-spout copper kettle into a sweet, thick paste. The theatrical pouring is the show at Tianjin and Beijing snack streets.

dishes.en: Tianjin Crispy Carp in Sweet & Sour
dishes.desc: A whole carp deep-fried to crunchy and doused with sizzling sweet-and-sour sauce, Tianjin's signature banquet fish. Found at old Tianjin restaurants like Defengyuan.
Pork, liver and kidney flash-fried together in a glossy brown sauce. A classic Tianjin home-style restaurant dish, best with rice.
Firmer than douhua, these chunks of tofu are drowned in sesame paste, chive-flower sauce and chili oil. A daily Tianjin breakfast with jianbing or youtiao.
Tofu skin rolled around a vegetarian filling and deep-fried crisp; often stuffed inside a jianbing guozi in Tianjin. Ask for 'juanquan' in your jianbing.
Famous meatless steamed buns from a century-old Tianjin shop with a stone doorstep. Packed with tofu, vegetables and sesame oil.
Tripe and chicken gizzard flash-fried in seconds to stay crunchy, a test of a Lu chef's wok skill. A Jinan banquet classic.
Battered pork strips in a tangy sweet-and-sour glaze, a Shandong-origin dish now loved across north China. A safe crowd-pleaser on any Lu menu.
Scored pork kidney 'flowers' flash-fried with vinegar and garlic, a Lu cuisine classic. Popular in Jinan restaurants.
Tofu slices coated in egg, pan-fried and then simmered in stock until it absorbs the broth - the 'guota' technique unique to Shandong.
Tender cattail shoots from Jinan's Daming Lake in a rich, milky-white stock. One of Jinan's signature soups.
A dry, paper-thin Shandong crepe (Tai'an/Linyi style) rolled around a whole raw scallion and bean sauce - the ultimate Shandong peasant food. Sold folded in stacks at markets.
Juicy pork buns from Jinan's century-old Caobao shop. Thin-skinned and full of savory broth.
Four large braised pork meatballs symbolizing happiness, wealth, longevity and good fortune. A Shandong banquet dish especially popular at weddings and New Year.
Chicken braised in a clay pot with mushrooms and peppers, served with rice. Born in Jinan, it is now one of China's most common fast-food chains (~20 RMB).
Pork belly slow-braised in a ceramic crock until meltingly tender. A century-old Jinan specialty from Fengjilou restaurant.
Layers of meats, fish, kelp and tofu slow-stewed in vinegar and sugar until bones soften, eaten cold. Every Zibo household makes it for Spring Festival.
Fried tofu blocks hollowed out like little boxes and stuffed with minced meat, then braised. A Zibo Boshan specialty.
Ultra-thin, crunchy sesame crackers baked on the inner wall of a clay oven, a Zibo souvenir with 100+ years of history. Sold in sweet and salty versions.
Whole squid or squid skewers grilled on iron plates and brushed with chili and cumin. Everywhere on Qingdao's beer streets and Taidong night market.
Soy-braised spare ribs ladled over rice with the sauce - Qingdao's everyday fast food. Every neighborhood has a paigu mifan shop.
Soy-braised pig's trotters from Liuting near the airport, a Qingdao favorite with cold beer.
A translucent jelly made from boiled seaweed, cut into strips and dressed with garlic and vinegar. A refreshing Qingdao summer cold dish.
Scallops on the half-shell steamed with garlic and glass noodles. A must-order at Qingdao seafood stalls where you pick live shellfish by weight.
Huge, dense, slightly sweet steamed buns from a Laoshan village, often shaped into flowers or fish for festivals. Sold at Qingdao markets.
Thin hand-pulled noodles in a light, savory fish broth, Yantai's signature breakfast noodle.
Hand-pulled noodles from Fushan near Yantai, regarded as the birthplace of Shandong lamian. Served with seafood topping or braised gravy.
Ornate decorated steamed buns (huabo) shaped like flowers, fish or animals, made for weddings and New Year across eastern Shandong.
Noodles steamed then stir-fried with green beans and pork so they absorb the flavor - a Henan everyday lunch (also called lumian). Ask for garlic sauce on the side.
Noodles cooked in a thick, porridge-like broth with vegetables and beans; the name means 'muddled'. A homey Henan comfort food.
Noodles simmered in tangy fermented mung-bean liquid with celery and sesame oil - a sour, earthy Luoyang classic.
The head dish of the Luoyang water banquet: finely shredded radish made to mimic bird's nest, topped with an egg 'peony'.
A thin mung-bean crepe that is never flipped, torn into a sour-peppery soup with seaweed and shrimp. A cheap Luoyang street classic.
A rich beef bone soup with sliced beef, eaten for breakfast with torn flatbread (bing). Free broth refills are customary.
A deboned duck stuffed with a chicken, which holds a pigeon, which holds a quail - all intact - in a clear soup. Kaifeng's showpiece dish; order ahead.
Peanuts and sugar pounded into flaky, crumbly layered bars. A traditional Kaifeng souvenir sold at night markets and old shops.
Small fish battered and fried then braised in a soy-based sauce, a Kaifeng home-style dish found in night markets.
Mashed sweet potato stir-fried in lard and sugar until glossy, a famous Kaifeng night market dessert.
A thin flatbread stuffed with minced lamb and griddle-baked until crisp. A Hui Muslim snack at Kaifeng's Gulou and Xisi night markets.
Battered pork strips fried crisp with Sichuan pepper, eaten as a snack or added to hot pot and soups. Henan claims it as its own.
A savory, peppery millet porridge with peanuts and greens, the mellower breakfast alternative to hulatang. Order a half-and-half bowl with hulatang (called 'liangjiaxing').

A whole boned duck stuffed with sticky rice and 'eight treasures' like chestnuts, mushrooms and ham, then braised until falling apart. A celebratory Shanghai banquet dish (famous at old restaurants like Shanghai Lao Fandian); often needs to be pre-ordered.

Spongy wheat gluten braised sweet and savory with mushrooms, wood ear and peanuts, served cold. A vegetarian Shanghai appetizer found at almost every local restaurant and deli; good choice for non-meat eaters.

dishes.en: Braised Pork Intestine with Clover Sprouts
dishes.desc: Red-braised pork large intestine rings served on a bed of stir-fried caotou (bur clover greens) splashed with liquor. A classic benbang dish beloved by older Shanghainese; order it at traditional spots like Lao Zhengxing.
Silky tofu in a rich orange sauce of hand-picked hairy-crab meat and roe. Best in autumn (October–November, crab season); spoon it over rice.
Halved crabs coated in batter, fried, then braised in a thick sweet-soy gravy, often with edamame or rice cakes. A homestyle Shanghai summer dish; messy, finger-licking eating.
Chewy oval rice cakes stir-fried with halved crabs so they soak up the crab-rich sauce. A popular autumn order at Shanghai local restaurants; the rice cakes are often the best part.
Tiny, silky wontons with a dab of pork in a light broth with dried shrimp, seaweed and egg ribbons. A cheap Shanghai breakfast or late-night snack (around ¥8–15) often paired with shengjian bao.

Large wontons stuffed with pork and chopped greens (jicai/shepherd's purse is the classic), served in soup or tossed dry with sesame-peanut sauce. Everyday Shanghai noodle-shop fare; ask for 'tang' (soup) or 'ban' (mixed dry).
Shredded radish in batter fried in a special ladle-shaped mold into a crunchy puck, sometimes topped with a small shrimp. Old-school Shanghai street snack — eat it hot from the stall.
A rectangle of pressed rice deep-fried until it has a crunchy shell and soft inside. One of Shanghai's classic breakfast 'Four Heavenly Kings' alongside dabing, youtiao and soy milk.
A crisp, sesame-crusted baked flatbread in sweet (round) or savory scallion (long) versions. Part of Shanghai's breakfast 'Four Heavenly Kings'; locals wrap a youtiao inside.

ingredients: scallion and lard filling or sweet filling
dishes.desc: A small round flaky pastry covered in sesame, named because its golden color resembles a cooked crab shell. Filled with scallion-pork or sweet fillings; a classic Shanghai teatime/breakfast snack.
Boiled glutinous rice balls rolled in dry red-bean powder instead of served in soup. A Shanghai specialty snack (Qiao Jia Zha is the famous shop); comes in sweet sesame or savory pork fillings.

ingredients: red bean paste or salted egg yolk & pork floss
dishes.desc: Bright green glutinous rice balls dyed with mugwort, traditionally filled with red bean paste. Seasonal around Qingming (April); Shanghai bakeries now sell trendy fillings like salted egg yolk and pork floss.
A soft, chewy glutinous-rice log rolled around sweet red bean paste and dusted with osmanthus. A traditional Shanghai teacake sold at old-style pastry shops like Shen Dacheng.

Light broth with spongy fried tofu puffs and glass noodles — the classic cheap partner to shengjian bao or xiaolongbao. Usually ¥6–12 at Shanghai dumpling shops; a version with gluten and tofu-skin rolls is called shuangdang (双档).
A thin, mildly curried broth with beef slices, sometimes with glass noodles. Shanghai shengjian shops' signature soup pairing (Xiao Yang Shengjian, Da Hu Chun); order it alongside the buns.
Thin Shanghai noodles topped with diced pork and bamboo shoots in a sweet-spicy sauce, served in soup or dry. A favorite cheap noodle-shop order; mildly spicy by Sichuan standards.
Noodles in a milky fish broth topped with fried yellow croaker and tangy pickled mustard greens. A beloved Shanghai/Ningbo-style noodle; pricier than pork noodles but considered a treat.
Noodles steamed, cooled and tossed with peanut butter sauce, vinegar and soy, often topped with a side of stir-fried toppings. A summer-only Shanghai favorite, usually ordered with small wontons.
Thick, chewy noodles stir-fried with pork and greens in dark soy. Known abroad as 'Shanghai chow mein'; in Shanghai ask for 粗炒 (cūchǎo) or 上海炒面.

dishes.en: Stir-Fried Rice Cakes with Pork & Greens
dishes.desc: Chewy sliced rice cakes stir-fried with shredded pork and shepherd's purse or napa cabbage. An everyday Shanghai home-style dish; also found with cabbage (白菜炒年糕).
A Shanghai take on Russian borscht made red with tomato and ketchup rather than beets, brought by Russian émigrés in the 1920s. A 'haipai' Western-style classic at old cafés and home kitchens.
Small crucian carp slow-braised on a bed of scallions until bones soften, then served cold in sweet soy. A classic benbang cold appetizer.
Assorted items (chicken feet, edamame, pork belly, duck tongue) soaked in a chilled, fragrant rice-wine-lees brine. A Shanghai summer favorite sold by weight at deli counters; pick-and-mix.
Duck braised in sweet dark soy until lacquered and mahogany, served sliced at room temperature. Sold at Shanghai roast-meat deli windows by the half or quarter duck.
Steamed sweet sticky rice dome studded with dried fruits and filled with red bean paste. A must at Shanghai Chinese New Year dinners; supermarkets sell ready-to-steam ones.
Crisp caramelized palmier cookies — a haipai legacy of Shanghai's Western bakeries. The Peace Hotel's and International Hotel's (国际饭店) versions draw long queues; a classic edible souvenir.
A clear broth with silky cubes of chicken and duck blood and bits of offal. Old-Shanghai street soup traditionally eaten with vegetable rice (菜饭); cheap and warming.
Tiny peeled river shrimp velveted and quickly stir-fried until translucent and tender, served with a dish of vinegar. A refined Shanghai restaurant classic; the crystal-shrimp version is 水晶虾仁.
Napa cabbage cooked down with shredded pork into a soft, thick, almost porridge-like stew. A comforting Shanghai home-style dish, especially in winter.
A dense roll of pressed tofu skin, sliced and braised in sweet soy — the name means 'vegetarian chicken'. A common Shanghai cold appetizer and noodle topping.

dishes.en: Red Bean Soup with Mini Rice Balls
dishes.desc: A sweet red-bean soup with tiny chewy glutinous rice balls and osmanthus. One of Nanjing's classic Qinhuai snacks, sold around Fuzimiao.
Noodles in broth topped with puffy fried pork skin, liver, sausage slices and greens. A hearty, cheap Nanjing breakfast/lunch noodle.
A smooth, lightly sweet congee of rice, soy milk and yam, named after Soong Mei-ling (Madame Chiang). A Nanjing restaurant favorite, especially at Nanjing Da Pai Dang.
Soft tofu pudding topped with dried shrimp, pickles, seaweed and chili oil — the savory Nanjing version of douhua. A cheap breakfast snack around Fuzimiao.
Fried tofu puffs re-braised in spiced soy broth with bean sprouts, served in a bowl. A Qinhuai street snack in Nanjing.
A boiled fertilized duck egg with a partly developed embryo, eaten with spiced salt. A popular, adventurous Nanjing street snack sold from carts in the evening.
Roast duck chopped on the bone and doused in a sweet-savory jus, a different style from Peking duck. Bought by the half from neighborhood duck shops; locals eat it alongside salted duck.
A light, slightly bitter egg-drop soup with juhuanao, a wild chrysanthemum green Nanjingers adore. A summer staple in Nanjing restaurants.
Noodles cooked individually in a small pot with your choice of toppings (pork, liver, kidney, beef). A late-night Nanjing classic; you pick the toppings at the counter.
Little cylinders of fluffy rice flour steamed to order with sweet sesame or red-bean filling. A nostalgic Nanjing street-cart snack.
Flower-shaped batter cups baked in iron molds and filled with red-bean paste, topped with colorful sugar. A common tourist-street snack in Nanjing and Suzhou old towns.
Tender river shrimp stir-fried with Suzhou's famous Biluochun green tea leaves. Suzhou's answer to Hangzhou's Longjing shrimp; best in spring.

ingredients: pork, or sweet nuts and seeds
dishes.desc: Flaky, layered mooncakes with sweet (five-nut, red bean) or savory fresh-pork fillings. A Suzhou specialty eaten warm; bakeries queue up around Mid-Autumn.
Suzhou's summer noodle in a clear white broth scented with fermented rice-wine lees, topped with tender pork belly. Only served in summer months (roughly June–August).
Thin noodles in a dark soy broth topped with crisp-fried, sweet-glazed fish pieces. One of the classic Suzhou soup-noodle toppings (浇头) alongside braised pork.
Noodles tossed with tuhuangyou — pure hairy-crab roe and fat cooked in lard. A luxurious Suzhou specialty (¥80+), best in autumn crab season.
Squares of pork belly braised a deep cherry red with red yeast rice and sugar. A seasonal Suzhou deli item sold around Qingming (spring); Lu Gao Jian is famous.
Small cubes of pork belly scored and braised glossy red so they resemble cherries. A classic Suzhou restaurant dish (Song He Lou).
Fresh chewy fox nuts — 'chicken-head rice' — in a light sweet soup with osmanthus. A prized Suzhou late-summer delicacy (August–September).
A flower-shaped batter cake with red bean filling, baked in iron molds with a caramelized sugar top. Classic Suzhou old-street snack.
A whole pork hock braised for hours until meltingly tender in sweet soy — the signature of Zhouzhuang water town near Suzhou. Sold everywhere in Zhouzhuang, also vacuum-packed as souvenirs.

The three 'whites' of Lake Tai — silverfish, white shrimp and whitefish — usually steamed or stir-fried simply. Order them at lakeside restaurants in Suzhou or Wuxi; whitebait omelette is a common form.
A delicate clear soup with tender liver of the small 'ba' fish, an autumn specialty at Mudu town near Suzhou. Famously praised by Yu Youren; seasonal (autumn).

ingredients: rose or red bean or sesame filling
dishes.desc: A small, soft pan-fried cake leavened with fermented rice wine, filled with rose, red-bean or sesame paste. A Suzhou spring snack; eat hot.
Small squares of dried tofu braised sweet and dark, chewy and snackable. A classic Suzhou souvenir snack sold in little packs.
Sweet glutinous rice porridge swirled with red-bean paste and osmanthus. A Suzhou/Nanjing comfort sweet; the Nanjing version with lotus root is 糖粥藕.
A diamond-cut steamed cake of 64 thin, sweet layers with lard and candied fruit. A Yangzhou morning-tea classic, usually ordered with three-diced buns.
Open-topped dumplings filled with sweet minced green vegetables that glow jade-green through the wrapper. A signature of Yangzhou morning tea at Fuchun.
A large carp head carefully deboned and stewed in a milky broth with crab, ham and shrimp. One of Huaiyang cuisine's three famous 'heads'.
Silken tofu sliced into hair-thin threads that float like a cloud in clear broth — a showcase of Huaiyang knife skills. Found at upscale Yangzhou restaurants.
Thin shreds of firm tofu blanched and served cold-ish in a soy-sesame dressing with ginger and dried shrimp. The lighter breakfast cousin of the braised version, eaten at Yangzhou morning tea.
Goose brined and poached until tender with juicy, pale meat. Yangzhou's everyday deli meat — buy it by weight from 'old goose' shops.
Tiny translucent whitebait from Lake Tai scrambled with egg into a fluffy omelette. Commonly ordered at Wuxi and Suzhou lakeside restaurants.
Pan-fried glutinous rice cakes with crisp bottoms, filled with pork, sesame or red bean. A classic Wuxi street snack; eat hot.
Shredded eel fried twice until crunchy and coated in a sweet soy glaze, served cold. A Wuxi specialty cold dish.
Ultra-fine, silky white noodles in a clear broth. Changzhou's signature noodle, usually with a toppings choice.
A flaky, sesame-covered oval flatbread baked crisp, sweet or savory. Changzhou's classic breakfast snack.
Tender strips of paddy eel stir-fried in garlic-pepper sauce — so soft they 'hang like a pocket' on chopsticks. The signature dish of Huai'an and Huaiyang cuisine.
Diced silken tofu in a thick, savory starch-thickened broth with chicken stock and seafood. A famous Huai'an dish said to have been served to Emperor Qianlong.
Crayfish cooked in a complex 'thirteen-spice' (十三香) sauce, from Xuyi county where China's crayfish craze began. Summer (May–August) is peak; ordered by the jin (500 g).

ingredients: flatbreads stuck to the pot rim
dishes.desc: Chicken stewed spicy in a big iron pot with flatbread stuck to the rim to soak up the sauce. A rustic Xuzhou favorite for groups.

ingredients: scallions and lard or sweet filling
dishes.desc: A round, golden sesame flatbread with dozens of flaky layers, from Huangqiao town in Taizhou. Famous across Jiangsu; savory scallion-lard or sweet versions.
Velvety pork slices poached in a fiery, numbing chili broth over vegetables. The pork sibling of water-boiled beef and fish.
Dark, firm spiced beef from the ancient town of Langzhong, named after the Three Kingdoms general. Popular vacuum-packed gift snack.
Pick-and-choose items boiled in a numbing, spicy broth, served in a bowl. Sichuan's original street version; pay by weight or skewer count.
Rabbit slices 'dive' briefly into a spicy pickled-chili broth so the meat stays tender. A Zigong specialty.
Fatty pork belly coated in seasoned rice powder and steamed over sweet potato until tender. Homestyle comfort food.
Whole fish fried then braised in a reduced chili-bean sauce until it clings to the fish. A Sichuan classic main.
Beef shreds fried until chewy and dry, then tossed with celery and chili. Great with beer.
Pan-fried tofu slices braised with pork and chili bean paste. Everyday Sichuan family cooking.
A cousin of twice-cooked pork: raw pork slices fried in doubanjiang with garlic sprouts. Common on local menus.
Chicken feet steeped in sour, spicy pickled-chili brine. Crunchy snack found in convenience stores and deli stalls.
Rice in a thick pea soup, often topped with braised meat or intestines. A homey Chengdu lunch for under ¥20.
Noodles in spicy red broth with chunks of braised beef. Sichuan's take on the classic; noodle shops everywhere.
Slightly sour fermented rice noodles in spicy broth, Nanchong's breakfast staple. Add a fried egg or beef topping.
Silky round rice noodles in a red-oil broth with braised meat, Mianyang's signature breakfast. Choose 红汤 (red) or 清汤 (clear).
Extremely long, thin slices of boiled pork from Lizhuang ancient town, eaten with a garlic chili dip. A Yibin specialty.
Small skewers grilled over charcoal and dusted with chili and peppercorn powder. Leshan's night-market scene, especially around Zhanggongqiao.
Craftsmen draw dragons and animals in molten sugar on a marble slab; spin a wheel to choose your design. Fun at Jinli and Kuanzhai Xiangzi.
A rich sweet paste of rice, soybeans and sesame stir-fried in lard, a traditional Chengdu dessert.
Pork meatballs rolled in glutinous rice and steamed until the grains shine like pearls. Classic Chengdu snack.
Smoked pork sausage seasoned with chili and peppercorn, sliced and steamed or stir-fried. Hangs everywhere before Chinese New Year.
Smoke-cured pork belly, stir-fried with garlic sprouts (蒜苗炒腊肉) or steamed. Winter staple.
Big boiled chunks of pork tossed in salt, chili and peppercorns, a festive dish of the Yi people in Liangshan.
Bite-size meats on skewers grilled over a charcoal basin at your table. Xichang's signature night out.
Fish cooked in spicy broth in the kitchen and served pre-cooked in the pot, then add hot pot sides. Popular in Chengdu suburbs.
Bouncy hand-beaten fish balls, the seafood counterpart to Chaoshan beef balls, often from Dahao in Shantou. Eaten in soup or with kway teow.
Despite the name it is not rice: whole fish poached in brine and served cold, dipped in fermented bean sauce. A Teochew seafood staple displayed in rows at dalĕng (cold cuts) stalls.
A Teochew night-stall feast of cold braised meats, chilled fish and pickles eaten with plain white congee. Point at the trays you want; priced by weight or plate.
Cubes of rice cake fried with egg and salty preserved radish, choose 'white' or 'black' (sweet soy). The Teochew original of Singapore's carrot cake.
Peach-shaped pink rice-dough dumplings filled with savory sticky rice, made for festivals but sold daily in Chaozhou snack shops. Steamed, then often pan-fried.
Translucent dumplings stuffed with chives, steamed then pan-fried crisp. A cheap snack at every Chaoshan kueh stall, a few yuan each.
Small bowl-shaped steamed rice cakes topped with savory fried preserved radish. A classic Chaozhou breakfast, sold in sets of 4-6.

ingredients: mung bean paste or sticky rice
dishes.desc: Dark green-black herbal rice-dough cakes pressed in wooden molds, filled sweet or savory. Traditional Teochew offering cake found in markets.
Little 'coins dropped in soup': boiled glutinous rice dumplings rolled in sugary crushed peanuts and sesame. A Chaozhou street dessert, especially on Paifang Street.
Flaky round pastry filled with a sweet-savory mix featuring red fermented tofu. A famous Chaozhou souvenir snack.
Pyramid sticky-rice bundles half-sweet, half-savory, the most famous from Laomagong in Shantou. Sold year-round in Shantou old town.
Golden fried tofu cubes, crisp outside and soft inside, dipped in chive-salt water. Cheap snack all over Chaoshan.
Crisp fried rolls with a filling of mung bean paste, pork and shrimp. Common at restaurants and snack stalls.
Soy-braised pork knuckle over rice, a Chaoshan specialty sold in chain shops across China. A filling ¥15-25 meal.
Fried taro sticks tossed in boiled sugar until coated in a sandy white crust. A classic Teochew banquet dessert.
Silky green puree soup of sweet potato leaves, linked to a legend of the last Song emperor. A signature of Teochew restaurants.
Date-shaped fried shrimp fritters, crisp and springy, served with tangerine jam. Teochew restaurant appetizer.
Whole crab steamed then chilled so the roe sets firm, eaten with vinegar. Pricey but a Teochew seafood icon.
Pork and water chestnut wrapped in bean curd skin and fried crisp. Known abroad as ngoh hiang/lor bak.
Airy hollow sugar candy wrapped in a thin crepe with peanuts and sesame - a Chaozhou old-town street sweet.
Dumplings whose wrapper is made from pounded fish paste, cooked in soup. Common alongside fish balls in Shantou.
Dark, cooling herbal jelly scooped warm or cold with sugar. A summer street dessert in Chaoshan.
Wenchang-style rice noodles in a sour-savory beef broth with peanuts. Breakfast at noodle shops in Haikou.
Thin noodles in rich pork broth with offal, from Wanning. Popular early-morning bowl.
Sanya fishing-port noodles in seafood broth topped with fish cake and pork.
Sticky rice steamed inside a whole coconut, sliced into wedges. Sweet-fragrant side or snack.
Short green noodles made from skunkvine leaves in brown sugar ginger soup. A Hainan folk dessert, despite the odd name ('chicken-dung vine').
Coconut milk jelly set inside the shell and served cold. Popular tourist treat in Sanya.
Puffed fried glutinous rice balls with sesame coating and sweet coconut-peanut filling.
Small glutinous rice cakes filled with sweet coconut, steamed in leaves. Market snack.
Rice in a peppery pork broth with offal - a Haikou comfort breakfast.
Fruit and milk 'stir-fried' on a frozen plate into icy mush. A night-market cooler.
Lightly fermented rice noodles in broth with sour sauce, from Danzhou.
Big square-ish zongzi stuffed with fatty pork and salted egg, Dingan's are most famous.
Poached chicken over rice cooked in chicken fat and broth. In Hainan you'll see it as 文昌鸡饭.
Snail shells stuffed with meat and snail and braised in spicy sauce. Guilin specialty.
Vegetables like tofu, bitter melon and peppers stuffed with pork - order a mixed plate in Yangshuo.
Tiny bowls of noodles with horse meat - locals eat a stack of them. A classic Guilin snack.
Steamed rice sheets rolled around minced meat and doused in sauce. Morning staple in Nanning.
Tangy fermented noodles pressed fresh in Nanning, in broth or dry.
Translucent steamed dumplings filled with pork and veggies, Nanning breakfast.
Thinly sliced raw fish with herbs and condiments, Guangxi-style.
Bitter herbal jelly, sweetened with honey. Wuzhou is its home.
Chicken marinated and fried in paper wrapping to lock in juice.
A spicy, sour hot pot of duck feet stewed in luosifen broth. Liuzhou late-night favorite.
Fried salt cod and potato balls, a popular snack at stalls on Rua do Cunha.
Crab cooked in rich Macanese curry, best at Taipa restaurants.
Soupy seafood rice served in a pot.
Portuguese sausage often flame-grilled tableside.
Noodles made by bouncing on a bamboo pole. Found in Macau noodle shops.
Crispy rolled cookies sold at souvenir shops on Senado Square.
Portuguese clams cooked in white wine, best with bread.
Charcoal-grilled sardines Portuguese style.
Baked rice with duck and sausage.
Blocks of ice cream between wafers from old shops.
Glutinous rice dough coiled on a stick and rolled in peanuts.
Frilly white leaves of beef tripe steamed with ginger and scallion — a classic small-plate yum cha order. Chewy and clean-tasting; often paired with honeycomb tripe on the same table.
A whole Cantonese sweet sausage wrapped in fluffy steamed bun dough, like a Chinese pig-in-a-blanket. Found in dim sum carts and bakery steamers; good for kids and breakfast on the go.
A chilled, film-like sheet of black sesame paste rolled into a spiral — looks like a roll of film. A light, nutty dessert dim sum at old-style tea houses.
A wobbly, amber jelly cake made from red jujube dates, served chilled in diamonds at dim sum. Sweet and floral, it's a classic end to yum cha.
A thick, warm, smooth purée of ground walnuts and rice — a Cantonese tong sui (sweet soup) believed to be good for the brain. Order it at dessert shops alongside black sesame soup.
Creamy hot sweet soup of ground roasted peanuts, a staple of Cantonese dessert shops. Often sold half-and-half with black sesame soup.
Bread spread with minced shrimp paste and deep-fried until golden and crisp. A fried dim sum and Cantonese banquet snack; eat hot.
A large steamed dumpling with a frilled top, traditionally holding shark fin, now usually mung bean vermicelli 'fins' in broth. A classic old-school dim sum item.
Duck feet tied into a bundle with fish maw, taro and roast pork by a strip of bean curd skin, then steamed in savory sauce. A retro yum cha favorite getting harder to find.
A peach-shaped steamed bun filled with lotus seed paste, tipped with pink. Served at birthday banquets for elders — order one for a birthday at yum cha.

dishes.pron: seung tong loong hah yee meen
dishes.desc: Wok-fried lobster pieces served over springy e-fu noodles that soak up the superior stock. A banquet showpiece priced by weight; a cheese version (芝士龙虾伊面) is also popular.
A clear, lightly sweet soup of silky white snow fungus simmered with rock sugar. A nourishing tong sui served warm or chilled at dessert shops.

dishes.roman: sai1 joeng4 coi3 zyu1 gwat1 tong1
dishes.pron: sai yeung choy jyoo gwut tong
dishes.desc: A classic Cantonese slow-cooked home soup of watercress and pork bones, often with sweet and bitter apricot kernels. Comes free as the 'soup of the day' at many local restaurants.

dishes.roman: haam4 coi3 wu4 ziu1 zyu1 tou5 tong1
dishes.en: Pickled Mustard & Pepper Pig Stomach Soup
dishes.pron: hahm choy woo jiu jyoo toe tong
dishes.desc: A peppery, warming soup of pig stomach and salted mustard greens. Popular in winter; the white pepper heat is the point.

dishes.en: Steamed Pork Patty with Salted Egg
dishes.desc: A flat patty of minced pork steamed with a salted duck egg cracked on top — homestyle Cantonese comfort food. Common as a claypot rice topping or set-lunch dish.
Lobster chunks wok-tossed with heaps of ginger and scallion in a glossy sauce. A seafood-restaurant signature; pick your lobster from the tank and pay by weight.
Pork chop pieces deep-fried and tossed with fried garlic, chili and salt-and-pepper. A dai pai dong favorite with beer.
Shell-on shrimp flash-fried crisp and tossed with garlic, chili and pepper-salt — eat shell and all. A staple of Cantonese seafood restaurants.
Bite-size pork ribs deep-fried and wok-tossed with pepper-salt and fried garlic. Crunchy, savory and very popular late-night.
A thick, starchy banquet soup loaded with crab, scallop and other seafood, finished with egg white ribbons. Add red vinegar at the table.
Stir-fried seafood served inside an edible deep-fried taro or potato 'nest'. A showy banquet and wedding dish.
Abalone slow-braised in a rich oyster-sauce gravy until tender — a luxury Cantonese banquet dish. Often served whole with mushrooms or goose web; priced per piece.
A silky, warm or chilled milk custard set with egg white — a simpler cousin of double-skin milk. Common at Guangzhou and Shunde dessert shops; ginger and red bean versions exist.
An assorted platter of Cantonese roast meats — char siu, crispy pork, roast duck or goose. The easy way to sample everything; order two- or three-meat combos (双拼/三拼) over rice too.
Battered pork ribs fried and tossed in a tangy sweet-and-sour sauce with peppers and onions. A home-style cousin of sweet and sour pork.

Crisp lettuce cups filled with a wok-fried mince (often squab or pork) with diced water chestnut, eaten by hand with hoisin. Also eaten at Lunar New Year for good fortune (生菜 sounds like 'growing wealth').
Steamed or claypot rice topped with seasoned minced beef and a raw egg that cooks in the heat — stir it all together. Cheap, filling set-lunch staple.
Short, chubby noodles with pointed ends, also called rat noodles (老鼠粉). Usually stir-fried with bean sprouts and char siu; great for a cheap breakfast.
Frog legs marinated and steamed on a lotus leaf, which perfumes the tender meat. 'Tin gai' (field chicken) is a common Cantonese menu item and tastes like chicken.

dishes.en: Duck with Taro & Aged Tangerine Peel
dishes.desc: Duck braised with creamy taro and fragrant aged tangerine peel, a homestyle Cantonese and Hakka dish. Rich and aromatic; share with rice.
A slow-cooked Cantonese soup of dried dragon-fruit-cactus flowers with pork bones, prized as 'cooling'. Look for it as a restaurant or home 'old fire soup'.
The classic Cantonese wedding-banquet soup of gelatinous shark fin strands in thick stock. Increasingly replaced by imitation fin; street versions are 碗仔翅.
Whole cuttlefish simmered in spiced lou seoi master stock and served sliced. Part of a lou mei platter at Chiu Chow-style shops.
Duck braised in fragrant spiced master stock, sliced and served with vinegar-garlic dip. A lou mei counter staple, often over rice.
A Hakka steamed bun stuffed with soy-braised pork belly (kau yuk) and preserved mustard greens. A popular snack in Hakka towns.
Chewy taro-and-starch nuggets shaped like abacus beads, stir-fried with mushrooms, dried shrimp and pork. A signature Hakka dish symbolizing wealth.
Pounded glutinous rice pulled into chewy pieces and rolled in crushed peanuts, sesame and sugar. A festive Hakka snack.
A whole deboned duck stuffed with seasoned sticky rice, then steamed or roasted. A Hakka banquet dish best ordered ahead for a group.
Chewy glutinous rice dumplings, sweet (peanut/sesame) or savory (radish, dried shrimp), steamed on leaves. Eaten with tea as a Hakka snack.
Pig cheek and ear braised in Teochew lou master stock, sliced thin with garlic vinegar. A must on any Chaoshan braised-meat (卤味) counter.
A tangy, appetizing soup of duck simmered with Teochew salted mustard greens and sometimes sour plum. Classic home and restaurant soup in Chaoshan.
Chicken stir-fried with fragrant peppercorn, garlic and chili — a numbing-savory Teochew home dish despite the Sichuan name.
Shrimp baked or wok-cooked with Teochew preserved olive-and-mustard relish, giving a salty, deep flavor. A common Chaoshan seafood restaurant order.

Watery Teochew-style rice porridge eaten with a spread of salty side dishes (杂咸) like pickled mustard, olive vegetable, salted egg and braised goose. Breakfast and late-night staple — pick sides from the counter.
Thin Teochew rice porridge cooked with fresh baby oysters and minced pork, seasoned with fish sauce and celery. Also called 蚝粥 / 蚝糜; best at night stalls.
Blood cockles quickly blanched so they stay red and juicy, dipped in garlic-chili soy. A beloved (and adventurous) Chaoshan seafood snack.
A clear, peppery soup of mixed fresh pork offal and lean meat, cooked to order. A popular Chaoshan breakfast with rice or rice noodles.
Pork trotters and skin simmered then chilled into a savory aspic, served sliced with vinegar. A cold dish found at Teochew braised-meat counters.
Thin wheat crepes wrapped around shredded vegetables, egg and crushed peanut — a fresh spring-roll street snack in Chaoshan.
Springy noodles with minced pork, fish balls and a vinegar-chili dressing — the ancestor of Singapore's bak chor mee. Order dry or in soup.
Translucent sago-skinned balls with a sweet filling, chewy and glossy — a classic Chaoshan snack sold in markets and dessert shops.
Lightly poached cuttlefish slices served on ice and dipped in sharp mustard. A refreshing Teochew cold dish at seafood restaurants.
Whole pomfret steamed with salted mustard greens, sour plum and tomato in a light, tangy broth. The signature Teochew fish dish.
Pressed slabs of bouncy fish paste, sliced and pan-fried or added to noodle soups. A Chaoshan market staple sold alongside fish balls.

Tender slices of beef fillet stir-fried with onions in a sweet-tangy ketchup and Worcestershire sauce, a cha chaan teng and Cantonese restaurant staple. Usually served as a dish to share or over rice as a lunch set for about HK$60–90.

Deep-fried pork ribs coated in a sweet mix of mayonnaise and condensed milk — a quirky Hong Kong-style 'soy sauce Western' creation. Found at cha chaan teng and dai pai dong; order it with rice or as a shared plate.
Ice-cold Coke topped with a scoop of vanilla ice cream, a retro cha chaan teng float. Ask for it by name at old-style cafes and bing sutt; it's a nostalgic treat on a hot afternoon.
Sprite or 7-Up with a scoop of vanilla ice cream floating on top, the lighter sibling of the Black Cow. A cha chaan teng and bing sutt classic named after the fairy-tale princess.
Cream soda mixed with fresh milk, a 1970s cha chaan teng favourite immortalised in the film 'Cream Soda and Milk'. Still on the menu at some old-school cafes — ask for it iced.
A raw egg stirred into sweetened boiling water so it turns silky — a cheap protein drink popular in 1960s Hong Kong. Now a nostalgic rarity found only at a few traditional cha chaan teng.
Hong Kong-style milk tea made with sweetened condensed milk instead of evaporated milk and sugar, giving a smoother, sweeter cup. Order 'caa zau' at any cha chaan teng, hot or iced (dung caa zau).
Battered, deep-fried chicken slices drenched in a sweet, glossy lemon sauce — a Hong Kong-Western classic. A popular rice-plate lunch at cha chaan teng and Cantonese restaurants.
Crispy battered squid tentacles sold on skewers or in paper bags at Hong Kong street snack stalls. Look for them in Mong Kok and Sham Shui Po; usually HK$20–35, eaten with curry sauce or sweet sauce.
Whole sweet potatoes roasted in a drum oven by winter street hawkers, often sold alongside roasted chestnuts. Sold by weight in paper bags — a warming snack on cold evenings.
Sticky golden maltose candy twirled onto a chopstick and sandwiched between two crisp soda crackers — a nostalgic Hong Kong street sweet. Found at traditional snack stalls for a few dollars each.
Firm, tart-sweet ruby-red slabs of set hawthorn paste, also called shanzha gao. Sold by weight at old-style pastry shops like Daoxiangcun; often sliced into cold dishes or eaten as a palate cleanser.
A classic Old Beijing street sweet: steamed glutinous rice rolled around sweet bean paste and sliced into rounds. Look for it at snack streets and Huguosi-style snack halls alongside lüdagun.
A soft, fluffy steamed sponge cake said to have come from Lama Temple traditions. Cheap and light; found in Beijing pastry shops and snack halls.
A thick, round, lightly sweet baked pastry from Manchu-era Beijing bakeries. Sold at traditional pastry shops; good with tea.
A small steamed rice cake stamped with a rooster, traditionally eaten on the Sun Festival (1st day of the 2nd lunar month). Not the same as Taiwan's flaky suncake.
Crisp-shelled, hollow choux-like fritters dusted with sugar, a Donglaishun specialty. Order them as dessert after a copper-pot hot pot meal.
Tender lamb slices glazed in a glossy sweet sauce — the name means 'it tastes like honey'. A Beijing halal (qingzhen) classic at places like Donglaishun and Hongbinlou.
Slices of firm buckwheat cake dressed with sesame sauce, vinegar, garlic and chili. A summer cold snack at Old Beijing snack halls.
Fried yam chunks coated in hot caramel that pulls into golden threads. Dip each piece in cold water to set the sugar before eating.
Thin, crisp fried strips of dough twisted into a lattice; sweet or salty. A staple of Beijing and Tianjin snack shops, sold by the bag.
A soft steamed cake of mashed chestnut, lightly sweet with osmanthus. An autumn treat at Beijing palace-style snack restaurants.
Pressed pork hock set in its own clear aspic, sliced cold and dipped in garlic vinegar. A popular cold appetizer with beer.
Old Beijing's answer to ham: pork leg cured in soy and air-dried, then steamed and sliced thin. Sold at old brands like Tianfuhao.
Whole hawthorn berries simmered in rock-sugar syrup until glossy — tart, sweet and served chilled. A winter favorite in Beijing homes and restaurants.
A rich stew of pork intestines and organs, the signature of the centuries-old Shaguoju restaurant. Strong flavors for offal lovers.
Crisp triangular fried pockets filled with pork and aspic that melts into a juicy filling. A classic Old Beijing snack.
Tofu-skin rolls stuffed and fried crisp, then glazed sweet-savory. A halal snack from Beijing's Niujie neighborhood.
Seasoned liver and meat wrapped in tofu skin and deep-fried, then sliced. An old-fashioned Beijing beer snack.
An oblong flaky pastry shaped like an ox tongue, sweet or with salt-and-pepper. Sold at Daoxiangcun and old bakeries.
A big basin-steamed cake of rice, beans and jujubes cut into slabs. A humble Old Beijing breakfast and street sweet.
Dense, slightly sweet baked buns once hawked at night in Beijing hutongs. Chewy and long-keeping.
Hollow cone-shaped steamed cornbread, a peasant staple turned nostalgic snack. Today's versions are small and sweet; eat with stews or pickles.
Rolls of yam and jujube fried and coated in sugar glaze. A halal-style Beijing sweet found in snack halls.
Small pressed cakes of sweet mung bean paste, melt-in-the-mouth and cooling. Eaten especially around Dragon Boat Festival.
Lamb intestine filled with blood custard, simmered and served with sesame sauce. A rare halal street snack from Old Beijing.
Pork and offal braised in a spiced broth — the Qing-court ancestor of luzhu huoshao. Some old shops still serve it with bread.
A seasonal spring pastry filled with fragrant wisteria blossoms. Look for it at Beijing bakeries in April–May.
A spongy, honeycomb-textured steamed cake, sometimes topped with dried fruit. Common breakfast or snack.
A fried pastry with three knife slashes, soaked in honey syrup and sprinkled with sesame. A traditional Beijing-Shandong confection.
A chilled sweet jelly of watermelon juice dotted with fruit — a summer dessert from Beijing banquets.
China's ultimate home dish: soft eggs with sweet-sour tomatoes. On nearly every casual menu — great with rice; also called fanqie chao dan.
A sweet sesame-topped baked flatbread filled with red bean paste. A cheap breakfast or snack at Beijing halal bakeries.
Pork strips in a light, fluffy egg-white batter, fried and dipped in pepper salt. An Old Beijing restaurant staple.
Small fish slow-braised in a sweet-vinegar sauce until even the bones are soft enough to eat. Served cold as an appetizer.
Whole fish poached in a hot, sour, peppery broth. A classic Beijing restaurant dish that wakes up the appetite.
Steamed (or fried) buns wrapped around fine strands of noodle-like dough, soft and slightly sweet. A Beijing banquet and dim-sum-style staple.
Cold noodles tossed in creamy sesame paste with shredded cucumber — Beijing's summer bowl. Cheap at any noodle shop.
A spiral-coiled flaky flatbread layered with sesame paste. An old Beijing breakfast bread.
Open-topped steamed dumplings from Duyichu, a Qianmen restaurant said to be named by Emperor Qianlong. Order a basket of the classic pork filling.
A charcoal hot pot of tangy fermented cabbage with sliced pork and blood sausage — the Northeast's winter hot pot (also called suancai huoguo).
Boiled pork belly and soft blood sausage sliced and dipped in garlic sauce, often with sour cabbage. A Manchu-origin Shenyang classic.

dishes.en: Pork Ribs Stewed with Green Beans
dishes.desc: A hearty Dongbei home-style stew of ribs and wide green beans, often with potato and corn. Portions are huge — share.
Catfish braised with eggplant in fermented soybean paste — a famous Northeastern home dish. Rich, saucy, great with rice.
Eggplant slices sandwiched with minced pork, battered and deep-fried crisp. Common at Dongbei restaurants; often with sweet-sour sauce.
Twisted steamed buns, often with scallion oil, eaten with stews or for breakfast. Cheap at any bun shop.
A fluffy steamed bun filled with sweet red bean paste, sold at breakfast stalls everywhere.
Thick, ridged noodles shaved by knife straight into boiling water — originally Shanxi, now common across the north. Watch the chef slice; order with braised beef.
Kaifeng's own roast duck, claimed as an ancestor of Peking duck from Song-dynasty Bianjing. Sold whole or half at local duck shops.
Crisp, puffy sesame flatbreads baked on the walls of a tall clay oven. A cheap breakfast staple; eat hot.

dishes.en: Braised Black Carp Head and Tail
dishes.desc: A classic Henan (Yu cuisine) restaurant dish: carp head and tail pan-fried then braised in a glossy sauce. Order at formal Henan restaurants.
Bite-size ribs in a sticky sweet-sour glaze, served as a cold or warm starter at Shanghai and Jiangnan restaurants.
Eggs simmered in spiced tea and soy until marbled. Sold for a few yuan from steaming pots at convenience stores and stalls.
Eel slices fried crisp and tossed in a sweet-sour glaze — a traditional Hangzhou restaurant dish.
Silky tofu from Mount Bagong in Huainan, legendary birthplace of tofu. Served braised or in tofu banquets around Huainan and Hefei.
A Chaoshan steamed then fried rice cake shaped like a horseshoe crab shell, filled with pork and shrimp. A local street snack.

dishes.desc: A slow-boiled Cantonese home soup of watercress, pork bones and sweet/bitter apricot kernels, believed to be cooling. Often a free soup-of-the-day.
A clear, gently sweet dessert soup of silver ear fungus, served hot or chilled at dessert (tong sui) shops.

Chicken dry-fried with three kinds of pepper — dried red chilies, fresh green chilies and Sichuan peppercorn — until fragrant and slightly chewy. A home-style Sichuan stir-fry found in neighborhood restaurants; good with rice and beer.

Poached chicken torn into shreds and tossed with red chili oil, numbing peppercorn, vinegar and sesame. A classic Sichuan cold dish (liangcai) ordered as a starter; often sold by weight at deli counters.
Braised beef tendon cut into cubes and stir-fried kung-pao style with dried chilies, peppercorn and peanuts in a sweet-sour-spicy glaze. Gelatinous and rich — a twist on the famous kung pao chicken.

Chengdu's summer-night street-side ritual: plastic tables, cold beer and a spread of cold-dressed and braised snacks like edamame, duck necks, snails and crayfish. Look for it on sidewalks from evening until late; you point and order small plates.
Tender slices of fish in a fiery, aromatic chili-and-peppercorn sauce. A staple on Sichuan menus — milder than shuizhuyu but still punchy; order with rice.
Pork spare ribs braised with springy konjac blocks in a red doubanjiang sauce. A homestyle Sichuan braise — the konjac soaks up the spicy sauce.
Duck tongues braised in spiced broth then coated in numbing-hot mala seasoning — a favorite Chengdu nibble with beer. Sold by weight at braised-meat (lu wei) shops alongside duck necks and heads.
Small golden patties of pumpkin and glutinous rice flour, pan- or deep-fried until crisp outside and chewy inside. A common sweet ending at Hunan restaurants and a cheap street snack.
Spare ribs seasoned with chili and fermented black beans, steamed inside a section of bamboo that perfumes the meat. Served in the tube at Hunan restaurants; often one tube per person.
Crunchy slices of lotus root stir-fried with tender peeled shrimp. A light, crisp counterpoint to Hunan's fierier dishes.
Diced chicken fried hard and tossed with heaps of dried chili and numbing peppercorn. A Hunan classic (also called Dong'an chicken's spicy cousin); great with rice and cold beer.

Wide, flat fresh rice noodles served in broth with minced meat, herbs and chili — the Dai-region cousin of mixian. A popular breakfast in Xishuangbanna and southern Yunnan; ask for 'mi gan' rather than 'mixian' for the flat version.
Small square blocks of tofu made with Shiping's mineral well water, grilled on a griddle until puffed and served with chili-salt dips. Sold by the piece at night-market grills across Yunnan.
A prized dry-cured ham from Weining in western Guizhou, served thinly sliced, steamed or stir-fried with chilies. Often used in place of bacon in Guizhou dishes.
Egg fried rice tossed with Guizhou's tangy fermented chili paste (zaola), often with cured pork or ham. A cheap, filling late-night and breakfast staple in Guiyang.
Thick, chewy wheat noodles stir-fried with pork shreds and bok choy in a dark, sweet soy sauce. Ubiquitous at Shanghai noodle shops and diners.
Thin noodles in broth topped with braised or fried eel. A seasonal topping at Shanghai's 'noodle with toppings' (jiaotou mian) shops.
Whole crucian carp fried then simmered until the broth turns milky white and rich. A comforting Jiangsu home-style soup, often cooked with tofu.

dishes.en: Wenzhou Pounded Fish with Three Shreds
dishes.desc: Fish fillets pounded thin with starch into silky sheets, cut into strips and served in clear broth with shreds of ham, mushroom and chicken. A signature Wenzhou dish.
Softshell turtle braised in a glossy sweet sauce of rock sugar, soy and Shaoxing wine. A classic, pricey Hangzhou banquet-style dish.

dishes.en: Salted Pork with Spring Bamboo Shoots
dishes.desc: Salt-cured pork stewed with tender spring bamboo shoots in a savory broth. A seasonal Hangzhou specialty best ordered in spring.
Thin rice noodles in hearty broth with pork intestines and offal, peppered and served with vinegar on the side. Wenzhou's beloved breakfast and late-night bowl.

dishes.en: Sizzling Rice Crust with Tomato Shrimp
dishes.desc: Crisp fried rice crust brought to the table and doused with hot tomato-shrimp sauce so it crackles and sizzles. Fun theater and a favorite in Hangzhou restaurants.
River shrimp coated in a fluffy egg batter and fried into golden, lacy balls. A traditional Shaoxing specialty, eaten hot.
Thin slices of pork topped with shrimp, cooked with fluffy egg white ('hibiscus') for a delicate, mild dish. An old-school Hangzhou classic.

A square block of Jinhua ham steamed until soft, then glazed in honey-sweet syrup and served with lotus seeds — often sandwiched in thin steamed buns. A famous Hangzhou banquet dish (also written 蜜汁大方).
A savory porridge-like paste of small river shrimp and rice flour from the ancient water town of Sanhe near Hefei. Eaten as a local snack, best with Sanhe rice dumplings.
Little dumplings whose wrappers are thin omelets folded around seasoned pork, then simmered in broth or in a hot pot. A farmhouse favorite in the Huizhou region.
A rich mixed stew of seafood, meats and vegetables named after the Hefei-born Qing statesman — sometimes called the origin of 'chop suey'. Served at Hefei restaurants.
Mountain stone frogs from Huangshan's streams steamed with ham and ginger for a clean, delicate broth. A prized Huizhou delicacy.
A soft folded steamed bun stuffed with braised pork belly, pickled greens, crushed peanuts and cilantro. A Minnan street snack (also written 割包), cousin of the Taiwanese version.
Carp from the Wanquan River in Qionghai, usually steamed or braised to show off its clean, sweet flesh. A local specialty of eastern Hainan.

Goose raised near the Xinglong hot springs in Wanning, poached or roasted and served with a tangy ginger-garlic dip. One of Hainan's famous 'four poultry dishes' alongside Wenchang chicken and Jiaji duck.
Thin noodles and wontons in a savory broth sprinkled with dried shrimp roe — a Huaiyang breakfast classic. Look for it at Yangzhou morning-tea houses.
